title: Urbanization Impacts on Evapotranspiration Across Various Spatio-temporal Scales
description:
The data in this release describe various aspects of the impacts of urbanization on evapotranspiration at local to global spatial scales. This data release is associated with the publication of these results in a concurrent journal article. Analyses in the journal article included comparisons between urban and non-urban ET in a variety of climate settings and spatial scales.  
Urbanization has been shown to locally increase the nighttime temperatures creating urban heat islands, which partly arise due to evapotranspiration (ET) reduction. It is unclear how the direction and magnitude of the change in local ET due to urbanization varies globally across different climatic regimes. This knowledge gap is critical, both for the key role of ET in the water cycle accounting for the majority of local precipitation, and for the high socioeconomic value of urban landscapes, where water resources are often in high demand. We explore and assess the impacts of urbanization on ET across a range of landscapes from local to global spatial scales, and monthly to mean annual timescales. Remotely sensed land cover and ET available at 1 km resolution are used to quantify the differences in ET between urban and surrounding non-urban areas across the globe. The observed patterns show the difference between urban and nonurban ET can be estimated to first order as a function of local hydroclimate with arid (humid) regions seeing increased (decreased) ET due to urbanization. Cities under cold climates also evaporate more than their non-urban surroundings during the winter as the urban micro-climate has increased energy availability resulting from human activity. Increased ET in arid cities clearly arises from municipal water withdrawals and increased irrigation during drought conditions further increases the ET from arid urban cities compared to non-urban ET. This information can help to inform planners for improved environmental conditions in designing urban landscapes.  
This data set will be updated with the full journal article citation when available. See also the metadata file for additional information, or contact the authors with questions.

title: VIIRS/JPSS1 Downward Shortwave Radiation Daily L3 Global 0.05Deg CMG V002
description:
The NOAA-20 Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) Downward Shortwave Radiation (DSR) Level 3 Climate Modeling Grid (CMG) product produced at 0.05 degree pixel resolution at daily intervals. DSR is the incident solar radiation over land surfaces in the shortwave spectrum (300-4,000 nanometers) and is a significant variable in land surface models (LSMs), receiving increased attention due to its importance for the management and operation of solar energy systems. 

The VJ118 algorithm adapts the narrowband look-up table (LUT) approach to estimate DSR. The LUTs consider different types of loadings of aerosols and clouds at a variety of illumination/viewing geometry. The Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document (ATBD) is forthcoming and will provide additional details regarding the methodology used to create the data. 

The VJ118C1 product is aggregated from VJ118A1 files and includes one set of global 3-hour DSR variables and one set of daily mean DSR.

title: WIND Toolkit Long-Term Ensemble Dataset
description:
WIND Toolkit Long-term Ensemble Dataset (WTK-LED), an updated version of the meteorological WIND Toolkit, is a meteorological dataset providing high-resolution time series, including interannual variability and model uncertainty of wind speed at every modeling grid point to indicate ranges of possible wind speeds. The data were produced using the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF). The vertical grid used in WTK-LED includes many vertical layers in the atmospheric boundary layer to provide information of atmospheric quantities across the rotor layer of utility scale and distributed wind turbines. The WTK-LED includes:  
(1) Numerical simulations of wind speed and other meteorological variables covering the contiguous United States (CONUS) and Alaska, with high-resolution (5-minute [min], 2-kilometer [km]) data for 3 years (2018-2020): WTK-LED CONUS, WTK-LED Alaska.
(2) Climate simulations from Argonne National Laboratory covering North America, including Alaska, Canada, and most of Mexico and the Caribbean islands. These simulations complement the new WTK-LED to offer a 4-km, hourly dataset covering 20 years (2001-2020): WTK-LED Climate.
(3) Specific long-term, high-resolution offshore simulations have been conducted separately for the U.S. coasts, Hawaii, and the Great Lakes, leading to the 2023 National Offshore Wind dataset: NOW-23. The data for Hawaii include land-based data and are part of WTK-LED Hawaii.

Because the accuracy of simulations from a mesoscale model, such as WRF, varies depending on the location and weather situation, and can reach up to several m/s for wind speed, we provide simulated wind speed uncertainty estimates to the community to be used in conjunction with the deterministic model simulations.

This dataset was developed to satisfy a wide group of stakeholders across various wind energy disciplines, including but not limited to stakeholders in the distributed and utility scale wind industry, the new emerging airborne wind energy field, grid integration, power systems modeling, environmental modeling, and researchers in academia, and to close some of the gaps that current public datasets have.

Based on our validation results to date, we suggest use cases and applications for each dataset of the WTK-LED as shown in "WTK-LED Use Cases" resource below.

title: WLCI - Important Agricultural Lands Assessment (Input Raster: Resource Index-Terrestrial-Agriculture-Important Agricultural Lands)
description:
The data contained in this report was compiled, modified, and analyzed for the Wyoming Landscape Conservation Initiative (WLCI) Integrated Assessment (IA). The WLCI is a long-term science based effort to assess and enhance aquatic and terrestrial habitats at a landscape scale in southwest Wyoming while facilitating responsible energy development through local collaboration and partnerships. The IA is an integrated synthesis and analysis of WLCI resource values based on best available data and information collected from multiple agencies and organizations. It is a support tool for landscape-scale conservation planning and evaluation, and a data and analysis resource that can be used for addressing specific management questions. The IA analysis was conducted using a Geographic Information System in a raster (that is, a grid) environment using a cell size of 30 meters. To facilitate the data in a regional context, mean values were summarized and displayed at the subwatershed unit (WLCI subwatersheds were subset from the National Hydrography Dataset, Hydrologic Unit Code 12/Level 6). A dynamic mapping platform, accessed via the WLCI webpage at http://www.wlci.gov is used to display the mapped information, and to access underlying resource values that were combined to produce the final mapped results.
The raster data used in the IA is provided here for use by interested parties to conduct additional analyses and can be accessed via the WLCI webpage. This data series contains 74 spatial data sets: WLCI subwatersheds (vector) and 73 geotiffs (raster) that are segregated into the major categories of Multicriteria Index (including Resource Index and Condition), Change Agents, and Future Change. The Total Multicriteria Index is composed of the Aquatic Multicriteria Index and the Terrestrial Multicriteria Index. The Aquatic Multicriteria Index is composed of the Aquatic Resource Index and the Aquatic Condition. The Aquatic Resource Index is composed of the following components: Groundwater, Special Management Areas, and Priority Areas. The Aquatic Condition is composed of the following components: Focal Species, Species of Concern, Focal Ecosystems, and Proper Functioning Condition. The Terrestrial Multicriteria Index is composed of the Terrestrial Resource Index and the Terrestrial Condition. The Terrestrial Resource Index is composed of the following components: Special Management Areas, Agriculture, and Priority Areas. The Terrestrial Condition is composed of the following components: Focal Species, Big Game, Species of Concern, Rare Plants, and Focal Ecosystems. The Change Agents are composed the following components: Roads, Energy, Mines, and Urban. The Future Change is composed of the following components: Oil-Gas-Coal, Wind, Minerals, Climate-Temperature, Invasive Species, and Urban.

title: WMO Climatological Standard Normals for 1991-2020 (NCEI Accession 0253808)
description: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Climatological Standard Normals are a large suite of data products that provide information about typical climate conditions for thousands of locations across the world. Normals act both as a ruler to compare today’s weather and tomorrow’s forecast, and as a predictor of conditions on a calendar basis. The Normals are calculated for a uniform 30-year period, and consist of monthly averages and statistics of temperature, precipitation, and other climatological variables observed in all member countries. Member countries follow a standard set of methods for performing these calculations, WMO No.1203. The Normals are generated every 10 years in keeping with the needs of our users and the requirements of the WMO. These data allow travelers to pack the right clothes, farmers to plant the best crop varieties, and utilities to plan for seasonal energy usage. Many other important economic decisions that are made beyond the predictive range of standard weather forecasts are either based on or influenced by climate Normals. Finally, they are used most commonly in broadcast meteorology. These valuable data are stored by the World Data Center for Meteorology - Asheville.

title: Western US Hydroclimate Scenarios Project Datasets
description:
This archive contains two datasets. Both cover the northwestern United States and part of southern British Columbia (N of about 38 degrees N and W of about 105 degrees W) at 1/16th (0.0625) degree resolution. Climate and hydrologic variables (21 total) in each are as follows: precipitation, temperature (avg./max./min.), outgoing longwave radiation, incoming shortwave radiation, relative humidity, vapor pressure deficit, evapotranspiration, runoff, baseflow, soil moisture (3-layers), snow water equivalent, snow depth, and potential evapotranspiration (5 vegetation references).
The first dataset, "Western US Hydroclimate Scenarios Project Dynamically Downscaled Data", contains daily dynamically downscaled climate projections and simulated land surface water and energy fluxes.  The downscaling is based on the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) regional model. WRF was run using boundary conditions from the ECHAM5 global model and the SRES A1B emissions scenario, one of the models from Phase 3 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP3), a critical source of data to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR4). title: iSnobal
description:
iSnobal is a physically-based distributed snowmelt model. Snowmelt is the principal source for soil moisture, ground-water re-charge, and stream-flow in mountainous regions of the western US, Canada, and other similar regions of the world. Information on the timing, magnitude, and contributing area of melt under variable or changing climate conditions is required for successful water and resource management. A coupled energy and mass-balance model iSnobal is used to simulate the development and melting of the seasonal snowcover in several mountain basins in California, Idaho, and Utah. Simulations are done over basins varying from 1 to 2500 km2 , with simulation periods varying from a few days for the smallest basin, Emerald Lake watershed in California, to multiple snow seasons for the Park City area in Utah. The model is driven by topographically corrected estimates of radiation, temperature, humidity, wind, and precipitation. Simulation results in all basins closely match independently measured snow water equivalent, snow depth, or runoff during both the development and depletion of the snowcover. Spatially distributed estimates of snow deposition and melt allow us to better understand the interaction between topographic structure, climate, and moisture availability in mountain basins of the western US. Application of topographically distributed models such as this will lead to improved water resource and watershed management.

A statistical release covering farm energy use was published on 15/08/2013.  This workbook contains comprehensive data tables, including some not shown in the statistical release.

Link to main notice: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-environment-food-rural-affairs/series/farm-business-survey#publications

If you require the data in a more accessible format, please contact fbs.queries@defra.gsi.gov.uk 

Survey details

Survey content and methodology
 
The Farm Business Survey (FBS) is an annual survey providing information on the financial position and physical and economic performance of farm businesses in England. The sample of around 1,900 farm businesses covers all regions of England and all types of farming with the data being collected by face to face interview with the farmer. To be eligible for the FBS, farm businesses must have a standard output of at least 25 thousand Euros.
 
In 2011/12 a sub-sample of around 200 farms in the FBS took part in an additional module to collect information on energy use.  The survey was designed to collect data for greenhouse gas calculations which will be reported on in late 2013.  Specific farm types were selected with a focus on those types which tend to have very dominant enterprises.  For this reason, horticulture, general cropping and mixed farm types were not surveyed.  It was also critical that full financial data was available for all responses, so the sample was restricted to those that completed that part of the FBS, although these represent over 90% of the full FBS sample.  The sample for cereals, dairy and grazing livestock farms was stratified into three strata, based on Standard Output.  This was not done for pigs and poultry farms.  The size breakdown of responses is close to the FBS population breakdown for some farm types but not for others.  
 
Full details of the characteristic of responding farms can be found at Appendix A.
 
Fuel volumes were converted into energy values (GJ) using factors extracted from the European Reference Life Cycle Database (ELCD) by Cranfield University.  These factors use a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) perspective which include energy used in the extraction, refinement and delivery of fuels, on top of the calorific value of the fuel itself.
 
For further information about the Farm Business Survey please see: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-environment-food-rural-affairs/series/farm-business-survey
 
Data analysis
 
The omission of some farm types from this survey means that the results are not representative of the farming industry as a whole and no results are reported on this basis.  Due largely to the low number of observations, no attempt has been made to weight up results.  As such, results in this release should not be regarded as representative of the FBS population.  Extreme care should be taken when drawing conclusions from this release.

title: Interim London Energy and Greenhouse Gas Inventory (LEGGI) 2014
description: The London Energy and Greenhouse Gas Inventory (LEGGI) 2014 shows greenhouse gas emissions and energy consumption for London. This is an interim version of the LEGGI 2014, which will be confirmed when final data on energy use is published by the Department of Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) and Transport for London (TfL), expected in late 2017. The LEGGI shows estimates of energy consumption and carbon dioxide equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions from homes, workplaces and transport within the Greater London area. It is produced by the Greater London Authority on an annual basis to measure progress against the Mayor's Climate Change Mitigation and Energy Strategy. The LEGGI uses sub-regional energy (electricity, gas and other fuels) and CO 2 e data published by DECC/BEIS for homes and workplaces, and data from the London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) for energy and CO 2 e data for transport. DECC/BEIS E mission F actors (EFs) are used to estimate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from stationary and mobile sources of energy use in the LEGGI. These EFs are produced annually based on the national greenhouse gas inventory two years prior. E.g. 2016 EFs are calculated using national GHG emissions and energy use inventory data from 2014. So, for this 2014 LEGGI we have applied DECC/BEIS 2016 EFs to 2014 energy use to provide a more accurate estimate of GHG emissions in 2014 that is consistent with UK inventory data for 2014. We have retrospectively applied this method for EF selection to data from 2010 onwards to ensure consistency of approach and allow trends in CO 2 e estimates to be assessed. Interim results show that in 2014, London’s CO 2 e emissions were 37.8 million tonnes. This is a 16 percent reduction on 1990 levels and a 25 percent reduction since the peak of emissions in 2000. This is despite an ever-increasing population – an increase of 26 percent since 1990. London’s per capita emissions were estimated at 4.4 tonnes of CO 2 e in 2014, their lowest since 1990.

title: NI 188 - Planning to adapt to climate change
description: Self reported measure of action against climate change. Level 1: LA has undertaken a comprehensive, local risk-based assessment of current vulnerabilities to weather and climate. Level 2. LA has identified effective adaptation responses to address the risks and opportunities, explicitly related to other council strategies, plans and operations. Level 3. LA has developed an adaptation action plan to deliver steps to achieve the existing objectives, and partnership arrangements in light of projected climate change. Level 4. LA has implemented an adaptation action plan and a process for monitoring and review to ensure progress with each measure.

title: National Household Model
description: The National Household Model (NHM) is delivered by the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS). It was developed on behalf of BEIS by the Centre for Sustainable Energy (CSE) as an open-source tool for projecting the effects of policy and other legislative changes on the energy and emissions of the UK domestic housing stock by the Department of Energy and Climate Change (DECC).  In order to be able to set up scenarios model users need to learn a specialist scenario language based on S-expressions (such as those used in the Lisp language) using the instruction manual found on the BEIS GitHub site.  This will allow them to run the model which acts on the data in the various UK housing surveys. UK Data Archive stores the datasets for this model on behalf of the Department for Communities and Local Government (DCLG). Users need to register at UK Data Archive in order to access the raw data and run a conversion program to create a full dataset. The NHM team encourages feedback on all aspects of the model and documentation.

title: 2017-18 Washington State CRDC Data - School Behavior and Climate
description:
The Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) is a biennial (i.e., every other school year) survey required by the U.S. Department of Education’s (Department) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) since 1968. The CRDC collects a variety of information including student enrollment and educational programs and services, most of which is disaggregated by race/ethnicity, sex, limited English proficiency, and disability. The CRDC is a longstanding and important aspect of the ED Office for Civil Rights (OCR) overall strategy for administering and enforcing the civil rights statutes for which it is responsible. 

Data was reported directly from the school districts to the Office of Civil Rights. This data process is not managed by OSPI and therefore the data is not validated or reviewed by OSPI before being reported to OCR. For this reason data presented in this file will not mirror  OSPI reports on similar student and school measures.  The 2017-18 data in the report represents the most recent data made publicly available by the CRDC as of 5/10/2021.

In some cases data was unavailable or suppressed by OCR to protect student privacy, for more information on this please visit the CRDC webpage. In addition, directory information for some schools is incomplete, as the names of the organizations provided in the CRDC data files did not match the names of organizations on record with OSPI.

For additional information or questions about this data please visit the CRDC webpage at https://ocrdata.ed.gov/.

This file is based on the 2022 - 2025 Energy Consumption database files available at https://transit.dot.gov/ntd/ntd-data

Data Tables organize and summarize data from the 2022 - 2025 NTD in a manner that is more useful for quick reference and summary analysis. 

Only Full Reporters report energy consumption. Other reporter types do not appear in this dataset. Demand Response Taxi (DR/TX) mode and type of service combination does not report energy consumption and does not appear in this dataset. Finally, Non-dedicated fleets report energy consumption but not miles traveled. Thus for some agencies the given data for miles traveled are incomplete. Non-dedicated fleets represent about 7% of the data reflected in this dataset.

Please note that the column "Dual Fuel" was added in the 2025 report year. Values for 2022-2024 will thus be null.

In versions of the data tables from 2014-2021, you can find data on fuel and energy in the file called "Fuel and Energy" available from the NTD program website.

title: GHG Reporting Program Publication
description: This dataset contains greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions data reported to the Washington State Department of Ecology from the state’s largest emitters. As of 2022, this dataset accounts for the majority of the state’s emissions and serves as an indicator of the statewide total. Ecology separately calculates the statewide emissions total through the Washington State Greenhouse Gas Inventory. Reported emissions vs. Covered emissions Some of the graphs showing this data distinguish between the total emissions reported to Ecology by large emitters called reported emissions and the subset of that total that is covered by the Climate Commitment Act called covered emissions. Reported emissions • These are the total emissions from large emitters: facilities, fuel and natural gas suppliers, and electric power entities that emit 10,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MTCO2e) or more annually. • These large emitters must report their emissions under WAC 173-441. Covered emissions • These are the emissions from a subset of large emitters that are regulated by the Climate Commitment Act (CCA): those that emit 25,000 MTCO2e or more of covered emissions annually. • This subset of large emitters is required to comply with the Climate Commitment Act under WAC 173-446. Notes • Emissions from biogenic fuels, as well as fuels used for agricultural, marine, and aviation purposes are exempt from the Climate Commitment Act under WAC 173-446-040. Because of this, some emitters’ covered emissions may be lower than their reported emissions. • To view data by reporter type, filter the Reporter Type column by Facility, Fuel Supplier, Natural Gas Supplier, or Electric Power Entity. Greenhouse gas emissions are in units of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents (MTCO2e) using global warming potentials (GWPs) as specified in Table A-1 of WAC 173-441-040. History Ecology has been collecting reported emissions from Washington’s industrial facilities since 2012. In anticipation of the state’s major climate policies taking effect, the Legislature directed Ecology to collect emissions data from all large emitters in Washington starting in 2022 by expanding mandatory reporting to additional sectors: fuel and natural gas suppliers, and electricity importers. Reporting timeline • Before EY2022: Some large facilities began reporting emissions in EY2012. - Natural gas suppliers back-reported to EY2015 to establish a baseline. • EY2022: Additional fuel suppliers and electric power entities began reporting. • EY2023: The CCA Cap-and-Invest Program took effect. - Covered emissions are now being calculated. - Third-party verification is now required for entities that report more than 25,000 MTCO2e per year. Updates to the dataset • Ecology publishes emissions from the most recent emissions year annually. • Data from earlier years may be updated if reporters submit corrections that Ecology (and in some case, the third-party verification body) reviews and approves. Where to learn more • Mandatory greenhouse gas reports • Third-party verification (3PV) •

title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions
description:
The monthly Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emission data represents Montgomery County Facilities and Fleet by month beginning July 2019.  
Facilities: The Facilities GHG data represents physical structures used by County residents and County staff who provide services for County residents. Examples include recreation, libraries, theater and arts, health and human services, liquor retail, courthouses, general services, maintenance facilities, correctional facilities, police stations, fire stations, volunteer fire stations, garages, parking lots, bus shelters and park & ride locations. Facilities use the following fuel sources: grid electricity, natural gas, propane and diesel fuel. 
Facilities GHG data DOES NOT include Montgomery County Public Schools, Montgomery College and Montgomery Parks Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC). 
Fleet: The Fleet GHG data represents Montgomery County vehicles used by County staff who provide services for County residents. Examples include mass transit buses, snowplows, liquor trucks, light duty trucks, police cars, fire engines and fire service equipment, etc. Each County  vehicle use different fuel sources (i.e. diesel, mobil diesel, compressed natural gas, unleaded and E-85).  
Fleet GHG data DOES NOT include Montgomery County Public School buses, Montgomery College and Montgomery Parks Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC) vehicles. 
GHG Calculation Method: Facilities and Fleet fuel sources are converted into one common unit of energy- 1 Million British thermal units (MMBtu) which are then used with emissions factors and 100-year global warming potential (GWP) to calculate GHG emissions into one common unit of measure- Metric Tons of CO2 Equivalent (MTCO2e). 
For more information go to: 
•	How to Calculate GHG emissions at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zq5wTjvLqnY&t=186s
•	Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID) at https://www.epa.gov/energy/emissions-generation-resource-integrated-database-egrid
•	Emission Factors for GHG Inventories at https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2018-03/documents/emission-factors_mar_2018_0.pdf
Update Frequency : Monthly

title: Residential Solar Investment Program (RSIP) Enrollment
description:
Through the Residential Solar Investment Program (RSIP), the Connecticut Green Bank, in partnership with a network of contractors and inspectors, helped more than 46,300 households access solar energy since 2012, surpassing the statutory target of 350 MW (reaching 378 MW) one year ahead of the December 2022 deadline.

Highlights
- $1.43B total investment
- $156M total incentive
- $0.41/W average incentive
- $3.79/W installed cost

How it works
- RSIP provided rebates and incentives to make rooftop solar more affordable for homeowners.
- When panels produce electricity, they save money and create Solar Home Renewable Energy Credits (SHRECs).
- Utilities entered into Master Purchase Agreements (MPAs) with the Green bank to buy SHRECs to comply with policy programs.
- Green bonds are created via SHREC revenue and purchased by both individual and institutional buyers.
- Revenue from MPAs and Green Bonds support RSIP incentives and cover administrative costs.

This dataset is an anonymized comprehensive listing of all approved and completed projects supported by the RSIP. It contains information on system costs, sizes, participating contractors, and other details gathered during the RSIP. More information and program evaluation reports can be found at https://www.ctgreenbank.com/strategy-impact/societal-impact/successful-legacy-programs/residential-solar-investment-program-rsip

title: 3D Microstructure Super-Resolution: Training, Validation, and Test Data
description: This dataset accompanies the study "Comparative Analysis of Neural Networks for the Super-Resolution of 3D Image Data on Porous Microstructures". It contains virtual 3D porous NMC microstructures generated using a stochastic model calibrated against experimental tomography data. The dataset supports training, validation, and testing of four deep learning-based super-resolution models (SRCNN, SRResNet, SRGAN, and SRUNet) at scaling factors of 2, 4, and 8. The associated study evaluates reconstruction quality using image-based, geometric, and transport-related metrics, including geodesic and effective tortuosity. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23240235

title: A 1 km gridded dataset of Northern Hemisphere permafrost active layer thickness (2000–2024)
description: This dataset provides annual active layer thickness (ALT) maps on a 1 km grid across the Northern Hemisphere permafrost region from 2000 to 2024. It was generated using a LightGBM–XGBoost ensemble trained with 2,373 quality-controlled annual ALT observations and multi-source climate, vegetation, topographic, soil, and biome predictors. The dataset includes annual ALT maps, relative site-resampling uncertainty layers, annual binary area-of-applicability (AOA) layers, and an AOA-frequency layer for 2000–2024. The uncertainty layers characterize sensitivity to monitoring-site composition, while the AOA layers identify environmental extrapolation. The dataset is intended primarily for regional- to hemispheric-scale analyses of spatial ALT patterns and long-term permafrost change. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23227837

title: A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning
description: This dataset provides a national-scale map of mean annual rainfall erosivity (R-factor) across China at a spatial resolution of 90 m, generated using a machine-learning framework combining Random Forest (RF) and Cubist models. The map was developed using environmental predictors representing geographic location, topography, climate, and vegetation conditions. It is provided in GeoTIFF format using the WGS 84 geographic coordinate reference system (EPSG:4326), with pixel values expressed in MJ mm ha-1 h-1 yr-1. The dataset provides a reliable baseline for accurate national and regional soil erosion assessment, spatially explicit soil erosion modelling, targeted soil and water conservation planning, and scalable integration with high-resolution earth system datasets. Due to the website uploading issues, the map was devided into 12 tiles. This dataset is asscoated to the "A 90 m rainfall erosivity dataset for China based on national hourly precipitation observations and ensemble learning" by Zeng et al. (Submitted). Manuscript citation: Zeng, R., Xu, J., Chen, T., Lin, D., Zhu, X., Teng, H., Yu, W., Fu, Z., Du, Y., Chang, J., Chen, S.,Shi, Z. title: A Computational Framework for Early Neurological Disorder Screening Using Speech Signals and Embedded System
description: Interpreting speech signals as nonlinear dynamical systems provides a promising foundation for the early diagnosis of neurological disorders. This research concentrates on Parkinson’s disease and ataxia, conditions in which subtle alterations in speech patterns emerge as early manifestations of neurodegeneration. We introduce a diagnostic framework that integrates deep learning techniques with statistical signal processing, drawing upon concepts from mathematical physics, including energy minimization and stochastic modeling. By conceptualizing speech variability as a dynamic field, the proposed method captures fine-grained perturbations and inherent uncertainty often overlooked by conventional approaches. Validation on well-established Parkinson’s speech datasets reveals enhanced classification accuracy and robustness relative to traditional models. Furthermore, the framework’s computational efficiency facilitates deployment on embedded systems and neuromorphic hardware, enabling real-time, portable applications. In addition to its clinical implications, this work advances the application of physics-informed methodologies to the analysis of complex biomedical signals, paving the way for future studies across a range of dynamical systems. title: A feature-group-aware burn severity prediction model using multi-source dataset
description: This dataset contains 50 environmental, climatic, vegetation, and fire-related predictor features developed for wildfire burn severity modeling across the western United States. The variables were extracted and processed using Google Earth Engine (GEE) from publicly available geospatial datasets. They represent terrain characteristics, pre-fire vegetation conditions, soil properties, antecedent climate, fire weather, drought conditions, historical fire activity, vegetation health, and seasonal characteristics. The 50 features are organized into 11 groups. Their order corresponds to the column positions in the dataset. Feature Groups and Description Terrain (Features 0–5): Six topographic variables, including elevation, slope, aspect, hillshade, topographic position index (TPI), and terrain ruggedness index. Pre-fire Vegetation Cover (Features 6–11): Six vegetation-cover variables derived from the Rangeland Analysis Platform (RAP): annual forb and grass cover, bare ground, litter, perennial forb and grass cover, shrub cover, and tree cover. Soil Properties (Features 12–18): Seven soil variables, including soil texture, soil organic carbon, bulk density, pH, soil taxonomy, clay content, and sand content. Antecedent Climate – One Year (Features 19–21): Mean precipitation, maximum temperature, and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) over the one-year period preceding fire ignition. Antecedent Fire Weather – 30 Days (Features 22–24): Mean precipitation, maximum temperature, and VPD during the 30-day period preceding ignition. Recent Weather Conditions (Features 25–30): Cumulative precipitation over the preceding 90 days, ignition-day precipitation, wind speed, minimum relative humidity, maximum relative humidity, and VPD. Fire Danger Indices (Features 31–37): Ignition-day 100-hour and 1000-hour dead fuel moisture, along with pre-ignition fire danger indicators, including Energy Release Component (ERC), Burning Index (BI), and dead fuel moisture over the specified preceding periods. Drought Indices (Features 38–39): Mean Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI) and Palmer Z-Index over the preceding 90 days. Historical Burn Frequency (Feature 40): Historical fire frequency derived from the Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS) dataset. Vegetation Condition and Health (Features 41–47): Pre-fire NDVI, NDVI trend, five-year mean NDVI, pre-fire NDVI anomaly, and NDVI spatial texture calculated using 3 × 3, 5 × 5, and 7 × 7 moving windows. Temporal Features (Features 48–49): Day of year and fire season. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24044649

title: ARCHITECTURAL CRITERIA FOR PLANNING MODERN RESIDENTIAL AREAS IN SAMARKAND CITY
description: Samarkand, a globally renowned UNESCO World Heritage site and Uzbekistan's second-largest urban center, faces an unprecedented surge in housing demand driven by rapid urbanization and demographic expansion. This study establishes a scientific framework of architectural and urban planning criteria for developing modern residential neighborhoods in Samarkand that reconcile high-density housing needs with UNESCO buffer zone regulations, arid microclimatic conditions, and high seismic risk (Zone 8–9 MSK-64). Structured according to the IMRAD format, the paper synthesizes national building standards (SHNQ 2.08.01-2019 and SHNQ 2.07.01-03), microclimatic thermal modeling, and traditional Central Asian passive cooling typologies (the traditional courtyard/Hayot). Results demonstrate that integrating climate-adaptive orientation, courtyard-based building envelopes, modular monolithic seismic framing, and 15-minute neighborhood green corridors achieves a 51.7% reduction in summer cooling energy demand while guaranteeing compliance with strict historical horizon preservation limits. Practical guidelines are provided for municipal authorities, urban masterplanners, and architectural developers. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23565970

title: ARCHITECTURAL-TRANSFORMATIONAL MODEL FOR ADAPTING EXISTING INDUSTRIAL BUILDINGS INTO MODERN FUNCTIONAL FACILITIES
description: Industrial degradation and post-industrial urban restructuring necessitate effective frameworks for converting redundant factory structures into modern, multi-functional urban assets. This paper presents a multi-criteria Architectural-Transformational Model (ATM) tailored for the adaptive reuse of existing industrial buildings. Grounded in structural engineering principles, building physics, and environmental life-cycle assessment (LCA), the study evaluates structural grid adaptations, thermal envelope retrofits, and spatial volumetric re-zoning. Empirical quantitative evaluations demonstrate that adaptive transformation achieves a 58.4% to 64.2% reduction in embodied carbon compared to complete demolition and new construction, while reducing capital expenditure by 22% to 35% and accelerating delivery schedules by 40%. The proposed ATM methodology synthesizes structural capacity assessments, microclimatic envelope upgrades, and flexible spatial layering (such as mezzanine insertion and atrium light-well carving). The findings provide municipal authorities, urban planners, and architectural practitioners with a standardized, actionable decision-making tool for sustainable post-industrial urban regeneration. description: This article examines the assessment of energy-resource efficiency across districts of the Kashkadarya region and proposes a differentiated management mechanism tailored to local energy profiles. District-level energy-efficiency indicators for 2019-2025 are analysed through an Integrated Energy Efficiency Index (IEFI), combining current-year efficiency, average efficiency over the observed period, the reduction in energy losses, and the share of solar energy. A common Min-Max normalisation base is used to make annual values comparable. Based on the final 2025 IEFI, 16 districts with comparable historical data are ranked into high, medium, and low groups. Kokdala district, established in 2022, is treated separately as a monitoring area because a standalone historical series for earlier years is unavailable. title: Aggregate data and reproducibility code for spatial-support diagnostics in LuTan-1 and Sentinel-1 comparisons with leveling
description: This dataset contains 57 deidentified aggregate CSV tables and Python standard-library code supporting a fixed-cohort comparison of delivered LuTan-1 and Sentinel-1 time-series products with leveling. The primary comparison retains 20 targets in five survey groups and five 2024 windows at 25, 50 and 100 m extraction radii in eastern Beijing. The tables document spatial-support diagnostics, within-group contrasts, loss decomposition, reference-energy subsets, calendar and projection sensitivity, and anonymous trajectory-deletion summaries. All adverse outcomes and existing aggregate values are retained. Ten replay runners verify released aggregate arithmetic; an additional temporary-copy test confirms that a deliberately corrupted value is rejected. The software reproduces aggregate calculations, not extraction from raw radar products, survey adjustment, calibration independence or physical object correspondence. Conventional per-target RMS is an algebraic rescaling of the contrast-dimension-weighted statistic, not independent evidence. Raw radar exports, survey workbooks, target coordinates, point-level links, source imagery, manuscripts, reviews and credentials are excluded. Group labels and anonymous count/trial identifiers are retained for reproducibility; this is a deidentified release, not a claim that the study region is anonymous. The data and documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0; Python source code is licensed under MIT. See LICENSE.md for the file-level scope. title: Arrival clouds, control calculations and code: Monte Carlo test of mean-free-path scaling for sputtered Cu, Ti and W atoms in argon
description: Data and code supporting the manuscript " Does Mean Free Path Organize the Arrival of Sputtered Atoms? A Monte Carlo Test for Cu, Ti and W in Argon " (Avdelkader Bouazza, L2GEGI Laboratory, University of Tiaret, Algeria). SUMMARY Arrival energy-angle clouds of sputtered Cu, Ti and W atoms transported through argon, generated by Monte Carlo simulation, together with the code, scripts and machine-readable results used in the paper. The study tests whether expressing the target-substrate distance in mean free paths (chi = L/lambda) makes the joint distribution of arrival energy and incidence angle the same for different materials, and which material property controls the differences. MODEL Point source on the target axis; cosine emission law; Thompson energy spectrum with E_ion = 500 eV; energy-independent hard-sphere mean free path in argon at 300 K; isotropic centre-of-mass elastic scattering from stationary argon atoms; coaxial disk substrate of radius L/5; chamber radius 0.15 m; thermalization below 1.5 k_B T; 300-step cap. Real-gas and collisionless (ballistic) runs of a seed share random numbers. Pressures 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 3 and 5 Pa; seeds 61001, 61002, 61003; 10^6 emitted particles per file. Two emission cutoffs are provided: E_max = 0.5 gamma E_ion (baseline) and E_max = gamma E_ion, where gamma = 4 m_Ar m / (m_Ar + m)^2. FILES (9) 1. clouds_production_baseline_cutoff.zip - 216 production clouds (Cu, Ti, W; chi = 4, 8; real-gas and ballistic), E_max = 0.5 gamma E_ion. 2. clouds_production_gammaEion_cutoff.zip - 216 production clouds, E_max = gamma E_ion. 3. clouds_control_baseline_cutoff.zip - 432 one-factor control clouds: Cu with a single property replaced (mass 47.867, 100, 183.84 or 300 u, or binding energy 4.85 or 8.68 eV), E_max = 0.5 gamma E_ion. 4. clouds_control_gammaEion_cutoff.zip - 288 control clouds (four variants), E_max = gamma E_ion. 5. clouds_decoupled_control.zip - 144 real-gas clouds in which the mass used in the collisions and the emission cutoff are varied separately. 6. clouds_same_gamma_twins.zip - 72 real-gas clouds for masses with the same energy-transfer factor gamma (25.1 u and 8.68 u). 7. clouds_chi1_chi2.zip - 108 real-gas clouds at chi = 1 and 2 (chi = 4 and 8 are in the production files). 8. clouds_matched_Gamma.zip - 108 real-gas clouds with matched Gamma = chi*gamma (L = Gamma*lambda/gamma). 9. Reproducibility_archive_v3_corrected.zip- transport and analysis code, production and control results tables for both cutoffs, scripts for every figure, the analytic verification scripts of the transport code and their results, file hashes, environment description and README. Each cloud zip contains MANIFEST.csv (geometry, arrival counts, SHA-256), SHA256SUMS.txt and README.md. FILE FORMAT NumPy .npz files named REAL_<material or variant>_P<pressure in Pa>_chi<value>_seed<seed>.npz (REAL = real-gas transport, BALL = collisionless transport). Each file holds E_arr (kinetic energy in eV of each atom reaching the substrate) and theta_arr (arrival angle in degrees from the substrate normal, 0-90). Control files store only these two arrays. The analytic verification of the transport code (uncollided arrival fraction, mean energy after n collisions, collision kinematics, sampling distributions) is included and reproduces its stored results exactly. Environment: Python 3.12, numpy 2.4.4, scipy 1.17.1 (see ENVIRONMENT.txt). LIMITS The data come from a reduced computational model (hard-sphere, energy-independent cross section; cosine and Thompson emission; uniform argon). No experimental validation is claime

title: BLE wearables under controlled Wi-Fi interference, shielded-chamber recordings
description: This dataset contains raw recordings of two Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) wearables streaming to a laptop while a controlled Wi-Fi load ran in an anechoic chamber. The sensors are a Polar H10 chest strap and a Corsano 287-2B wristband. Setup. The chamber held a single test access point on Wi-Fi channel 6. A Raspberry Pi 3 Model B+ sent iperf3 UDP traffic through it to the laptop, at configurable rates and duty cycles. The receiver was a ThinkPad T14 Gen 5 with an Intel Bluetooth 5.3 controller, running Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy. An nRF52 BLE sniffer captured the over-the-air traffic. Before each session, the laptop's built-in Wi-Fi was disabled and a scan confirmed that no other networks were present. Conditions. The runs cover a baseline calibration, a long connection-parameter watch, a Wi-Fi duty-cycle sweep (0–100 %), the BLE link forced onto the channels that overlap the Wi-Fi channel (no load to maximum load), and a headroom series that adds k = 0–8 extra BLE channels. Each condition was repeated, typically three times. Contents. There are two sessions with 120 runs in total: 20261007_105222_chamber_1 : 108 runs (51 Polar H10, 57 Corsano) 20261008_010249_chamber_2 : 12 runs (Polar H10) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23750299

All plant and inverter identifiers are anonymized, and precise coordinates are restricted to the state level to protect asset owners while preserving regional climatological resolution. BR-PVGen is intended to support research in photovoltaic generation forecasting, performance benchmarking and loss decomposition, fault diagnosis, power quality assessment, and microgrid control validation. The simulation period is set to 10/01/2027–10/01/2031 to match the embedded tidal series. The rain gage reads SF_rainfall_RCP85_CCSM4_2026-2045.dat from the same folder. SF_rainfall_RCP85_CCSM4_2026-2045.dat: hourly rainfall, 2026–2045 (near-term period). SF_rainfall_RCP85_CCSM4_2086-2099.dat: hourly rainfall, 2086–2099 (end-of-century period). Rainfall data: daily precipitation from the MACAv2-Livneh statistically downscaled CCSM4 projection under RCP 8.5 for the San Francisco study area, disaggregated to hourly depths. Format: SWMM user-prepared rain gage file (columns: Station, Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, Value). Values are hourly rainfall depth in inches. Station ID: RCP85_CCSM4. Note on disaggregation: these files are a corrected hourly disaggregation of the daily rainfall used in the paper. The corrected series takes each day’s within-day pattern from observed San Francisco storms (2018–2025), and daily and annual totals are identical in both versions. Re-simulating the base-rainfall scenarios with the corrected series changed total CSO volume by −1.2%, the rainfall-intensification multiple changed from about 2.5× to 2.45×, and treatment-plant flows changed by less than 1.5%. Overflow volumes at individual outfalls may differ more than system totals. The corrected series uses present-day storm shapes, so it may understate future within-storm intensification. Sea-level rise scenarios are represented by raising the outfall tidal boundary, and groundwater intrusion by adding inflows at submerged pipes (see the paper’s Methods and Supporting Information). title: Bandwidth-Invariant MTPA Speed Control of Induction Motor Drives With Application to Airborne Wind Energy Systems
description: Efficiency-oriented control of induction motor drives reduces rotor flux at partial load, but the resulting reduction in speed-loop gain degrades closed-loop bandwidth under fixed-gain control. The maximum torque per ampere (MTPA) constraint permits an exact resolution. Enforcing MTPA as a structural control law reduces the conventional two-input field-oriented-control plant to a single-input single-output system. Its linearized transfer function is a second-order plant with a real zero at twice the rotor-flux pole frequency. A gain-scheduled proportional-integral controller, whose gain is inversely proportional to the stator-current magnitude, cancels the operating-point dependence and maintains constant crossover frequency and phase margin without a flux observer or look-up table. Four strategies are compared in simulation and experimentally on an 18.5 kW induction machine under airborne-wind-energy pumping cycles: standard field-oriented control, fixed-gain MTPA, the proposed SISO-MTPA, and loss minimization. SISO-MTPA is the only strategy that improves both net harvested energy and speed tracking relative to the FOC baseline while remaining undominated: its energy is within 10% of the MTPA-optimal strategies, its speed-error RMSE is approximately 1.7 times lower, and its maximum deviation is over 40% lower. Against an industrial drive under high-power generation, it reduces speed-tracking RMSE by 47% with comparable generated energy. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23243453

title: Baton Rouge Car Paint and Ceramic Coating Weather Dataset, 2006–2025
description: Open data on how Baton Rouge, Louisiana weather stresses automotive paint (UV, heat, humidity and rain), and on how often it allows a ceramic coating to be applied and cured. It includes a 12-city U.S. comparison and the 1950–2025 record of 90°F days at Baton Rouge Metro Airport. Headline findings: Baton Rouge averaged 111 days at or above 90°F and 117 days with a peak UV index of 8 or more each year from 2016 to 2025. 59% of all hours were at 80% relative humidity or higher, and 21 "hot-sun rain days" a year brought rain on a 90°F, very-high-UV day. Days at 90°F+ have risen about 2.9 per decade since 1950 (Sen's slope; Mann-Kendall p = 0.014). Airport hourly observations show 165 days a year (2016–2024) when a coating could be applied at 50–86°F and 80% humidity or less with no rain for the next 24 hours. That falls to about 2 days in July and 2 in August, against about 21 in October. On a combined paint-stress score, Baton Rouge ranks 3rd of 12 U.S. metros, after Tampa and Miami. Files: daily Baton Rouge records 2006–2025 (station and NASA POWER model values, with cure-window flags), the 12-metro benchmark, monthly and annual profiles, the 1950–2025 heat record, a threshold sensitivity table, EPA AQI context, stats.json with every headline figure and validation result, a methods PDF with the data dictionary, charts, and the Python code that rebuilds everything from public sources. Sources: NOAA NCEI GHCN-Daily and ISD-Lite; NASA LaRC POWER Project (hourly API); U.S. EPA AirData. title: Benggang susceptibility maps for southern China under current and future climate at 500 m grid spacing
description: This dataset contains Benggang susceptibility maps for seven provinces of southern China: Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Jiangxi, Hunan, Hubei, and Anhui. It accompanies the study “Climate Change Redistributes Tea Plantation Exposure to Benggang Erosion in Southern China” and provides spatial susceptibility outputs supporting the study’s tea plantation exposure assessment. The archive includes 87 GeoTIFF files on a 500 m grid, covering the reference period (1995–2014) and 28 future scenario–period combinations. Future projections span four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5) and seven ten-year windows: 2031–2040, 2041–2050, 2051–2060, 2061–2070, 2071–2080, 2081–2090, and 2091–2100. Three products are provided for each of the 29 reference or future combinations: • Susceptibility score (score/): continuous ensemble scores ranging from 0 to 1. • Susceptibility class (class/): five classes coded from 1 (Very low) to 5 (Very high), using thresholds of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8. Values equal to a threshold are assigned to the higher class. • Inter-algorithm variability (algorithm_iqr/): the interquartile range of scores across eight algorithms. Reference-period scores are calculated as the median across eight algorithms. Future scores are calculated by first taking the median of five global climate model-specific predictions within each algorithm, then taking the median across the eight algorithms. Future inter-algorithm variability is calculated from the eight algorithm-specific climate-model medians.  All rasters share a common valid prediction domain and use a custom WGS 84 / Albers Equal Area coordinate reference system embedded in each GeoTIFF. NoData values are −9999 for susceptibility scores and interquartile ranges, and 0 for susceptibility classes.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23389801

title: Binding energy distributions and associated optimised structures for Nitrogen- and Sulphur-Bearing Species on Amorphous Solid Water Ice
description: Datasets associated with the following publication. Title: Binding Energy Distributions of Nitrogen- and Sulphur-Bearing Species on Amorphous Solid Water Ice Authors: Aneesa Ahmad (1)(1: University of Leeds, UK) Description of contents of all_xzy.tgz : This tar archive contains the optimised geometries of ten nitrogen- and sulphur-bearing molecules (adsorbates) bound to 12-molecule amorphous solid water clusters for which a binding energy was derived: 2096 structures on fifteen water clusters, in ten folders, one per species (n2, hcn, hnco, nh3, h2s, ocs, so2, cs, ch3sh and so), plus a ReadMe. Each .xyz file contains Cartesian coordinates in Ångström, with the 36 atoms of the 12 water molecules listed first, followed by the atoms of the adsorbate. File names follow [species]_w12_[number]_[site].xyz, where [species] is the species name, [number] identifies the water cluster, and [site] identifies a unique binding site, e.g. nh3_w12_20_0018.xyz. The water clusters are numbered 1–3, 5, 6, 10–16 and 18–20, with the same numbering as the dataset for methanol and related species (doi:10.5281/zenodo.20764134), so a given [number] denotes the same water cluster in both datasets. The second line of each file gives the model name. Geometries were optimised at the MPWB1K-D3BJ/def2-TZVP level (UMPWB1K-D3BJ/def2-TZVP for the SO radical). The binding energy for each structure is listed in BE_lists.tgz under the same model name. System requirements for all_xzy.tgz : These are standard xyz files (the first line lists the atom count, followed by a comment line, then rows of each element in the structure and its x y z position). They can be opened and read by any text editor and inspected and plotted with any molecular visualisation software running on any operating system, for example, VMD, Avogadro, PyMOL, OVITO, Jmol, or ASE GUI. Description of contents of BE_lists.tgz : This tar archive contains 10 text files, one per species, plus a ReadMe. The file name gives the species, e.g. nh3_be_list.txt lists the binding energies of NH3 on all fifteen clusters. Column 1 gives the model name (matching the structure files in all_xyz.tgz) and column 2 the binding energy in Kelvin at the ωB97X-V/def2-TZVP level, corrected for basis-set superposition error with the counterpoise method and for the change in zero-point vibrational energy (ΔZPVE) using unscaled GFN2-xTB harmonic frequencies. The arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (n−1) are listed at the bottom of each file; these are the values reported in the Research Note.  System requirements for BE_lists.tgz : Plain machine-readable text files that can be opened with any text editor or read by any code, on any operating system. title: Bioacoustic and optical dataset
description: Data for this dataset were collected in a recirculating aquaculture tank. The acoustic subset ( acoustic/ ) contains 4,000 labelled vocalisation clips, 800 for each of five behavioural states (normal, feeding, stressed, starved and weakened). Each clip is 0.1 s long (12,800 samples, 128 kHz, 16-bit PCM, mono) and was segmented from continuous hydrophone recordings by a dual-threshold endpoint detector based on short-term energy and zero-crossing rate, then labelled against synchronised video recordings. The optical subset ( optical/ ) contains 2,075 tank images with 2,075 YOLO-format annotation files and 10,648 annotated instances covering three visible states: active (7,347 instances), weakened (1,203) and dead (2,098). Images were sampled at 1 s intervals from the tank videos and annotated with LabelImg. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with its modality, behavioural class and audio properties. CAMELS-IND-Proj: Daily streamflow projections for 472 Peninsular Indian catchments under future climate scenarios
description: Data Description We introduce CAMELS-IND-Proj ( C atchment  A ttributes and  ME teorology for  L arge-sample  S tudies –  India  - Proj ected Streamflow ), a dataset containing meteorological forcings and projected streamflow for the 472 Peninsular Indian catchments as specified in CAMELS-IND (Mangukiya et al., 2025). The projected streamflow (cumecs) at daily time scale is provided for the 13 CMIP6 GCMs (General Circulation Models) under the four SSP (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways) scenarios (SSP126, SSP245, SSP370 and SSP585), for the time period spanning from 2015 to 2100. The simulated streamflow values are also provided under the historical period for each GCM model. The forcing datasets comprising the meteorological variables such as precipitation (mm), maximum temperature (°C) and minimum temperature (°C) are also provided for the historical as well as the future period under each SSP scenario for each GCM model. This dataset aims to foster large-sample hydrological research in India, enabling the inclusion of Indian catchments within global hydrological studies. The file 'Confidence_flag.csv' provides a confidence indicator (under the column named 'confidence'), for the catchments with available observed streamflow. Of the total 472 catchments, 239 are flagged: the 159 catchments used to train the LSTM model and 80 additional catchments with observed streamflow that were not used in training. For the 159 catchments, the perfomance metrics were computed for the test period (2005-2014). For the 80 additional catchments, the trained model was applied to the same test period, and its simulations were compared with the observed data. The file also includes a 'low_reason' column which indicates the metrics which are failing, causing the poor model performance of the model. The remaining 233 catchments lack the observed streamflow for the testing period or the complete training and testing period considered in this study and are therefore left unflagged. The absence of a flag should not be interpreted as indicating either good or poor model reliability. The zip file also contains a python script named as ‘filter_catchment_model_scenario.py’ which enables users to extract forcing and streamflow data. User can specify a custom list of GCM models, SSP scenarios, and gauge IDs, or select the ‘All’ option to extract all items of that category. For example, if the user needs to download the data for the models ACCESS-CM2 and INM-CM4-8 for the SSP scenarios SSP245 and SSP585 for all the 472 catchments then provide the inputs for selected models as [“ACCESS-CM2”, “INM-CM4-8”], selected scenarios as [“ssp245”, “ssp585”] and target gauge ids as “All”. ------------------------------------------- ### Contribute to CAMELS-IND-Proj ------------------------------------------- If you are working with a data set covering Indian catchments and would like to contribute meteorological and projected streamflow data to CAMELS-IND-Proj , please get in touch. title: CERRA-Based Meteorological Cutouts for High-Resolution Wind Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: CERRA-Based Meteorological Cutouts for High-Resolution Wind Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain This repository provides high-resolution meteorological cutouts derived from the Copernicus European Regional ReAnalysis (CERRA) dataset for wind energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula. The cutouts have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. The cutout includes only the meteorological variables required by atlite to model onshore and offshore wind generation using logarithmic vertical wind speed extrapolation: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level ( wnd100m ). Surface roughness length ( roughness ). The original CERRA data are provided on a Lambert conformal grid. To ensure compatibility with atlite, the relevant variables are regridded to a regular latitude-longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.05° (approximately 5 km). Wind speed is regridded using bilinear interpolation, while surface roughness is interpolated using the nearest-neighbor method to preserve abrupt spatial variations associated with changes in land cover and surface features. A continuous hourly time series is constructed by combining CERRA analysis fields, available every three hours (00:00, 03:00, 06:00, …, 21:00 UTC), with short-range forecast fields. Specifically, the intermediate hours are obtained from the first two forecast lead times (+1 h and +2 h) of the preceding analysis cycle. Users wishing to rely exclusively on CERRA analysis fields should configure PyPSA-Spain to use a time step of 3 hours. The dataset is distributed as an atlite-compatible NetCDF cutout and retains the era5 module identifier to ensure compatibility without requiring modifications to the atlite code. Data Source All meteorological data are derived exclusively from CERRA, available through the Copernicus Climate Data Store: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ Configuration and Usage To use this dataset in PyPSA-Spain, the CERRA cutout must be explicitly selected in the configuration file for the onwind and/or offwind technologies.  Since the CERRA cutout contains only wind-related meteorological variables, an additional standard atlite cutout must be specified as the default_cutout to provide the meteorological inputs required for other technologies and applications, such as solar PV, hydropower, and temperature-dependent processes. These default cutouts can be obtained from the PyPSA-Eur cutout repository . For example, the YAML configuration file can be modified to run a simulation for the year 2023 as follows: alite: default_cutout: europe-2023-sarah3-era5 renewable: onwind: cutout: iberia-2023-cerra resource: method: wind interpolation_method: logarithmic offwind: cutout: iberia-2023-cerra resource: method: wind interpolation_method: logarithmic Licensing and Attribution The cutouts are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, subject to the attribution requirements associated with the original data sources. Users of these cutouts should acknowledge the original CERRA dataset and cite their corresponding sources in scientific publications and derived products. Availability of additional cutouts Cutouts for other European regions can be prepared upon request. Interested users are encouraged to contact the corresponding author for further information. title: CLARES: monthly and annual downward surface solar radiation over China, 1980–2025
description: CLARES is an all-sky downward surface solar radiation dataset over China constructed from CLARA-A3 and CERES EBAF Ed4.2.1. This release provides monthly data from January 1980 to December 2025 and annual data for 1980–2025 on a regular 0.5° latitude–longitude grid. Grid centers span 17–54°N and 73–136°E, with values outside the study’s China analysis domain designated as missing. Calendar-month mean–variance adjustment was fitted independently at each grid cell over 2001–2024. Adjusted CLARA supplies the record before March 2000, whereas CERES EBAF supplies the subsequent record. Annual values are calculated as equal-weight means of the 12 monthly values. This release represents the baseline reconstruction used for the updated regional analyses in the associated study. The data are provided in two compressed NetCDF files. The primary variable, rsds, represents mean surface downwelling shortwave radiation in W m⁻², with a missing-value sentinel of −9999.0. Domain masks, source identification, and negative-value screening flags accompany the data. A flagged negative monthly reconstruction value is retained for reproducibility and documented in the README. The README also describes processing methods, variable definitions, source attribution, and usage considerations. The associated manuscript, “Reassessing long-term downward surface solar radiation changes over China based on an integrated satellite record,” is currently under review at npj Climate and Atmospheric Science and has not yet been accepted or published. title: COACH AUTONOMY SUPPORT, BASIC PSYCHOLOGICAL NEEDS AND SELF-DETERMINED MOTIVATION IN KICKBOXERS: A CONCEPTUAL MODEL AND DIAGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK
description: Kickboxing is a full-contact combat sport that places high physical, technical and psychological demands on athletes. While the physical preparation of kickboxers has been studied extensively, the psychological mechanisms that sustain long-term training engagement remain insufficiently explored, particularly in Central Asian contexts. This article aims to develop a theoretically grounded conceptual model explaining how the coaching climate influences the quality of kickboxers' motivation, and to propose a corresponding diagnostic framework. The study is based on an integrative review of the literature on self-determination theory (SDT), the hierarchical model of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and the motivational model of the coach–athlete relationship. The proposed model describes a sequence in which coach autonomy support versus controlling coaching affects the satisfaction or thwarting of athletes' basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness, which in turn determines autonomous or controlled motivation and its behavioural and affective outcomes. A diagnostic battery comprising four validated instruments (ASCQ, BNSSS, PNTS and SMS-II) is proposed, along with a four-stage assessment procedure and need-specific coaching recommendations. The model provides a basis for future empirical research and for the design of motivational interventions in kickboxing. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23311963

title: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF ELECTRIC VEHICLE BATTERY TECHNOLOGIES: PERFORMANCE, SAFETY, AND SUSTAINABILITY
description: Electric vehicles (EVs) depend on rechargeable batteries to provide driving range, power, and reliable operation. Battery chemistry affects vehicle mass, charging time, cost, safety, and environmental impact. This article reviews the main battery technologies used in electric vehicles: lead–acid, nickel–metal hydride (NiMH), lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC), nickel cobalt aluminum oxide (NCA), lithium titanate (LTO), sodium-ion, and solid-state batteries. A comparative literature-review approach is used to assess energy density, durability, thermal behavior, charging performance, and application suitability. Lithium-ion batteries remain the leading technology for modern electric vehicles. LFP batteries offer favorable thermal stability and durability, while NMC and NCA batteries generally provide higher energy density. Sodium-ion batteries may become useful in cost-sensitive applications, while solid-state batteries require further development. Battery selection should consider vehicle requirements, climate, safety, lifecycle cost, and recycling. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23643394

title: COMPOSITE RISK INDEX AND EARLY DETECTION ALGORITHM FOR STRESS AND LOW-ENERGY INJURIES AMONG MILITARY PERSONNEL
description: Abstract.   Based on an examination of 220 military personnel aged 18–45 years, a composite risk index for stress and low-energy injuries was developed, incorporating 10 clinical, physical load-related, and bone metabolic indicators. The index demonstrated good discriminative performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.825 (95% CI 0.763–0.887), a sensitivity of 68.4%, and a specificity of 81.2%. Injury rates in the low-, moderate-, and high-risk groups were 7.1%, 23.5%, and 65.8%, respectively (p<0.001). A two-stage early detection algorithm was developed, comprising initial screening at the military unit medical facility followed by comprehensive assessment at a military hospital. The first-stage screening achieved a sensitivity of 94.7%, enabling the identification of military personnel at increased risk of injury before the onset of pronounced clinical manifestations. description: A river or lake can still hold water after it has ceased to provide suitable habitat for some species. For the Aydar-Arnasay, Sudochye, and Tudakul–Kuymazar systems, it identifies ecologically important seasons and proposes monitoring indicators. Aligning water allocations with fish spawning and bird migration, conserving shoreline habitats, and pairing hydrological measurements with biological surveys would help managers assess conservation outcomes. title: CSIRO - UNSEEN - CEAA PNW heatwave case study
description: This store contains the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) submission to the 2021 Pacific Northwest Heatwave case study of the Common Event Attribution and Assessment (CEAA) project of the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) Explaining and Predicting Earth System Change (EPESC) Lighthouse Activity.  To calculate the likelihood (expressed as a return period in years) of the 2021 Pacific Northwest Heatwave, the UNprecedented Simulated Extremes using ENsembles (UNSEEN) approach was applied to decadal forecast data from nine models that contributed to the Decadal Climate Prediction Project (DCPP) . The UNSEEN implementation used by CSIRO is documented by Stellema et al (2025) . The Tier 1 netCDF data file (`CSIRO_UNSEEN_tier1.nc`) contains the estimated return period for each of the nine models, as well as the uncertainty bounds on those estimates and the sample size for each model. The return periods were calculated via extreme value analysis, as described in detail in the file metadata. The Tier 2 netCDF data file (`CSIRO_UNSEEN_tier2_<model>.nc`) for each model contains the annual maximum daily maximum temperature (TXx) samples used to calculate the return periods. The data processing steps performed to produce the samples are described in the file metadata. The TXx samples from six of the models required bias correction (BCC-CSM2-MR, CMCC-CM2-SR5, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0), whereas the remaining three models did not require bias correction (CanESM5, EC-Earth3 and NorCPM1). The Tier 3, 5-day sequence netCDF data files for each model (`CSIRO_UNSEEN_tier3_<model>_5day.nc`) contain spatial fields of surface temperature, mean sea level pressure and 500hPa geopotential height for the five days leading up to and including the day of the top ten most extreme TXx values simulated by the model. The Tier 3, climatology netCDF data files for each model (`CSIRO_UNSEEN_tier3_<model>_climatology.nc`) contain spatial fields corresponding to the 1991-2020 climatology (June-July) of surface temperature, mean sea level pressure and 500hPa geopotential height.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22804782

title: CURRENT STATE, TECHNOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT AND PROSPECTS OF SOLAR WATER STILLS: A CRITICAL REVIEW
description: This article critically reviews the current state, design solutions, heat and mass transfer mechanisms, and prospective development directions of solar-powered water desalination systems. In addition to conventional solar stills, the review covers phase change materials (PCMs), nanofluids, nano-enhanced PCMs, photovoltaic/thermal (PV/T) systems, external collectors, evacuated-tube heaters, thermoelectric modules, and hybrid desalination technologies. The literature indicates that the main advantages of conventional solar stills are their simplicity, low operating cost, and limited dependence on the electrical grid, whereas their principal limitations are relatively low productivity and strong dependence on solar radiation. Recent studies have achieved substantial productivity improvements through thermal energy storage, enlargement of the evaporation surface, enhanced condensation, and hybridization of energy sources. However, transferring high laboratory-scale performance to real operating conditions remains challenging because of the long-term stability of PCMs, environmental risks associated with nanomaterials, salt deposition, fouling, maintenance requirements, and the lack of comprehensive life-cycle assessment. For future systems, the article identifies the 4E approach—energy, exergy, economic, and environmental analysis—together with digital modeling and artificial-intelligence-based optimization as priority directions [1–8]. title: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Macroeconomic Forecasting with Climate-Related Information? A Leakage-Free Out-of-Sample Evaluation for OECD Countries
description: This study asks whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based models produce more accurate one-year-ahead GDP-growth forecasts than conventional econometric benchmarks, and whether climate-related information improves them. Using a balanced panel of 38 OECD economies over 1995–2023 (N = 1,102) built from World Bank national accounts, International Energy Agency renewable-energy data, Copernicus/ERA5 country-level temperature anomalies and EM-DAT disaster records, we compare a per-country AR(1) benchmark, a random walk, a Fixed Effects panel regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting and an equal-weight forecast combination. Forecasts are strictly ex ante: in an expanding-window rolling-origin design over 2010–2023, every predictor enters with a one-year lag, all preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning are nested inside each training window, and forecasts are evaluated against realised, un-winsorised growth. Accuracy differences are tested with a Diebold–Mariano test that is robust to cross-sectional dependence, complemented by block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Random Forest (RMSE = 3.35) and Fixed Effects (3.38) reduce RMSE by about 8–9% relative to the AR(1) benchmark (3.67), but no individual model is statistically superior to it. The forecast combination is the most accurate approach (RMSE = 3.23; 12.0% below AR(1); two-sided p = 0.09; 95% bootstrap interval of the loss differential excluding zero). Climate variables account for about one-third of mean absolute SHAP importance, mainly through temperature anomaly and renewable share, yet a feature-set ablation shows that they add no out-of-sample accuracy: macro-only specifications forecast at least as well. Ex-ante climate-uncertainty proxies are not associated with larger forecast errors across countries, and only one proxy shows a positive within-country association. AI gains in OECD GDP forecasting are therefore modest and statistically fragile, and SHAP importance should not be read as evidence of forecasting value. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23340566

title: Can China's policy-driven greening be sustained under future climate risks?
Can soluble organic fertilizers and/or manure reach the agronomic and environmental performance of synthetic fertilizers in drip-fertigated crops?
description: The substitution of synthetics by organic fertilizers, which is the current pillar of circular economy, has been broadly evaluated. However, varying results were obtained on nitrous oxide (N2O) and nitric oxide (NO) emissions as well as crop yields. Besides, in irrigated semi-arid croplands, drip fertigation has been suggested to be an effective practice for mitigating N2O and NO emissions while maintaining or enhancing agronomic performance. However, the promising combination of drip fertigation and organic fertilization remains poorly studied. By setting up melon (Cucumis melo L.) during 2022, and maize (Zea mays L.) during 2023, we aimed to evaluate the effect of different combinations of nitrogen (N) fertilizers: control without N fertilization, 100% of the N rate as solid manure (100OrM), 50% of the N rate as solid manure and 50% as urea (50OrM–50Syn), 50% of the N rate as solid manure and 50% as soluble organic (50OrM–50OrS), 100% of the N rate as urea (100Syn) and 100% of the N rate as soluble organic (100OrS). Urea and soluble organic fertilizers were supplied via drip fertigation. N-oxides (N2O and NO), methane (CH4) and ecosystem respiration (CO2) fluxes, mineral N (ammonium [NH4+] and nitrate [NO3−]), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and crop parameters were analysed. As regards N2O, no differences were observed between treatments in melon crop, whereas in maize crop, the cumulative emissions were the highest in 100OrM, followed by 50OrM–50Syn.
