description: Release 2026.10: 1,278 rows in 6 tables, as CSV and Parquet. Aggregates only: no listing identifiers, descriptions, photos, addresses, agency identities or user data. Luxembourg housing asking prices by commune and month (https://chathome.lu/en/data/commune-asking-prices): Asking prices per square metre of living area for apartments and houses offered for sale or rent in each of Luxembourg's 100 communes and in the 24 official quarters of Luxembourg City. Values are the median and the 25th and 75th percentiles of the residential listings that were active on ChatHome when the statistics were computed; ChatHome collects these listings from estate-agency websites. The data has four segments (sale apartment, sale house, rent apartment, rent house), a current snapshot per commune and per quarter, and a monthly history in long format that grows with each release. A median or quartile is published only when at least 5 listings support it; otherwise the cell is empty, never zero. With few listings, a median or quartile can equal a single advert's asking price per m²; the adverts are public, so this reveals no private data. For reference, the commune snapshot also carries, where available, two official Observatoire de l'Habitat series from data.public.lu: the mean asking rent over a rolling 12-month window and the mean registered apartment sale price. These differ from the ChatHome figures in statistic (mean, not median), window, source and coverage, and the registered price is a transaction figure while every other price here is an asking price. Each commune row carries the official 4-digit commune code used by STATEC and data.public.lu. Tables: commune_prices_latest, commune_prices_monthly, city_quarter_prices_latest, commune_registry. Advertised homes and asking prices by energy class, Luxembourg and border regions (https://chathome.lu/en/data/energy-class-asking-prices): How the homes advertised for sale and for rent in Luxembourg and in the neighbouring areas of France, Belgium (Wallonia) and Germany are distributed across energy-performance classes, and what they ask per square metre in each class. Each country keeps its own certificate scheme and headline indicator: the Luxembourg CPE primary-energy class (A+ to I), the French DPE energy-consumption class (A to G), the Walloon PEB class (A++ to G) and the German Energieausweis class (A+ to H). Letters are never pooled or converted across schemes. A listing whose class is missing, on another axis or outside its scheme's scale counts as not stated, and not-stated rows are published so the gap stays visible. The source is a one-day snapshot of the public ChatHome catalogue of active listings, which ChatHome collects from estate-agency websites. Counts and shares need at least 5 listings, because smaller counts are unreliable; the adverts are public and this is not a confidentiality guarantee, as a hidden count can sometimes be worked out from the shares. Median, 25th and 75th percentile asking prices per m² and new-build shares need at least 10. A second table gives the class mix by Luxembourg canton. The shares describe advertised stock on the snapshot date. They are not the national certificate registers and not the housing stock. Tables: energy_class_asking_prices, canton_energy_class_mix. Correction 2026-10-18 (release 2026.10): commune_rent_price_quarterly is withdrawn. Release 2026.08 labelled it as Observatoire de l'Habitat advertised rents, but it came from ChatHome's retired rental_price_index: it carried size brackets, medians and quartiles that the Observatoire does not publish, and 4,428 of its 9,470 rows had fewer than 5 observations. Correction 2026-10-18 (release 2026.10): commune_sale_price_quarterly and commune_asking_price_annual are no longer published. They copied official Observatoire de l'Habitat series that could not be rebuilt reproducibly: the history is no longer stored and the stored commune codes were not the official ones. Use the originals on data.publ

title: Circulation analogue dates for the ClimaMeter attribution of 33 high-impact African heatwaves, floods and tropical cyclones (2019-2024)
description: This dataset contains the dates of the circulation analogues used in Faranda et al. (2026), "Attribution of the most impactful heatwaves, cyclones and floods hitting Africa in the period 2019-2024 to climate change", Weather and Climate Extremes, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wace.2026.100967. Together with the ERA5 reanalysis, these dates are sufficient to reproduce the results of the article.   The article analyses 33 high-impact African events (10 heatwaves, 13 floods and 10 tropical cyclones) with the analogue-based ClimaMeter approach. For each event, analogues of the daily mean sea-level pressure pattern were searched in ERA5 over the event domain, separately in a past (1950-1985) and a present (1987-2022) period. Pressure fields were averaged over the event duration and deseasonalised, candidate days were restricted to the calendar month before to the calendar month after the event month, and the event window and the seven days before and after it were excluded. The analogues are the best 1% of candidate days in terms of Euclidean distance (about 33 per period, 21 or 22 when the seasonal window is truncated at the calendar-year boundary). The present-minus-past differences of temperature, precipitation and wind averaged over these analogue days give the detected changes discussed in the article.   The MAT-file contains a structure array (Events) with, for each event, its name, hazard type, dates, averaging window, analysis domain and the analogue dates of the two periods (yyyymmdd), plus a structure (Info) describing the conventions. description: This repository contains a climate and geospatial database for Jezero Crater, Mars (18.44° N; 77.45° E), developed to represent Martian microclimatic conditions in the  EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) format and support building energy and thermal performance simulations for space engineering and extraterrestrial architecture applications. The primary data were collected by the MEDA ( Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer ) environmental sensor suite aboard NASA's Perseverance rover during the Mars 2020 mission. The analyzed period covers mission sols 1–687, corresponding to approximately one Martian year. Repository structure The database comprises four main products: MARS_JEZERO_MEDA.epw  — A synthetic annual weather file containing 8,760 hourly records, constructed by sampling representative sols from the four Martian seasons and modeling the components of solar radiation. MEDA_selected_days_8760.xlsx — An Excel spreadsheet containing the hourly time series and meteorological variables integrated into the EPW file. MEDA_all_sols_hourly.xlsx — A tabular database containing raw and processed records of the environmental variables monitored by the rover during the analyzed period. Sol selection and seasonal coverage To adapt the duration of a Martian year to the standardized EPW format, which comprises 365 days and 8,760 hours, uniform sampling based on linear interpolation of indices was applied, followed by a duplicate-removal procedure. Climate change shifts Arabica coffee suitability upslope and constrains long-term cultivable land: implications for coffee cultivation and forest conservation in montane northern Vietnam
description: Arabica coffee is highly sensitive to warming, yet its suitability is rarely assessed alongside the ecological and legal limits on forest conversion. We mapped land suitability in montane northern Vietnam on a 30 m grid from twelve climatic, topographic and soil criteria, weighted by a literature-based fuzzy analytic hierarchy process and screened by a non-compensatory ecological exclusion overriding high scores elsewhere. Projections cover 2041–2070 under two high-emission pathways (SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5) with five global climate models. Climatically suitable land covers 55,182 km²; the exclusion removed 26.6% of the domain. On the ensemble mean it contracts by 19.9–24.4%, and by 16.7–19.8% where at least three of five models agree; the highly suitable class loses 64–69%, and the median elevation of suitable land rises 127–161 m. Intersected with the baseline and a non-agricultural mask, that area yields long-term cultivable land of 44,094 km² (SSP3-7.0) and 41,862 km² (SSP5-8.5). Of that, 6.5% lies in special-use forest, treated as legally unavailable for coffee; 30.4% in protection forest, where statutory ceilings leave of the order of 4,000 km² usable; about 60% is under tree cover, leaving 17,815 km² unforested. Discrimination is good (AUC = 0.846, 95% CI 0.820–0.872), but absence data come from one province and absolute areas respond more to classification thresholds than to the climate signal: these maps screen rather than authorise land. Because the suitable belt rises while the topographic ceiling and forest estate do not, adaptation itself risks driving forest conversion; it should favour shade-grown coffee on farmland, not standing forest. title: Climate-Hazard Screening and the Limits of Calendar Adaptation for Global Endurance Events under CMIP6 Projections (Code and Data)
description: This repository contains the data, code, intermediate outputs, validation results, and figures associated with the study: “Climate-Hazard Screening and the Limits of Calendar Adaptation for Global Endurance Events under CMIP6 Projections.” The study assesses climate-related disruption risks for 28 major endurance events (18 marathons and 10 Ironman triathlons) using CMIP6 climate projections. The analysis combines heat and heavy-precipitation hazards through the Endurance Event Disruption Index (EEDI), evaluates present and future exposure at current event dates, and explores the potential and limitations of calendar adaptation under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. The repository contains both the analysis code and the datasets generated or processed for the study. Repository structure Code.zip Analysis and processing scripts used to reproduce the main calculations, sensitivity analyses, figures, and derived results presented in the manuscript and Supplementary Material. data.zip Processed and derived datasets used in the analyses, including event-level and monthly climate-hazard indicators and EEDI results. timeseries.zip Time-series data used to calculate the climate indicators and event-level statistics. Because of their size, these files are provided separately from the more compact processed datasets. era5_validation_results.zip Outputs from the validation of the daily WBGT reconstruction against hourly ERA5 reanalysis at the 28 study locations for 2011–2020. These results support the evaluation of temporal-aggregation and WBGT-reconstruction uncertainty reported in the manuscript and Supplementary Material. figures.zip Figures generated for the manuscript and Supplementary Material. aci.zip Additional analysis outputs and supporting files used in the study workflow. Main methodological components The repository supports reproduction of the principal analyses described in the paper, including: climate-hazard screening at the current seasonal position of each event; calculation of the Endurance Event Disruption Index (EEDI); monthly climatological EEDI profiles; identification of optimal and quasi-optimal calendar windows; SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 future projections; inter-model spread and agreement analyses; sensitivity to WBGT thresholds and time-of-day assumptions; sensitivity to the event-date sampling window; sensitivity to the quasi-optimal tolerance parameter; validation of the daily WBGT reconstruction against hourly ERA5. Data provenance The climate projections used in the study are derived from the NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 dataset. Hourly ERA5 reanalysis data are used for the independent evaluation of the daily WBGT reconstruction. Large original climate-model and reanalysis archives are not redistributed in this repository. The deposited files contain the processed, extracted, and derived data required for the analyses described in the study, together with the corresponding analysis code. Reproducibility The repository is intended to provide the material necessary to reproduce the reported analyses and figures from the deposited processed datasets. Users wishing to reconstruct the complete workflow from the original climate archives should obtain the corresponding NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 and ERA5 source data from their official providers. Please cite both the associated publication and this Zenodo record when reusing the data or code. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23785746

title: Climate-robust plantable zones for macadamia outside forest-planning land in northwestern Vietnam
description: Suitability maps guide perennial-crop expansion but are rarely converted into units that planners can allocate, tested for robustness to analyst choices or checked against presence records. We assessed land suitability for macadamia ( Macadamia integrifolia ) in four provinces of northwestern Vietnam, where a national programme targets 75,000–95,000 ha by 2030, using twelve FAO-rated criteria weighted by fuzzy AHP under baseline and 2041–2070 climates (five CMIP6 models, two scenarios). We delineated plantable zones: contiguous blocks of at least 1000 ha that keep a suitability index of 0.75 or more in all eleven runs, lie outside forest-planning land on slopes of at most 20°. Before the minimum-area rule, this land forms more than 100,000 patches, and projected changes in suitable area changed sign at high thresholds. Delineation produced 89 zones covering 346,945 ha, whose location changed little across weight sets (Jaccard ≥ 0.78), largely because the exclusion masks fix where zones can lie. Of 88 presence records not used to set class limits, 69% lay within 3 km of a zone, against 39% of the region, also after spatial thinning; mask-only zones did as well, so the agreement reflects the masks and cannot test the index ranking. Within the criteria used, warming relaxes the cold limit, but the best low-lying zones decline most. The zones cover 3.7–4.6 times the 2030 target, yet half their area carries tree cover and a quarter is cropland, so land availability, not qualifying area, is the likely constraint (Sustainable Development Goals 15 and 2). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23450272

title: Climatic mass balance dataset for Svalbard glaciers between 1990 and 2025
description: Dataset of annual climatic mass balance for all glaciers in Svalbard. Results were extracted from a preliminary dataset for 1990-2025, produced using the coupled energy balance firn model (EBFM; Van Pelt et al. 2019 , 2021 ), forced with CARRA reanalysis data, on a 500-m resolution grid. Compared to Van Pelt et al. (2019) , the model contains new descriptions for seasonal snow compaction (following Van Kampenhout et al. 2017 ) and turbulence (following Fitzpatrick et al. 2017 ). Model calibration follows as similar procedure as in Van Pelt et al. (2019) for melt and accumulation parameters using stake mass balance data across Svalbard. Additional calibration of snow compaction parameters was done using bulk snow pit densities measured by Uppsala University and the Norwegian Polar Institute. A manuscript on this dataset is currently in preparation. Climatic mass balance is calculated per mass balance year using a start date of 15 September. The MATLAB file ( CMB_data_Svalbard_EBFM_1990_2025.mat ) contains a table MB_Svalbard with the following columns: Year_start : Start year of the annual mass balance Year_end : End year of the annual mass balance CMB_in_Gt : Climatic mass balance in gigatonnes (Gt) per year   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23943913

title: Climatic-niche metrics for 1,516 bird species in China
description: Species temperature indices (STIs) summarize the climatic conditions associated with species’ geographic ranges and are used to calculate community temperature indices. We present a climatic-niche dataset for all 1,516 species listed in the China Bird Report Checklist v12.0. Four STI variants—Chinese breeding-range, wintering-range, combined-range, and global breeding-range indices—were calculated by intersecting BirdLife International range polygons with WorldClim v2.1 climate layers aggregated to a 0.25° grid. The dataset also includes temperature-niche breadth, mean annual precipitation, precipitation breadth, temperature seasonality, residency annotations, and a documented crosswalk between IOC and BirdLife taxonomies. Comparisons with eBird-derived estimates yielded correlations of 0.806 for breeding-season indices (895 species) and 0.870 for wintering-season indices (776 species). Comparison with published estimates for 60 species from Thousand Island Lake yielded a correlation of 0.687. Species rankings were highly consistent across other four independent climate baseline periods (r ≥ 0.9998). The dataset can support reproducible analyses of climatic-niche position and breadth, community composition, and climate-associated biodiversity change in China. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23631573

title: Code and data for: Climate, not its geography, governs present-day speciation rates
description: Code and Data Availability Repository Overview This repository contains the code and processed data required to reproduce the main analyses and figures presented in the associated manuscript. The repository is organized into three R scripts, a directory containing processed datasets for the four tetrapod classes, and a directory containing the geographic grid shapefiles used in the spatial analyses. All scripts are annotated to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. Folder Structure clim_space_statistics.R geo_clim_path_analysis.R geo_clim_spaces_maps.R combined_spaces_df/ geo_clim_space_amphibians.rds geo_clim_space_birds.rds geo_clim_space_mammals.rds geo_clim_space_reptiles.rds other_files/ Grids/ GriMap100_clean.shp and associated shapefile components R Scripts 1. clim_space_statistics.R Purpose: Performs the main statistical analyses evaluating how climate itself and the geography of climates relate to present-day speciation rates. The script uses mammals as an example but can be adapted to the other tetrapod classes. Analyses include: Effects of mean temperature and precipitation on speciation rates. Effects of climate area and climate isolation on speciation rates. Summary statistics and visualizations. Additional analyses involving climatic niche evolution rates, using temp_bamm and prec_bamm as predictors where appropriate. Reproducing analyses for other tetrapod classes: The script uses mammals as an example. To reproduce the analyses for amphibians, birds, or reptiles, replace the input dataset with the corresponding file from combined_spaces_df/ . 2. geo_clim_path_analysis.R Purpose: Performs path analyses examining the relationships between climatic and geographic tropicality, climatic niche evolution, and present-day speciation rates. Analyses include: Associations between climatic tropicality and speciation rates. Associations between geographic tropicality and speciation rates. Relationships between temperature-niche evolution and speciation rates. Path coefficients, model fit statistics, path diagrams, and summary tables for the main figures and supplementary material. Reproducing analyses for other tetrapod classes: The script uses mammals as an example. To reproduce the analyses for amphibians, birds, or reptiles, replace the input dataset with the corresponding file from combined_spaces_df/ . 3. geo_clim_spaces_maps.R Purpose: Generates the geographic-space and climate-space visualizations used in the manuscript. Outputs include: Geographic maps of speciation rates estimated using BAMM, ClaDS, DR, and MiSSE. Climate-space visualizations of speciation rates. Maps and visualizations of climate area and climate isolation. Combined figure panels used in the study. Reproducing analyses for other tetrapod classes: The script uses mammals as an example. To reproduce the analyses for amphibians, birds, or reptiles, replace the input dataset with the corresponding file from combined_spaces_df/ . Data Files 1. combined_spaces_df/ This folder contains the processed datasets combining geographic and climatic information for amphibians, birds, mammals, and reptiles. Each .rds file contains species-level evolutionary rate estimates and associated geographic and climatic information, with records corresponding to species × climate-bin or species × geographic-grid-cell combinations, depending on the dataset. Variables included: geoID : Unique geographic grid-cell identifier. long , lat : Longitude and latitude of the geographic grid-cell centroid. species : Species name. grid_presence : Indicates species presence within a geographic grid cell. BAMM_spec : Species-specific speciation rate estimated using BAMM. DR : Species-specific speciation rate estimated using the DR metric. misse_spec : Species-specific speciation rate estimated using MiSSE. claDS : Species-specific speciation rate estimated using ClaDS. temp_bamm , prec_bamm : Temperature- and precipitation-niche evolution rates estimated using BAMM.

Code and data: Seven-decade climate trends and ML temperature forecasting at an ERA5-Land grid point, Punjab–Balochistan border region
description: Code, processed data and results supporting the study "Seven-Decade Climate Trends and Machine-Learning Temperature Forecasting at a Grid Point in the Punjab–Balochistan Border Region, Pakistan: A Single-Location Case Study". The study analyses hourly ERA5-Land data (1950–2026) at one 0.1° grid cell (30.5°N, 69.0°E). It applies Mann–Kendall and Sen's slope trend tests to annual temperature and precipitation (1950–2025), and compares next-day temperature forecasts from Random Forest, LSTM and a persistence baseline. Contents: - CP5.ipynb: analysis notebook (preprocessing, trend tests, feature engineering, Random Forest and LSTM models, figures) - data/processed/: daily, monthly and annual ERA5-Land series and the daily feature table - results/: trend results, decade-wise statistics, model metrics, feature importance and test-set predictions - figures/: figures used in the study - lstm_five_seed_numpy.py: five-seed LSTM re-run (NumPy re-implementation of the notebook's Keras architecture) Raw data source: ERA5-Land hourly data, Copernicus Climate Change Service (ECMWF), doi:10.24381/cds.e2161bac. Raw ERA5-Land files are not redistributed here. Authors: Moavia Naeem, Muhammad Mekhmoor, Muhammad Usman, Sibtain Ejaz (The Islamia University of Bahawalpur, Pakistan). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24076650

title: Code and dataset for "Do the Time Constants of the Canadian Fire Weather Index System Hold in Humid Subtropical China?"
description: # Code and dataset for "Do the Time Constants of the Canadian Fire Weather Index System Hold in Humid Subtropical China?"   This archive (Code S1 and Dataset S1 of the paper) holds the analysis and figure code behind the paper, together with the derived tables the figures and the paper's numbers are drawn from.    ## What the code does   The paper asks whether the time constants written into the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System (about 2/3 day for fine fuels, 15 days for duff, 53 days for deep organic matter) have a counterpart in humid subtropical China. The pipeline builds a daily 0.1 degree cell-day sample for Jiangxi Province over 2003-2024, trains a dilated convolutional network on 90 days of raw weather, recovers the memory kernel with integrated gradients, and cross-checks the result with three tests that do not depend on the network architecture. It also fits the fire-weather response of the two fire seasons and compares pooled against regime-specific models.   ## Contents   ``` README.md                this file code/                    36 Python files, the analysis pipeline in run order   requirements.txt       package versions the results were produced with   MANIFEST.csv           script -> output -> figure/table mapping, machine readable   LICENSE                MIT dataset/                 derived data (CC BY 4.0)   tab_*.csv              27 tables the figures and the paper's numbers come from   tab_precip_shap_share.csv  share of each precipitation window in the precipitation-group                          SHAP (Figure 3c), transcribed from the log of 44_memory_check.py   access_0p1.csv         population and road covariates per 0.1 degree cell   grid_mask.csv          the 0.1 degree grid: cell centre, share of the cell inside Jiangxi                          (frac; the 1530 analysis cells have frac >= 0.5) and elevation statistics   MANIFEST.csv           list of the files in this archive with their sizes ```   ## Paths   Every script writes to three directories that are referenced through short absolute paths at the top of the file:   ```python INT = r'I:\jxwork\interim'   # intermediate arrays OUT = r'I:\jxwork\out'       # tables and logs FIG = r'I:\jxwork\paper2\fig'  # figures ```   `I:\jxwork` was a junction to the working directory and `I:\jxdata` a junction to the raw data directory. To run the code elsewhere, edit those constants at the top of each file, or recreate the two junctions. The paths were left as they were run rather than rewritten for release, so that the deposited code is the code that produced the numbers.   ## Environment   Python 3.9 on Windows 10, 22 CPU threads, no GPU. The sequence models were trained on CPU. See `requirements.txt` for versions. Installation:   ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ```   `torch` is the CPU build. `captum` is needed only for the integrated-gradient scripts (42, 74, 84), `shap` only for 81, `statsmodels` and `patsy` only for 79.   ## Input data   None of the raw data is redistributed here. All of it is public.   | Dataset | Source | |---|---| | MODIS C6.1 active fire (MCD14ML) | https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/download/ | | VIIRS SNPP VNP14IMG (screening cross-check only) | https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/download/ | | CMFD V2.0 meteorological forcing | https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/ | | CHM_PRE V2.1 daily

title: Code and derived data for "Cascading vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo"
description: This repository accompanies the article "Cascading Vulnerability in the Limboto Basin, Gorontalo: Dry-Season Drought, Tree-Cover Loss, and Vegetation, Lake, and Rice Responses, 2001–2025" by Pramono Putra S. Pido (Department of Geography, Universitas Indonesia). The article tests whether dry-season drought amplified by El Niño propagates from rainfall to soil moisture, vegetation, tree cover, Lake Limboto, and rice production in Gorontalo Province, on the northern arm of Sulawesi, Indonesia. The analysis compares three non-overlapping zones within the province (the North zone, the South zone, and the Limboto Basin) and also covers the province as a whole; tree-cover loss is examined in the HydroBASINS level 8 watershed unit that contains Lake Limboto and in the province. The analysis combines openly available satellite, reanalysis, and climate-index data with official rice statistics: CHIRPS v2.0 rainfall, expressed as the 1- and 3-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-1 and SPI-3), and ERA5-Land soil moisture and skin temperature for 1981–2025; GPM IMERG rainfall and SMAP L4 soil moisture as comparison products; the MODIS Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI) for 2001–2025, computed with and without pixel-quality filtering; Hansen Global Forest Change v1.12 tree-cover loss and ESA WorldCover 2021 at 30 m; FIRMS active-fire detections on a 1 km grid and MODIS MCD64A1 burned area; the water area of Lake Limboto from JRC Global Surface Water (1984–2021) and Sentinel-2 (July–October, 2019–2025); MODIS EVI over cropland in the Limboto Basin (2018–2024); the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the monthly Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly, and the Dipole Mode Index (DMI); and rice harvested area, yield, and production for 2018–2025 from BPS-Statistics Indonesia and BPS-Statistics of Gorontalo Province. The Python scripts compute July–October (dry-season) composites; lagged correlations with an effective sample size, prewhitened cross-correlations, and bidirectional Granger causality tests, including conditional tests, along the monthly chain from rainfall to soil moisture to vegetation; correlations, partial correlations, and Granger tests between the climate indices and SPI-1; zone-specific regressions of the vegetation indices on SPI-3 and a pooled Zone × SPI-3 model with standard errors clustered by year; comparisons of tree-cover loss between dry-season drought years and other years; a two-way (cell and year) fixed-effects model that relates the tree-cover loss rate of 1 km cells to active-fire detections, together with a partition of the excess loss in dry years between fire-detected cells and cells without fire detections; annual summaries of the water area of Lake Limboto; summaries of rainfall, soil moisture, and cropland EVI by cropping-season window, set against the rice statistics; and a simulation of the effect of the ONI running mean on the Granger test. The archive Limboto_cascading_vulnerability_v1.0.zip contains the Google Earth Engine scripts that extract the satellite and reanalysis data; the Earth Engine exports and the small external input files used in the reported run; the Python scripts that compute the numbers, tables, and figures reported in the article and its Supplementary Material; the outputs of that run; Figures 1–10 in English and Indonesian; and a manifest that lists the size and SHA-256 checksum of every file. The README, which is also provided as a separate file, gives the order in which the scripts are run and links each table and figure in the article to its output files. The station data, the publications read by two of the scripts, and the FAO GAUL boundaries and the zone polygons derived from them are not redistributed; the README explains how to obtain or recreate them. title: Code and results: When Do Time Series Foundation Models Help Forecast Wind Energy Droughts? A Preregistered Evaluation
description: Code, NWP covariates, per-window scores and logs for the article "When Do Time Series Foundation Models Help Forecast Wind Energy Droughts? A Preregistered Evaluation" (Q. Dai, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering). The study evaluates time series foundation models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, Moirai-2) against climatology, model output statistics, quantile regression and a recurrent network for probabilistic forecasts of the cumulative wind energy deficit in 16 regions in Europe, Australia and the US. The protocol was registered on OSF (https://osf.io/ph7nr/) before the prespecified main analysis of the sealed test period (January 2024 to September 2026) was scored once. Subsequent post-hoc analyses included additional forecasts and rescoring. The archive contains the code of every step, NWP covariates derived from ECMWF IFS HRES forecasts (CC BY 4.0), the per-window scores of all methods, run logs, and the post-hoc fairness analyses; the registered protocol is on OSF. Observed wind power is not redistributed; the released scripts download it from its sources. See README.md. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23872120

title: Code and source tables for Agroecological Pest Spillover Dynamics (APSD) v3: potential host-mediated pest pathways under climate-driven shifts in fruit crop suitability
description: Analysis code, supplementary tables, figure source data and provenance files for the revised manuscript "Accounting for climate-driven shifts in fruit crop suitability reorders the priorities of potential host-mediated pest pathways" (Kim and Do, Journal of Pest Science, under review). Agroecological Pest Spillover Dynamics (APSD) ranks potential host-mediated pathways between fruit crop pairs. Each directed pest–donor–receptor edge combines current pest climatic suitability, the projected gain in donor crop suitability outside current production (the crop frontier), receptor crop area within a 3 × 3 cell neighbourhood and the shared EPPO host record, summed across a 0.5° global grid. Contents - apsd_v3/: R and Python scripts for steps 1–8 of the workflow, with a README giving the order of execution (R 4.6, Python 3.12). - tables/: Tables S1–S21 of Online Resource 1, as CSV files and as one Excel workbook. - figure_source_data/: source data for Figs. 1–5. - provenance/: GBIF record identifiers and API query parameters, taxon key resolution, intermediate scores and diagnostics, and the analytical decision log (analysis_decision_log.md), which lists the analysis plan and every change made after it was fixed, with reason and timing. Data not redistributed Raw GBIF occurrences, EPPO Global Database host records, WorldClim 2.1 rasters, CROPGRIDS v1.08 and MapSPAM 2020 layers are available from their original providers. Occurrences come from three GBIF downloads of 8 May 2026 (DOIs 10.15468/dl.rn4pfg, 10.15468/dl.p8a8pg, 10.15468/dl.bm3wk8) and a public GBIF API retrieval of 30 October 2026; the identifiers of all API records are listed in provenance/gbif_api_retrieved_ids.csv.gz. EPPO host records were retrieved through API v2 on 14 May 2026. Relation to the earlier archive This record replaces the code and tables deposited with the submitted manuscript (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20502270). Crop area and crop frontier layers are now derived from CROPGRIDS and crop suitability models projected with five CMIP6 models; pest models use target-group background and 5° spatial blocks; host records are merged into 689 taxonomic units with non-host records excluded; and the score includes a spatial neighbourhood term. Results of the earlier archive should not be used with the revised manuscript. File names beginning with "robust_" in provenance/ refer to the assumption-stable core. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24072007

title: Code, Data and Per-Seed Results for Analogue-Anchored Crude Oil Price Forecasting (FTGN-A2)
description: Complete computational record for a study on interpretable monthly crude oil price forecasting. The deposit contains the input price series, all 16 scripts implementing the proposed analogue-anchored model and its comparators, and the per-seed outputs behind every table and figure in the associated manuscript. The input series is the monthly West Texas Intermediate spot price published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration, January 1986 to June 2026, 486 consecutive observations with no gaps. Series for Brent, copper, natural gas and a combined commodity panel, plus a daily WTI series, support additional runs. Results cover a main comparison of 31 models trained across 20 random seeds under a single chronological, leakage-controlled protocol; three crude oil literature methods (VMD-GRU, CEEMDAN-GRU and pattern sequence forecasting) evaluated under the identical protocol; leave-one-out ablations; controlled isolations of individual design elements; a learned-versus-frozen retrieval metric comparison; explanation-stability measurements comparing native retrieval weights against post-hoc gradient-times-input saliency; and directional, residual and tail diagnostics. Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman-Nemenyi test workbooks, run logs with wall-clock timings, and a seed-0 model checkpoint are included. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24050393

title: Coral growth data for the research article "Reconstruction of long-term sub-lethal effects of warming on a temperate coral in a climate change hotspot" in Journal of Animal Ecology
description: This repository contains the coral growth data files used to generate the results for the following article:   MJ. Vergotti, JP. D’Olivo, T. Brachert, P. Capdevila, J. Garrabou, C. Linares, P. Spreter, DK. Kersting (2024) Reconstruction of long-term sub-lethal effects of warming on a temperate coral in a climate change hot-spot. Journal of Animal Ecology . https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.14225   Abstract: The impact of warming on zooxanthellate corals is widespread, from tropical to temperate seas, with their associated mortalities causing global concern. The temperate coral Cladocora caespitosa is the only zooxanthellate coral with reef-building capacity in the Mediterranean Sea, a climate change hotspot with warming rates triple the global average. Over the past two decades, C. caespitosa populations have suffered severe mortality events associated with marine heatwaves (MHWs). However, with monitoring efforts beginning, at best, in the 2000s, the occurrence of MHWs before to that period, as well as the sub-lethal effects of these events remain poorly understood. Here we use sclerochronology to reconstruct the histories of past stress events and long-term sub-lethal effects on C. caespitosa in three locations within the NW Mediterranean Sea, each with different environmental conditions. Skeletal extension, density and calcification rates were compared to the in situ seawater temperature of each site to assess their relationship. Additionally, we assessed the occurrence of skeletal growth anomalies to reconstruct stress events between 1991 and 2021, a period that encompasses the onset and evolution of warming-related mass mortality events in the NW Mediterranean Sea. Our results reveal a positive association between calcification and temperature, following a latitudinal temperature gradient. However, the evolution of the likelihood distribution of growth rates in the warmest site (Columbretes Islands) since the 1990s indicates a decrease in linear extension and calcification rates during the most recent years. With the increase in the frequency of MHWs and growth anomalies during the last decade, this decline suggests a recurrence in physiological stress events. These results unravel information on the long-term impacts of warming on coral growth and highlight the potential of applying sclerochronology to reconstruct sub-lethal effects of warming using C. caespitosa .      Funding : This research is supported by the Horizon 2020 program of research and innovation of the European Union under the MaCoBioS grant agreement, by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation, project no. 401447620) and by the Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities under the project UndResCoral (project no. PID2022-137539OA-C22). D.K.K. was supported by a Ramon y Cajal postdoctoral grant funded by the Ministry of Science and Innovation (PEICTI 2021–2023; grant no. RYC2021-033576-I).  C.L. acknowledges the support by ICREA Academia. title: Correlative Operando X-Ray Imaging and Diffraction Revealing Mechanical Failure Pathways in Sulfide-Based All-Solid-State Batteries
description: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) based on sulfide solid electrolytes and lithium metal anodes promise high energy density and enhanced safety. However, their practical implementation is hindered by coupled electro-chemo-mechanical instabilities. Here, we combine operando X-ray computed tomography (XCT), operando X-ray diffraction (XRD), and pressure monitoring to elucidate degradation mechanisms in LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) | Li 6 PS 5 Cl (LPSC) | Li cells under realistic cycling conditions. By directly correlating particle- and stack-level morphological evolution with lattice-scale structural and strain dynamics, we establish a multiscale understanding of failure processes. Operando XCT reveals reversible volume changes of the NCM composite cathode during (de-)lithiation. Spatially resolved operando XRD uncovers heterogeneous lithiation fronts and depth-dependent electrochemical activity across the cathode thickness, while also identifying a partial release of internal microstrain at the NCM|LPSC interface associated with oxidative decomposition of LPSC. At the LPSC|Li interface, XCT visualizes crack propagation, lithium infiltration into the solid electrolyte, and interfacial void formation, ultimately leading to mechanical disconnection and soft short-circuiting. Notably, these mechanically induced degradation phenomena exhibit partial reversibility during cycling. The presence of soft shorts is independently confirmed by characteristic cell pressure reversals. This multimodal operando framework provides critical insight into degradation pathways and establishes design principles for mechanically robust sulfide-based ASSBs. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19866288

description: Daily Photovoltaic Electricity Generation Dataset from Adıyaman, Türkiye (2021–2024) This dataset contains 1,330 daily electricity generation observations collected from a grid-connected photovoltaic power plant with a nominal capacity of 110 kW, located in Adıyaman, Türkiye. The observations cover the period from 13 May 2021 to 31 December 2024. The dataset is provided in Microsoft Excel format (.xlsx) and was used to investigate the statistical characteristics of photovoltaic electricity generation and the temporal variation in forecasting model performance. The associated research examines seasonality, volatility, heteroskedasticity, and forecasting superiority using statistical and nonlinear forecasting approaches, including Naive, Seasonal Naive, ETS, SARIMA, Theta, STL-ETS, TBATS, and NNAR. The dataset is intended to support reproducibility and further research on renewable energy forecasting, statistical regime identification, and adaptive forecasting model selection. title: Daily oxygen, water temperature and wind records, hypoxic episodes and model outputs for 358 United States rivers, 2010–2024
description: The dataset supports an analysis of how long United States rivers stay hypoxic and of the weather on the days when hypoxic episodes begin and end. It holds a screened daily panel for 358 river and stream sites (4,538 site-summers, 800,141 valid days; 1 May to 31 October, 2010–2024) with daily minimum, mean and maximum dissolved oxygen, daily mean water temperature and daily mean discharge from the U.S. Geological Survey National Water Information System (NWIS), and daily wind speed, 2 m air temperature and shortwave radiation from the ERA5 reanalysis for the 0.25° cell containing each site. Derived tables give within-river anomalies of each driver, 3,929 hypoxic episodes (daily minimum at or below 2 mg L -1 ; 10,175 at or below 4 mg L -1 ), the entry and exit risk sets used in discrete-time hazard models, site-summer statistics, within-episode contrasts, river-level wind coefficients and model coefficient tables. The package also contains the Python code that builds every derived table from the screened inputs ( code/ ), the numbers behind each figure, and a data dictionary. The ERA5 hourly fields are not redistributed. Stations with continuous oxygen sensors are not a random sample of United States rivers. Wind and radiation are reanalysis values for a 0.25° cell, not measurements at the reach. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23643437

title: Data Supporting a Dose-Response Model for Weather-Induced Colour Change in Wood
description: This dataset contains the climatic, colourimetric, and model-development data used to establish and validate a dose-response framework for predicting weather-induced colour change in wood exposed to outdoor environments. The data originate from natural weathering experiments conducted across multiple European exposure locations and include monthly climatic variables, weather dose calculations, colour measurements, and model outputs used in the development of universal weathering response functions. Climatic variables include air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, relative humidity, and wind speed. In addition, the dataset contains engineered interaction terms between climatic variables, cumulative weather descriptors, calculated weather doses, and colour response parameters. Colour changes are reported in the CIE L a b* colour space and include source measurements, processed datasets used for model fitting, and universal response curves describing the evolution of lightness (L*), redness-greenness (a*), and yellowness-blueness (b*) as a function of accumulated weather dose. The dataset also includes prediction outputs and model evaluation metrics used during calibration and validation. The purpose of this dataset is to provide transparent access to the data underlying the development of the dose-response model and to facilitate reproducibility, independent validation, and future research on climate-driven weathering of wood and other bio-based materials. The deposition of these data responds to reviewer requests for public availability of the source data supporting the associated manuscript. Included Data Monthly climatic data for multiple European exposure sites. Weather variables: temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, relative humidity, and wind speed. Derived climatic interaction variables and cumulative weather descriptors. Weather dose calculations and dose increment values. Measured CIE L*, a*, and b* colour data. Universal weathering curves for colour response modelling. Model calibration, prediction, and evaluation datasets.  Keywords Wood weathering; Dose-response model; Weather dose; Colour change; CIE L a b*; Natural weathering; Climate exposure; Service life prediction; Wood durability; Norway spruce. title: Data and Code for "Becoming resident in a warming world: Food availability shapes seasonal partial migration"
description: Abstract In migrating wildlife, plasticity in migratory behaviour is an important trait for responding to seasonal environmental variation and coping with anthropogenic change. Although partial migrants with a high level of migratory plasticity seem to be more robust to rapid climate change than full migrants, we have limited knowledge about the mechanisms behind migratory responses to the environment in partial migrants. Using a dataset of 691 fall migration seasons from 339 GPS-tagged partially migrant red kites ( Milvus milvus ), we quantify how two key environmental factors, deviation from the average temperature and food availability, affect migratory behaviour. Warmer than average temperatures tended to delay fall migration among migrants. Within a sub-sample of territorial adults, a supplementary feeding experiment revealed that supplemented individuals delayed migration and showed considerably higher residence rates (68%) than controls (43%) while the temperature effect was difficult to estimate because only few of the food-supplemented birds migrated. These results provide experimental evidence that future positive temperature deviations may affect migratory decisions of partial migrants mainly via enhanced food availability. This plastic, food-dependent migration behaviour predicts future increases in the proportion of residents in partial migrant populations, as well as increased resident occurrence in areas with favourable food conditions. This repository holds the data and code to generate the output described in the publication Witczak et al. 2027 (DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2026.2371). To replicate the analyses presented in the paper, use the file "REKI_mig_departure_decisions.R", which includes the complete analysis and figures. This file reads in some prepared datasets that are stored in the 'data' folder and were prepared using the script 'dataprep'. The script "REKI_mig_departure_MS_numbers.r" summarizes the sample sizes presented in the text of the manuscript. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23412693

title: Data and Code for "Linearly stabilizing active stress drives hyperchaos in contractile polar fluids"
description: This package contains the code and data supporting "Linearly stabilizing active stress drives hyperchaos in contractile polar fluids" by Z. Cui (Fayetteville State University). The Python code solves a two-dimensional active polar fluid with variable polarization modulus in Stokes flow, using a fully resolved pseudospectral method with an exact energy budget as a runtime check. It includes the solver, an analytic tangent map, Lyapunov-spectrum and covariant-Lyapunov-vector routines, a symbolic derivation of the linear stability operator, and one script for each computation reported in the paper. The data include run logs and resumable checkpoints for the Lyapunov spectra, convergence tests, defect statistics, the energy-injection analysis and the hysteresis test, together with the four figures and the manuscript source. Requires Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and SymPy. The README maps every figure and quoted number to its script and data file. A small number of values come from earlier runs whose raw data were not retained; these are marked, and the included scripts regenerate them. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23267214

Data and R scripts for: Climate-sensitive periods of tree growth advance under cold, delay under heat, and widen under drought
description: This Zenodo deposit contains the R scripts and processed datasets needed to reproduce the figures and supplementary tables of the manuscript "Climate-sensitive periods of tree growth advance under cold, delay under heat, and widen under drought." Fourteen scripts cover the main mixed-effects models, the figures, the nine sensitivity analyses added during the first revision, and the across-group summaries and Supplementary Table 6 added during the second. The deposit starts from processed analysis tables rather than from raw tree-ring and climate series. Extracting the climate-sensitive periods from daily ERA5-Land data takes roughly three months of computation for about 3,000 sites, so that step is documented in the README rather than bundled here. The raw correlation surfaces and the scripts that reduce them are available from the corresponding author on request. Processed inputs include the analysis table ( modelling_data_r1.rds ), its counterparts built from SPEI and vapour-pressure deficit, the window coordinates under all seven extraction rules, and site-level metadata for the 2,926 chronologies in the analysed network ( meta_data.csv ). A complete output/ folder from the run behind the manuscript is included, so every figure and table can be inspected without running anything. Because Zenodo stores files as a flat list, the two directories are deposited as data.zip and output.zip ; extracting both at the deposit root, alongside the scripts, rebuilds the layout the scripts expect. The README describes how to run each script, which manuscript item it produces, and how the derived data files were built. Supplementary Data 1 reports the per-group trend estimates and diagnostics obtained under each of the seven window-extraction rules; Supplementary Tables 4 and 5 are drawn from it and are also provided as separate files. Supplementary Data 2 and 3 provide the full model outputs for the analyses of CSP shifts. Supplementary Data 2 reports models fitted at the climate zone × clade level, Supplementary Data 3 those fitted at the genus × climate zone level. Each includes complete fixed-effect estimates (intercept and year terms), chronology-level random-intercept estimates, variance components for the random intercept and residual, and key model fit and diagnostic metrics: log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, residual σ, AR(1) ρ, convergence information, and summary residual diagnostics. Relative to the previous version of this record (v3.0.1), this version adds 14_group_summaries.R, which writes Supplementary Table 6 and the across-group means and standard errors quoted in the text. Scripts 01 to 13, the data and their outputs are unchanged. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23560296

title: Data and code for "Climate change is decoupling fixed calendrical knowledge from the natural events it once predicted"
description: Data and code for "Climate change is decoupling fixed calendrical knowledge from the natural events it once predicted"   Jun Guo, Enze Song, Yi Liu, Lixiang Song, Xinyu Chang, Shengchu Zhang, Yang Xiao, Xinyi Liu, Yunhui Bai, Shuhui Yang, Xiaojiong Xu, Yongchuan Zhang, Hui Qin. Contact: Jun Guo (prof_guojun@hust.edu.cn).   - Licences: `dataset/` under **CC BY 4.0**; `code/` under the **MIT License** (see `dataset/LICENSE` and   `code/LICENSE`, and section 4 for exceptions).   This folder holds everything needed to reproduce the results and figures of the paper. Many Chinese agricultural proverbs tie a natural event (river thaw, last frost, first snow, insect emergence) to a fixed calendar date such as a solar term, a nine-day winter period or a lunar date. We call that date the **anchor**. The anchor does not move with climate but the event does, so the number of days between them measures whether a proverb still holds. The paper evaluates 805 such proverbs at Chinese weather stations for 1951–2024 and projects them to 2100 with five downscaled CMIP6 models.   The folder has two sub-folders:   | Folder | Content | Size | |---|---|---| | `dataset/` | Annotation layer of 20,606 proverbs, test units, station-year events, coupling results, projections, station and model inventories (14 data files + `LICENSE`) | 21.5 MB | | `code/` | Analysis and figure scripts, annotation protocol and validator, station list, map boundaries (19 files + `LICENSE`) | 17.9 MB |     ---   ## 1. Conventions used in all files   - **Dates** are day of year (DOY, 1 = 1 January). **Trends** are Theil–Sen slopes in days per decade. - **Offset** = event DOY − anchor DOY, wrapped into (−182, 183] days so that a winter anchor paired with an   autumn event does not produce a spurious offset of about ±365 days. - **Season of an event** follows from its proxy: upward temperature crossings, last frost and last snow are   *spring-side* events; downward crossings, first frost and first snow are *autumn-side* events. - **Warm-side offset W** = −offset for spring-side events and +offset for autumn-side events. W > 0 means the   event falls on the warm side of its anchor (spring event earlier, autumn event later than the anchor). - **Coupled**: a unit whose mean offset over a period lies within ±15 days of its anchor (about one solar-term   interval), i.e. the proverb holds at that station. Sensitivity columns use ±7.5 and ±30 days. - **Annual hit rate**: share of individual years in which the event fell within ±15 days of the anchor. - **Unit**: one proverb tested at one station in its province of circulation (`pid` × `sid`). - **Station ids** (`sid`) are GHCN-Daily ids (`CHM000` + 5-digit WMO number). - Missing values are empty cells (CSV) or `null` (JSON). Text fields are UTF-8; proverb texts, province names and   basin names are in Chinese (an English key for basins is given in section 2.8). - Frost and snow events end in 2019 (minimum-temperature reporting at many Chinese GHCN stations deteriorates   afterwards); temperature-crossing events run to 2024.   ---   ## 2. `dataset/` — file by file   ### 2.1 `pheno_annot_all.jsonl` — annotation layer (20,606 lines, 7.9 MB)   One JSON object per anchored entry of the Jicheng layer (*Zhongguo Yanyu Jicheng*, 26 provincial volumes), 4–80 characters long. 5,907 entries are testable assertions.   | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `id` | str | Entry id (`Y` prefix = Jicheng layer) | | `text` | str | Proverb text (simplified Chinese) | | `province` | str | Province of the volume (Chinese) | | `counties` | str | County-level circulation record where the volume gives one (empty for 6,421 entries) | | `source_volume` | str | Volume title, e.g. 中国谚语集成·宁夏卷 | | `printed_page` | int / null | Printed page number in the vo

title: Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
description: Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability . This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70 ) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming. description: Aggregate results and analysis code for a national re-rating of England's domestic Energy Performance Certificate register under the reformed Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard, which pairs a fabric metric with a secondary route met by the heating system or smart readiness. title: Data and code for: Forest cooling is not natural-vegetation cooling: pair-specific and environmentally conditioned land-cover thermal contrasts across India
description: This repository contains the processed datasets and Jupyter notebooks supporting the study entitled “Forest cooling is not natural-vegetation cooling: pair-specific and environmentally conditioned land-cover thermal contrasts across India”. The study examines daytime, nighttime, seasonal, and spatial variations in land-surface temperature (LST) contrasts among seven major land-cover classes – forest, shrubland, savanna, grassland, cropland, urban land, and barren land – across India using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) observations. The analysis covers 2003-2022 for LST, with land-cover stability assessed over 2001-2022. The study employs a spatially matched moving-window framework, environmental-gradient analyses, statistical regression methods, and machine-learning approaches to investigate pair-specific thermal contrasts and their associated biophysical characteristics. Repository contents 1. analysis_plotting_jupyter_notebooks.zip This archive contains the Python scripts and Jupyter notebooks used for data processing, analysis, and visualisation, including: Quality screening and preprocessing of MODIS datasets. Construction of spatially matched land-cover pairs using the moving-window framework. Additional quality screening and filtering to generate the final analysis datasets. Statistical and machine-learning analyses of land-cover thermal contrasts and associated biophysical variables. Scripts used to generate the figures presented in the main manuscript and supplementary information. 2. data_generated.zip This archive contains the final processed datasets generated after the screening, spatial matching, and filtering procedures. It also includes the Excel files containing statistical results and summary outputs produced by the Python analysis scripts. These datasets and outputs support the analyses, figures, and reported findings presented in the main manuscript and Supplementary Information. Data sources and reproducibility The analyses are based on publicly available MODIS Collection 6.1 products, including land-cover classification, land-surface temperature, surface albedo, leaf area index, evapotranspiration, latent heat flux, and vegetation productivity datasets, together with Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) elevation data. The original satellite products are available through NASA's Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center (LP DAAC). The repository provides the processed data, analysis workflows, and visualisation scripts to support transparency, reproducibility, and further research on land-cover thermal contrasts and associated biophysical processes. Users should refer to the accompanying manuscript and supplementary information for detailed methodological descriptions, data-selection criteria, statistical procedures, and interpretation of the results. title: Data and code from: Early-life viral immune challenge alters behavior and growth trajectories in zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)
description: Early-life immune challenge (ELIC) is particularly costly as neonates are antigenically naïve and limited to an innate immune response when exposed to pathogens outside the maternal repertoire. As the post-natal period requires extensive energy for processes like somatic growth, reallocation of resources toward pathogen clearance may alter developmental trajectories. Our objective was to evaluate the effects of an early-viral immune challenge on nestling behavior and growth trajectories in zebra finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ) using polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid (poly I:C), an agonist of innate viral pathways. Nestlings were challenged with poly I:C, saline, or simply handled (no injection) on post-hatch day (PHD) 5. Behaviors associated with sickness responses were quantified from videos recorded over the following 10 days. Growth was monitored through PHD 60 using repeated measures of mass, wing chord, and tarsus length. Poly I:C-challenged nestlings exhibited classic sickness behaviors, including reduced begging 1-day post-injection (DPI) and reduced parent-directed begging and feeding 4 DPI. Although behavioral changes largely resolved within 7 DPI, both poly I:C and saline-challenged birds exhibited persistently lower body mass and condition than non-injected controls. Structural measures of body size and fledging age were unaffected by treatment, suggesting that nestlings prioritized development of traits critical for fledging despite reduced overall body mass. These findings show that early-life immune activation can alter nestling behavior and produce lasting effects on growth trajectories. These results support life-history theory predictions that investment in immune defense during development requires energetic trade-offs and highlights the importance of early immune experiences in shaping developmental outcomes. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23700087

description: This data set contains the plotted data and scripts for the figures of Scholz, Danilov, Klingbeil and Banerjee, "Discrete variance decay of temperature and salinity in the global Finite volumE Sea-Ice Ocean Model (FESOM2)", submitted to the Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems (JAMES). Model setup Model and mesh: the Finite volumE Sea-Ice Ocean Model (FESOM2; Danilov et al. 2017) on the unstructured CORE2 mesh, with a nominal resolution of about 1°, refined to about 25 km north of 50°N, to about 1/3° in the equatorial belt and to about 65 km in the Southern Ocean, and 47 z* layers (48 level depths). Vertical mixing: the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) scheme of Gaspar et al. (1990), via CVMix. Eddy parameterizations: isoneutral (Redi) diffusion and the Gent-McWilliams parameterization, with a diffusivity of 1000 m² s⁻¹ at 100 km resolution that scales linearly with the local resolution. Initialisation and forcing: initialized from the PHC3 winter climatology (Steele et al. 2001) and forced with JRA55-do v1.4.0 (Tsujino et al. 2018) over a single forcing cycle (1958 to 2019). (2014), "K14": the total DVD rate, which uses a heuristic definition of the second-moment fluxes. Banerjee et al. (2024), "B24": the DVD rate computed at cell faces from the first-moment fluxes of the model. title: Data for [Experimental Constraints on Ion Irradiation–Induced Remanent Magnetization in Extraterrestrial Samples]
description: Remanent magnetization (RM) in extraterrestrial materials preserves key information on Solar System processes. However, in samples from airless bodies affected by space weathering, the effects of plasma irradiation on magnetic properties and RM remain poorly constrained. Here we conducted hydrogen ion irradiation experiments with various energy (10, 20, and 30 keV) and fluences (1, 4.5, and 9 × 10 17 ions cm -2 ) on magnetic meteorites and magnetite to simulate space plasma exposure, combined with hysteresis, demagnetization, and anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) measurements. Our results reveal that intense irradiation can impart irradiation-induced remanent magnetization (IIRM) under weak ambient fields (<50 μT) without modification of bulk magnetic properties, whereas low-energy or low-fluence irradiation produces negligible effects. Comparison of IIRM with ARM suggests that implantation-driven internal stresses may perturb magnetic energy states and promote remanence acquisition. These findings provide a potential mechanism for magnetic recording in irradiated extraterrestrial materials and constrain their exposure environments. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23467420

title: Data from: The legacy of past climate warming: strong local adaptation in rear-edge populations
description: Improving forecasts of species’ responses to climate change has become a central challenge in ecology and evolution as species distributions are increasingly disrupted by ongoing climate warming. Insight into this challenge may be gained through a better understanding of evolutionary responses to past climate change. The rear edges of species’ distributions are typically relict populations persisting in former glacial refugia at warmer range limits. As such, they form natural laboratories to study the evolutionary outcomes of past climate warming. Three such outcomes have been proposed for rear-edge populations: maintenance of high diversity due to long-term persistence, strong genetic drift following habitat decline, and strong local adaptation allowing persistence despite environmental change. Empirical studies rarely explicitly test these alternate outcomes limiting our understanding of evolutionary responses to warming climates. We tested all three evolutionary outcomes at the rear edge of the North American herb Campanula americana , by assessing genetic variation in a genome-wide population genetic study, drift load as measure of fitness decline due to drift in a controlled crossing study, and local adaptation in a transplant study. Rear-edge populations exhibited reduced genetic diversity within populations and high differentiation among populations, typically interpreted as evidence of genetic drift, yet show limited drift load. Instead, these populations expressed strong local adaptation, thriving in rear-edge habitats that were unsuitably warm for populations in the expanded range. This indicates that warm-edge populations may persist under warming climates by gradually adapting, even in the face of genetic erosion. Our findings highlight the importance of explicitly testing for all evolutionary outcomes, and particularly going beyond measures of genetic variation, when inferring evolutionary history. More broadly, these findings identify rear-edge populations not as relics of decline, but as underappreciated models for studying successful adaptation under long-term climate change. Three different EarthCARE approaches were validated; 1D radiative transfer model (RTM) along-track estimates (1x1 km), 1D RTM across-track extension using the Scene Construction Algorithm (Qu et al., 2023), and 3D RTM estimates (5x21 km). To infer cloud-induced discrepancies, the cloud modification factor (CMF) was calculated. The corresponding results of the longwave irradiance can be found in BSRN_ECA_LW_AlongTrack.csv. description: This dataset provides source transcriptions, numerical inputs, analytical code, derived tables, figures, and verification procedures for an examination of company cash flows and direct state payments to energy suppliers reported by JIRAMA, Madagascar's national electricity and water utility. The analysis uses JIRAMA's first-half 2026 financial recovery monitoring report, including monthly company cash-flow records and supplier-payment schedules covering electricity producers and petroleum suppliers. The supplier-payment summary reports MGA 195.04 billion in direct state settlements as paid by the end of June 2026. The dated annexes assign MGA 64.14 billion of these settlements to July, leaving MGA 130.89 billion attributable to April–June. Across both payment routes, explicitly July-labelled settlements total MGA 77.05 billion, representing at least 17.44% of the MGA 441.76 billion reported as paid for the supplier invoice cohorts. The company cash-flow decomposition identifies a deterioration of MGA 56.25 billion per month between January–April and May–June 2026. Purchased-electricity and petroleum payments account for MGA 46.00 billion, or 81.78%, of that change. Under explicitly stated assumptions concerning payment-route separation, inclusion of company-paid cohort settlements, and completeness of the company payment categories, the documented combined payment amount is at least MGA 564.89 billion, with a conditional lower bound of 23.17% for the direct state-payment share. The archive contains six CSV input files, ten analytical tables, two figures supplied in SVG, PNG, and PDF formats, source provenance records, methodological documentation, calculation scripts, independent numerical tests, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. Scientific calculations use Python 3.12 or newer and its standard library. The default reproduction workflow operates offline. It regenerates the analytical outputs and checks their SHA-256 hashes against the distributed reference files. Optional graphical dependencies support regeneration of the PNG and PDF illustrations. The numerical reconstruction and integrity checks were successfully executed under Windows using Python 3.12.10. The scientific outputs reproduced their reference SHA-256 values. The original institutional reports and third-party publications are referenced through source documentation and are not redistributed. The archive contains author-prepared transcriptions and derived materials. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23333294

title: Dengue, climate and marginalization in Mexico, 2021–2025
description: This repository contains the data and R code needed to reproduce a Bayesian spatiotemporal analysis of weekly confirmed dengue cases in Mexican municipalities from 2021 to 2025. Case data come from the national epidemiological surveillance system (SINAVE, Dirección General de Epidemiología), climate exposures (dewpoint temperature, air temperature and precipitation) from the ERA5-Land reanalysis, and municipal marginalization from the 2020 CONAPO index. The main model is a negative binomial model fitted with R-INLA, with a BYM2 spatial effect, distributed lag effects of climate over 0 to 10 weeks and state-specific seasonality. Because many municipality-weeks are not reported to surveillance, the analysis treats unreported weeks as missing rather than as zero cases, restricts the main sample by weekly reporting coverage, and assesses reporting bias with several sensitivity analyses, including multiple imputation. The numbered R pipelines run from sample construction to the final figures and tables. A single README file describes all datasets and scripts. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23889257

title: Designing the side frame of an electric-vehicle battery enclosure for oblique pole impact
description: The side frame of an electric-vehicle battery enclosure must absorb pole-impact energy before the battery modules are damaged. Enclosure optimisation studies usually limit intrusion into the cell zone and so treat any contact between frame and modules as failure. This study examines how that choice changes the optimal frame. A subsystem model of an enclosure section under a 32 km/h, 75° oblique pole impact was built in the open-source explicit solver OpenCourant. The aluminium model was validated against axial-crush tests on AA6063-T5 extrusions (mean crushing force and absorbed energy within 9%), and the modules were represented by homogenised blocks calibrated against published module indentation tests. Frame wall thickness, number of frame cells and tray and cross-member thicknesses were varied in 61 simulations, combined with Kriging surrogates and NSGA-II. Under the no-contact criterion a single-cell frame was lightest, but by no more than 3%. Under a damage criterion of 5 mm module indentation the ranking reversed: the single-cell frames absorbed 16–23% less energy before module damage, and a two-cell frame with 3.2 mm walls raised this energy by 28% for 12% more mass. Frames whose peak force before module contact exceeded about 130 kN damaged the modules earlier, so their energy fell although their mass rose. This stiffness limit persisted when the module strength was varied by ±33%. Tray and cross-member thickness changed the result by less than 4%. All input decks and scripts are openly released DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23903832

title: Dissemination of Climate Change Program in Indonesia in Accordance with the Sustainable Development Goals SDG-13 Based on Demographic Characteristics
description: Climate change has a significant impact on communities worldwide, including in developing countries like Indonesia. The Sustainable Development Goals, specifically Goal 13, Climate Action, reflect this. This study examines how demographic factors influence community strategies for adapting to climate change and its mitigation in Indonesia. 2024 was the hottest year on record, with the global average temperature reaching 1.55°C above the pre-industrial era (1850–1900). For the first time, the global annual temperature increase exceeded the 1.5°C threshold set in the Paris Agreement in 2015. The last ten years (2015–2024) were the hottest in recorded history, demonstrating a consistent global warming trend. In Indonesia, 2024 was also the hottest year since observations began in 1981, with an average temperature of 27.5°C and an anomaly of 0.8°C compared to the 1991–2020 normal. Sea level rise, based on satellite data, shows an upward trend of 4.3±0.4 mm/year. This study provides new empirical evidence from Indonesia on the role of communities in shaping adaptation responses to climate change. The approach used is based on the concept of climate change knowledge management and the knowledge management system cycle, with exploratory factor analysis and regression analysis methods for model development. The results obtained are the existence of several new factors that can be used as indicators of success in strengthening community capacity and resilience in facing climate change now and in the future. Double boundary drift: geographical indication boundaries under climate change and administrative reorganisation - the case of Son La coffee, Vietnam
description: Geographical indications (GIs) link a product to its place of origin. Where that place is written as a list of administrative units, the legal description and the land it denotes can come apart. We conceptualise this as double boundary drift : institutional drift, when the units describing a GI area are renamed, amalgamated or abolished, and ecological drift, when land sustainably suited to the product shifts under climate change. We argue that administrative reform opens an amendment of the area that climate change alone rarely triggers, and that this amendment is the moment to re-anchor the boundary. We examine the Son La coffee GI (Vietnam), registered in 2017 as 24 communes, combining the 2025 commune amalgamation with an Arabica suitability model under five global climate models, two shared socioeconomic pathways and forest zoning. The amalgamation left 16 of the 24 names without a referent, and 10 of the 13 successor communes extend beyond the GI area. Only 61.5% (1067 km²) of the area is sustainably suitable, against 90.7% suitable. The gap is almost entirely protection and special-use forest, a misalignment present at registration, whereas modelled climate change lowers the grade of sustainable land (highest class from 16.4% to 4–5%). Institutional drift and ecological misalignment fall on different communes. Renaming would add about 785 km² without raising the sustainable share. Excluding protected forest raises the share to 90.3%; a hybrid boundary reaches 98.8% and keeps all producers but needs a digital map. Boundaries should be written in geographical criteria and reviewed periodically. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23435068
