title: Dynamic DAG Overlay Rewiring
description: Problem. DAG-based ledgers like IOTA suit decentralized IoT. The peer-to-peer overlay that carries their transactions and content is usually static or ignores device energy and storage. Making it adaptive creates a risk: if peers rewire toward neighbors that advertise the most resources, a Byzantine node can attract links just by exaggerating its state. Design. The paper proposes an overlay that adapts to resource state while limiting the influence of false reports: Nodes estimate peers’ state by latency-weighted diffusion with coordinate-wise trimming of extreme values. Self-reported state is checked by audits and trust factors. Rewiring follows a payoff-driven evolutionary rule, with an in-degree cap and random anchor links. Each rewiring is validated by a one-hop quorum, so the cost depends on neighborhood size, not network size. Tip selection and caching use the same resource and popularity signals. Theory. It proves quorum safety and liveness, a trimming bound, a closed-form probability that a neighborhood breaks the fault assumption (A1), and finite convergence of rewiring under frozen state. It also corrects several errors in the original draft: the equation weights, the quorum size, the caching threshold direction, the tip-age sign, and the smoothing and diffusion updates. Evaluation. The experiments are an epoch-level simulation of 500 heterogeneous nodes, with 3 to 5 seeds, paired tests and 95% confidence intervals. The baselines are a static random overlay, cluster overlays, simplified Perigee-style and Cyclon-style overlays, conventional LRU plus uniform tip selection stacks, and LRU, LFU and fixed-threshold caching. PBFT is compared analytically only. Findings. Versus the static overlay, sensor energy per confirmed transaction is about 21% lower and mean retrieval latency about 13% lower. Throughput and confirmation delay do not change. Rewiring is the only component whose removal clearly worsens service. Resource-aware tip selection cuts confirmation delay by roughly 10%. With 20% of nodes falsifying their state, the overlay sharply reduces the share of honest links pointing to Byzantine nodes. Audits matter most. The share of neighborhoods violating A1 matches the binomial prediction, and equivocation throttles rewiring without hurting throughput. Under churn it keeps its energy advantage, and the cluster overlay fragments more. In the accelerated lifetime run, more sensors survive than with the static overlay. The energy saving also grows with network size, up to N = 1000. Negative results, stated openly. A Perigee-style overlay beats it on sensor energy and latency. LRU and LFU caching beat its adaptive cache. Cluster overlays use the least energy but fail a quarter or more of retrievals and concentrate load. Anchors, diffusion and the probability floor show no benefit in clean runs. The earlier draft’s claims (41% energy saving, 1,240 tx/s, big throughput and load-balancing gains) are withdrawn. Limitations. The device constants are assumed and the evaluation is simulation-only. The runs are short with few seeds. The Perigee and Cyclon baselines are simplified re-implementations. The attack is one specific falsification-and-blackholing behavior. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23682004

title: ECOLOGICAL BURDEN OF LARGE CITIES AND HYGIENIC CHANGES IN BIOLOGICAL MARKERS OF URBAN POPULATIONS
description: the rapid expansion of large urban centers has heightened ecological pressures that significantly influence the biological markers of exposed populations, creating complex hygienic challenges that affect public health at molecular, physiological, and systemic levels. As urban environments experience intensified anthropogenic activities, including industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust, waste accumulation, reduced green spaces, and altered microclimates, residents are increasingly exposed to pollutants, toxicants, bioaerosols, noise, and psychosocial stressors, all of which contribute to measurable changes in biological markers associated with hygiene, inflammation, oxidative stress, immune function, endocrine regulation, and metabolic balance. This study examines the ecological burden of large cities and evaluates its impact on hygienically relevant biological markers, employing an integrated assessment combining environmental monitoring, biomarker analysis, epidemiological profiling, and predictive modeling. Environmental datasets include air pollutants (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, NO₂, SO₂, CO, VOCs), microbial contamination levels, noise exposure, water quality indicators, microclimate measurements, and urban-form metrics. Biological markers investigated include cortisol, C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukins (IL-6, IL-1 β ), oxidative stress indicators (MDA, 8-OHdG), heavy-metal accumulation (Pb, Cd, Hg), microbiome diversity indices, epigenetic methylation patterns, and antioxidant enzyme activity. The findings demonstrate that populations living in areas with high ecological loads exhibit significant alterations in inflammatory, endocrine, metabolic, and immunological biomarkers compared to those in less polluted or suburban regions. Predictive modeling indicates that biomarker deviations closely correlate with cumulative ecological exposure, lifestyle factors, and spatial distribution of urban stressors. The study proposes a hygiene-oriented biomonitoring framework and adaptive public-health strategies to mitigate the physiological impact of urban ecological burdens. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of how environmental pressures in large cities translate into measurable biological responses, highlighting the need for integrated hygienic policies to protect the health of urban populations. title: ECOLOGICAL DYNAMICS OF CRUSTACEAN ZOOPLANKTON AND THEIR CONTRIBUTION TO THE FOOD WEB OF TUDAKUL RESERVOIR
description: Crustacean zooplankton represents an important component of freshwater ecosystems and plays a significant role in the transfer of energy from primary producers to higher trophic levels. The present study considers the ecological characteristics of crustacean zooplankton inhabiting the Tudakul Reservoir, with particular attention to representatives of the classes Cladocera and Copepoda. The ecological importance of these organisms was assessed in relation to seasonal changes, environmental conditions, trophic interactions, and their contribution to the natural food resources of fish. Published data indicate that zooplankton communities of Uzbek reservoirs are composed of rotifers, cladocerans, and copepods, while Tudakul Reservoir has previously been reported to contain representatives of all three major groups. Crustacean zooplankton, particularly cladocerans and copepods, contributes substantially to the transfer of organic matter and energy within aquatic food webs. These organisms consume phytoplankton and particulate organic matter and, in turn, serve as food for fish and other aquatic consumers. The ecological significance of crustacean zooplankton in Tudakul Reservoir is therefore associated not only with its taxonomic diversity but also with its role in maintaining trophic interactions, supporting fish productivity, and responding to environmental changes. Monitoring the abundance and composition of Cladocera and Copepoda may provide useful information for evaluating the ecological condition and biological productivity of the reservoir. title: EL-VPD: A High-Resolution Globally Validated Vapor Pressure Deficit Record from 1951 to near present
description: Overview Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) is a fundamental measure of atmospheric moisture demand, with far-reaching implications for plant water stress, land-atmosphere interactions, ecosystem productivity, wildfire risk, and hydroclimatic extremes. This repository presents EL-VPD, a globally consistent daily VPD dataset covering the entire terrestrial domain (90°N–90°S, 180°W–180°E) from 1951 to near-present at 0.1° spatial resolution. Its combination of long temporal coverage, fine spatial resolution, and regular updates as new input data become available makes EL-VPD well suited for hydrologic, climate, ecological, agricultural, and broader environmental research. The repository also provides the MATLAB script VPD_Computation.m, which implements the annual EL-VPD production workflow, including the processing of required meteorological inputs and VPD computation. The provided Figure_#_*.m scripts replicate the analyses and visualizations presented in the accompanying manuscript.  Data Availability Because of the large volume of the complete EL-VPD archive (approximately 1.5 TB), the daily dataset is not distributed directly through this repository. The full dataset can be accessed through: http://140.112.67.11/public_datasets/EL-VPD/ .  Access credentials are provided as: User ID: user  and Password: public_user . Data Organization The archive is organized as monthly NetCDF-4 files stored within year-specific directories. Each file contains a three-dimensional array with dimensions: time × latitude × longitude, where time = number of days in the corresponding month, latitude = 1801 grid cells spanning 90°N to 90°S at 0.1° resolution, longitude = 3600 grid cells spanning 180°W to 180°E at 0.1° resolution. VPD values are stored in hectopascals (hPa). Files follow the naming convention as Daily_VPD_Y<YEAR>_M<MONTH>.nc . For example, daily VPD estimates for January 2024 are located at /daily/Year_2024/Daily_VPD_Y2024_M1.nc . File Contents Each NetCDF-4 file includes daily VPD values, latitude coordinates, longitude coordinates and time coordinates (days since reference epoch). The files also contain comprehensive metadata describing dataset name and version, spatial and temporal resolution, variable definitions and units, valid data ranges, and missing-value indicators. Citation If you use the EL-VPD dataset, or any portion of this repository in your research, please cite the associated dataset and accompanying manuscript. Proper citation helps support continued development, maintenance, and dissemination of open environmental data products. A formal citation for the dataset and manuscript will be provided upon publication.  Contact For questions, technical clarifications, or collaboration inquiries, please contact: Sandipan Paul 📧 sandipan.paul.ess@gmail.com 🌐 https://sites.google.com/view/sandipan-paul   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23940603

title: ELECTROCHEMICAL PROPERTIES AND APPLICATION  PROSPECTS OF ELECTROACTIVE COMPOSITE SUPERCAPACITORS BASED ON POLYANILINE
description: This article examines the operating principles of electrochemical energy storage devices—supercapacitors—and analyzes the physical limitations of conventional electrode materials. To overcome challenges such as large overall dimensions, low active surface density, and poor oxidation resistance in currently utilized supercapacitors, an approach employing polyaniline (PANI)-based electroactive composite materials is proposed. It is established that charge accumulation in the composite system proceeds via both the electric double layer (EDLC) mechanism and Faradaic reversible redox reactions. Conjugating the polyaniline matrix with an active substrate successfully eliminates the mechanical brittleness inherent to pure conducting polymers. Furthermore, the practical significance of symmetric supercapacitors for industrial power factor correction is demonstrated. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23336408

title: ENBLOC: Survey-Based Database of Housing Cooperative Residents for LLM-Based Agent-Based Modelling in Czechia and Poland
description: This dataset contains survey-based resident data prepared within the ENBLOC research project to support the development and application of an LLM-based agent-based model (LLM-ABM) investigating collective decision-making on photovoltaic investments in housing cooperatives in Czechia and Poland. The original ENBLOC survey included respondents living in both housing cooperatives and homeowners' associations. As the LLM-ABM focuses exclusively on housing cooperatives, the database was restricted to respondents living in housing cooperative buildings. The resulting dataset contains 2,754 individual records , including 754 respondents from Czechia and 2,000 from Poland , with 33 variables covering housing tenure, household composition, sociodemographic characteristics, technological and environmental attitudes, energy-related behaviour, financial concerns, neighbourhood relationships, trust, and participation in collective decision-making. The repository includes: database_all.xlsx: A combined Czech–Polish database of survey respondents living in housing cooperative buildings, containing the variables relevant to agent characterisation and modelling. variable key for database_all.xlsx: A data dictionary describing the variables, their definitions, and coding schemes. The dataset provides the empirical basis for constructing and characterising resident agents in the ENBLOC modelling framework. It complements the separately published country-specific model input configurations and the Python implementation of the LLM-ABM. Data anonymisation The survey data were provided to the ENBLOC research team by the research agencies responsible for data collection in anonymised form. The research team did not receive respondents' personal identifiers or any information enabling their direct identification. The published dataset contains a subset of these anonymised survey records, restricted to respondents living in housing cooperative buildings. The materials are intended to support methodological transparency, reproducibility, and further research on resident heterogeneity and collective energy investment decision-making in housing cooperatives. title: ENERGY SECURITY AND MACROECONOMIC STABILITY: THE ROLE OF SUPPLY RELIABILITY, AFFORDABILITY, AND DIVERSIFICATION IN CENTRAL ASIA
description: Energy security is usually treated as an energy-sector objective, yet its macroeconomic role in Central Asia, where five economies combine very different resource endowments and pricing regimes, is poorly documented. This article asks how supply reliability, energy affordability and diversification relate to macroeconomic stability in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, and through which mechanisms. Using a qualitative-comparative design, it synthesises ten peer-reviewed studies and several institutional reports located through scholarly search, compares the concentration of national power systems using 2026 Eurasian Development Bank figures, and examines four country cases. The evidence indicates that (i) unreliable supply imposes measurable real-economy costs, most visibly in hydropower-dependent Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan; (ii) affordability achieved through below-cost tariffs shifts costs onto public budgets, as Uzbekistan’s subsidy experience shows; and (iii) every country depends on a single source for 63–99% of its supply, which amplifies exposure to seasonal, price and import shocks. For the energy exporter, Kazakhstan, oil prices transmit to inflation through exchange rates. The article concludes that energy security supports macroeconomic stability chiefly when reliability and fiscally sustainable pricing are achieved together, and proposes a five-country panel design for formal testing. title: ERA5–SARAH-3 Meteorological Cutouts for Renewable Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain
description: Description This repository provides a 30-year collection of meteorological cutouts for renewable energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula and nearby offshore areas. The datasets combine ERA5 meteorological information with satellite-derived solar radiation data from SARAH-3 and have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. ERA5 provides the meteorological variables required for wind, temperature-dependent and hydrological modelling, while SARAH-3 supplies the direct and diffuse surface solar radiation fields used for photovoltaic generation modelling. The cutouts are defined on a regular latitude–longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.3° × 0.3° (approximately 30 km) and hourly temporal resolution. SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are retained over land and offshore grid cells located within 50 km of the coastline. All variables are integrated into a common atlite-compatible NetCDF structure, enabling the modelling of wind, solar and other weather-dependent energy-system processes. Data Sources ERA5 ERA5 is the global atmospheric reanalysis produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). ERA5 provides most of the meteorological variables contained in these cutouts. The variables derived from ERA5 are: height : Surface elevation wnd100m : Wind speed at 100 m above ground level wnd_azimuth : Wind direction information derived from the 100 m wind field roughness : Surface roughness length influx_toa : Top-of-atmosphere solar radiation albedo : Surface albedo temperature : Air temperature at 2 m above ground level soil temperature : Soil temperature at level 4 runoff : Surface and subsurface runoff information used by the atlite hydrological workflow Source: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ SARAH-3 Solar radiation data are obtained from the Surface Solar Radiation Data Set – Heliosat, Edition 3 (SARAH-3), developed by the EUMETSAT Satellite Application Facility on Climate Monitoring (CM SAF). SARAH-3 provides satellite-derived surface solar radiation information over the study region. The following radiation variables are derived from SARAH-3: influx_direct : Direct surface solar radiation influx_diffuse : Diffuse surface solar radiation The cutouts also include solar position variables calculated during data processing: solar_altitude : Solar altitude angle solar_azimuth : Solar azimuth angle Within these cutouts, SARAH-3-derived radiation variables are provided over land and offshore grid cells located at most 50 km from the coastline. For marine grid cells located farther than 50 km from the coast, these variables are set to NaN . title: EUSFlux: Mapping Forest Carbon Uptake in the Eastern US from Upscaled Flux Tower Data
description: This repository provides annual maps of Net Ecosystem Productivity (NEP) for eastern US forests at 500 m resolution, 2003–2023. NEP is predicted by a Random Forest model trained on AmeriFlux and NEON eddy covariance observations and applied to gridded MODIS, solar-induced fluorescence (GOSIF), Daymet and ERA5-Land predictors. Predictions are made for 16-day periods, gap-filled, and summed (day-weighted) to annual NEP. From 51 candidate predictors (Table 2 of the paper), permutation importance across 100 repetitions of 5-fold spatial cross-validation retained 13; daylength was added, giving 14: forest type, NDVI, EVI, LSWI, the 30-day LSWI anomaly, NIRv, MOD09A1 surface reflectance Bands 2, 4 and 7, LAI, SIF, root-zone soil temperature, shortwave radiation and daylength. The Random Forest (100 trees, max_features = 0.33) was tuned by nested spatial cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret it. The Zenodo repository includes: The preprocessed flux tower training dataset (NEE_flux_unh_sif_8.csv), containing 16-day site-level NEE observations and co-located predictor variables from AmeriFlux/NEON sites in eastern US forests; • An independent evaluation dataset of monthly FluxCom NEE estimates at seven held-out flux tower test sites (test_sites_monthly_fluxComNEE_2003_2021.csv; column NEE_gC_m2_d1); • The study area boundary shapefile (StudyArea.shp); • Python scripts, Slurm job scripts and one Jupyter notebook implementing the full workflow, in four folders: input data download and checks, predictor selection and model tuning, NEP prediction and annual forest maps, and the analyses and figures of the paper (run on Indiana University’s Big Red 200 cluster; file paths must be adapted); • Annual NEP GeoTIFFs (NEP_annual_YYYY.tif, 2003–2023) at 500 m resolution. NEP is reported in units of gC m⁻² year⁻¹ in annual rasters, with positive values indicating net carbon uptake and negative values indicating net carbon release. Pixels outside each year’s NLCD forest mask are NoData. The sign convention follows NEP = −NEE; flux tower data and intermediate prediction rasters are in NEE convention and are sign-flipped in the analysis scripts. A README provided within the deposit describes the contents, formats, column names, units, and provenance of all shared data files and code. Predictor variables and benchmark data are derived from the following external datasets, which are not included in this deposit and must be obtained separately: MODIS MOD09A1, MOD13A1, MOD15A2H, MCD12Q1 and land surface temperature products (NASA LP DAAC); GOSIF SIF (University of New Hampshire); Daymet v4 (ORNL DAAC); ERA5-Land (ECMWF / Copernicus Climate Change Service); AmeriFlux/NEON flux tower observations; FLUXCOM RS+METEO (Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry); NLCD land cover (USGS), 2003–2023; forest carbon removals from Harris et al. (2021) (Global Forest Watch); and a forest stand age raster for 2010. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23848971

title: EcoPro Tree Mortality Drought Indexes
description: BCMv8_indexes.nc4 holds annual (water-year) climate and water-balance variables and multi-year drought indexes for California on the 270 m grid of the USGS Basin Characterization Model version 8 (BCMv8), for water years 2006–2024. The drought indexes are the standardized precipitation index (SPI), the standardized precipitation–evapotranspiration index (SPEI) and the cumulative precipitation and water balance they are computed from, each accumulated over 1 to 6 water years. All standardized indexes use the water years 1980–2005 as the reference period. Source data and provenance All variables come from the monthly BCMv8 grids: Flint, L.E., Flint, A.L., Stern, M.A., Seymour, W.A., and Zamora-Reyes, D., 2021, The Basin Characterization Model – A monthly regional water balance software package (BCMv8) data release and model archive for hydrologic California: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P9PT36UI . (CC0 1.0.) The model itself is described in Flint, L.E., Flint, A.L., and Stern, M.A., 2021, The basin characterization model – A regional water balance software package: U.S. Geological Survey Techniques and Methods 6–H1, 85 p., https://doi.org/10.3133/tm6H1 . We downloaded the monthly grids for water years 1980–2020 from the child item “BCMv8 climate inputs for water years 1896–2020” and the parent item (September 2023), and those for water years 2021–2024 from the child items “BCMv8 climate inputs and outputs for water year 2021” through “…2024”. We used ten variables: aet, cwd, pck, pet, ppt, rch, run, str, tmn and tmx (October 1979 – September 2024). We did not change the values in the source grids. Our processing did the following: Read the monthly ASCII grids and stacked them into one monthly data cube ( convert_bcm_v8.py , merge_bcm.py ). Aggregated each grid cell to water years ( aggregate_bcm_v8.py ; see below). Computed the cumulative and standardized indexes ( append_climate_indexes.py ). Wrote the result to NetCDF-4 with zlib compression, level 9 ( zarr_to_nc4.py ). Grid, time and file format Projection: NAD83 / California Albers (EPSG:3310), stored in the spatial_ref variable. Grid: 3486 ( easting ) × 4477 ( northing ) cells of 270 m × 270 m, identical to BCMv8. Coordinates are cell centres in metres: easting runs from −374,360.8 to 566,589.2, northing from 592,501.7 to −616,018.3. Time: year = water year, 2006–2024 (19 values). Water year \(t\) runs from 1 October of calendar year \(t-1\) to 30 September of calendar year \(t\) (e.g. water year 2015 = Oct 2014 – Sep 2015). Dimensions: every data variable is (year, northing, easting) . Cells outside the BCMv8 domain, and windows with any missing month or year, are NaN. Types: the base variables, PR and PRET are float32; SPI and SPEI are float64. Notation For grid cell \(s\) and water year \(t\), let \(m \in t\) denote the twelve months of water year \(t\), and let \(\mathrm{ppt}_m\), \(\mathrm{pet}_m\), … denote the monthly BCMv8 values. \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the quantile function of the standard normal distribution. Base variables (single water year) Water-year aggregates of the monthly BCMv8 grids. Fluxes and storages are summed over the twelve months, \(X(t)=\sum_{m\in t} X_m\); temperatures take the monthly extreme. A water year with any missing month is NaN. title: Ecological Terminology in Karakalpak Publicistic Discourse: Semantic and Functional Analysis
description: . This article examines the semantic and functional characteristics of ecological terminology in Karakalpak publicistic discourse. The study draws on environmental materials published in the Karakalpak newspapers Erkin Qaraqalpaqstan and Qaraqalpaqstan jasları. Descriptive, contextual, semantic, comparative, and functional-stylistic methods are used to analyze terms related to water resources, environmental conditions, climate change, biodiversity, protected areas, environmental security, and the consequences of the Aral Sea disaster. The findings indicate that ecological terms generally preserve their core conceptual meanings in newspaper discourse, while their communicative functions are adapted to a broad readership. Some terms are used without explanation because they have become familiar to the public, whereas others occur with descriptive or semantically related expressions. The analysis also identifies lexical variation, illustrated by expressions corresponding to water scarcity and water shortage. Such variation can improve textual accessibility, but it may also create challenges for terminological consistency when conceptually distinct units are treated as interchangeable. The article argues that publicistic discourse plays a dual role in ecological terminology: it disseminates specialized vocabulary and makes environmental concepts socially recognizable, while also providing evidence of variants that may require further terminological assessment. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23656478

title: Effect of limited water availability on forest litter decomposition processes
description: Litter decomposition is a central biogeochemical process that regulates carbon and nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems. Litter has a critical role in improving soil nutrition, maintaining biological activity, preserving biodiversity, and supporting the overall forest ecosystem. However, there is limited knowledge on the release of macroelements during litter decomposition, particularly for different monoculture and mixed-species stands.  The study was conducted on experimental plots in the Miechów Forest District in southern Poland (50.19621°N, 20.06509°E). Litter of the following six tree species were examined: Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.), European larch (Larix decidua Mill.), pedunculate oak (Quercus robur L.), European ash (Fraxinus excelsior L.), European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.), and European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus L.). Both single-species and mixed-species litter were evaluated, with mixtures containing 75%, 50%, and 25% of deciduous and coniferous species.  The prominent effect of drought on litter decomposition emphasizes the importance of climatic factors in regulating decomposition rates and nutrient release from litter, which is crucial for maintaining forest ecosystem in the current global climate change scenario DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23676049

title: Effects of elevated carbon dioxide on growth performance and physiology of juvenile RAS-based Eurasian perch (Perca fluviatilis)
description: The present 105-day experiment studied the influence of exposure to carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in its dissolved form on the growth performance, somatic condition, blood plasma biochemistry, and fin integrity of Eurasian perch ( Perca fluviatilis ) juveniles reared in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Eurasian perch juveniles (mean initial body weight of 117.7 ± 28.2 g) were divided into three CO 2 groups in triplicate: Low (5 mg L -1 , control), Medium (15 mg L -1 ), and High (30 mg L -1 ). The exposure to dissolved CO 2 had a significant effect on total length, whereby the juveniles exposed to Low CO 2 achieved significantly greater length as compared to Medium and High treatments ( p = 0.009). Fulton’s condition factor (K) was significantly higher in Medium (2.35 ± 0.32) and High (2.34 ± 0.22) groups in comparison with the Low group (2.11 ± 0.24; p ≤ 0.001). Mean final body weight, standard length, specific growth rate (SGR), thermal growth coefficient (TGC), feed conversion ratio (FCR), and survival rate (as high as 99.33%) were not significantly different among the treatments ( p > 0.05). Analysis of the somatic indices showed the trade-off between gonadosomatic index (GSI) and kidney/fat somatic indices, while no significant differences in blood plasma biochemical parameters were found ( p > 0.05). The fin condition was very high, with an intact fin percentage ranging from 84% to 100%. Results indicate that chronic exposure to dissolved CO 2 concentrations up to 30 mg L -1 does not compromise the welfare or production performance of juvenile Eurasian perch in RAS but may induce subtle physiological adjustments associated with altered energy partitioning and somatic development, reflected in increased condition factors and shifts among somatic indices. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23529241

title: EliseGallois/Above_v_Below_Phenology: rootpheno_2025
description: The below-ground growing season often extends beyond the above-ground growing season in tundra ecosystems and as the climate warms, shifts in growing seasons are expected. However, we do not yet know to what extent, when and where asynchrony in above- and below-ground phenology occurs and whether variation is driven by local vegetation communities or spatial variation in microclimate. Here, we combined above- and below-ground plant phenology metrics to compare the relative timings and magnitudes of leaf and fine-root growth and senescence across microclimates and plant communities at five sites across the Arctic and alpine tundra biome. We observed asynchronous growth between above- and below-ground plant tissue, with the below-ground season extending up to 74% (~56 days) beyond the onset of above-ground leaf senescence. Plant community type, rather than microclimate, was a key factor controlling the timing, productivity, and growth rates of fine roots, with graminoid roots exhibiting a distinct ‘pulse’ of growth later into the growing season than shrub roots. Our findings indicate the potential of vegetation change to influence below-ground carbon storage as the climate warms and roots remain active in unfrozen soils for longer . Taken together, our findings of increased root growth in soils that remain thawed later into the growing season, in combination with ongoing tundra vegetation change including increased shrub and graminoid abundance, indicate increased below-ground productivity and altered carbon cycling in the tundra biome. title: Enhancing energy delivery does not remove the acutely blocked but surviving margin: a unified biophysical analysis of radiofrequency, cryo and pulsed field ablation in myocardial walls of different thickness
description: Background. Acute electrical endpoints, pulmonary vein isolation, loss of local electrograms, non-inducibility, are achieved in almost every radiofrequency (RF), cryo and pulsed field ablation (PFA) procedure, yet conduction recovers in a substantial fraction of patients. Each modality has been enhanced to enlarge lesions: higher power and shorter duration, contact-force and dose indices for RF; second-generation and constant-pressure balloons, colder cryogens and tailored dosing for cryo; optimised waveforms, higher voltage, repeated applications and larger footprints for PFA. We asked whether these enhancements eliminate the tissue that is electrically silent at the end of the procedure but survives. Methods. Axisymmetric finite-volume models of a catheter or balloon on a myocardial slab 2–10 mm thick, with blood above and epicardial fat behind, were solved for 18 clinically representative settings, bipolar delivery between catheters on the two faces of the interventricular septum (6–15 mm, blood on both sides) was modelled separately, and a three-dimensional model of a circular multi-electrode bipolar catheter with real device electrode geometry was solved for seven further settings. RF was modelled with the Laplace and Pennes equations and Arrhenius damage; cryo with an enthalpy formulation including phase change; PFA with the Laplace equation and field-dependent conductivity, plus Joule heating. Tissue perfusion was present during energy delivery and absent afterwards. For each modality a lethal criterion (Arrhenius index Ω ≥ 1; minimum temperature ≤ −30 °C; field ≥ 636 V/cm, or 423 V/cm after repeated applications) and an acute-block criterion (Ω ≥ 0.1; tissue frozen; field ≥ 318 V/cm) defined the permanent lesion and the acutely blocked but surviving margin. Lesion lines were analysed through critical spacings for a lethal and for an acutely blocked midpoint. Results. Every setting produced a surviving margin. Its maximal lateral width was 0.8–2.9 mm for RF, 1.2–2.2 mm for cryo and 1.0–4.8 mm for PFA, and in 8-mm walls the surviving-to-lethal volume ratio ranged from 0.58 (repeated septal bipolar PFA) to 6.8 (double focal freeze). Enhancements that prolong or intensify the same field, longer RF duration, double or longer freezes, higher PFA voltage, larger footprint, deepened the lesion but widened the margin in absolute terms. Enhancements that concentrate dose, high-power short-duration RF and repeated PFA at a fixed outer field, narrowed the margin to 0.8–1.6 mm but did not remove it. In 3-mm walls, lines spaced more closely than a modality-specific critical spacing (3.8–6.8 mm for RF and ultra-low-temperature cryo; 7–20 mm for PFA) killed the midpoint, whereas a window of 1.6–8.0 mm beyond it produced midpoints that appeared blocked acutely but survived. In 8-mm walls no unipolar setting produced a transmural lethal line, and surviving but blocked tissue persisted at the midpoint for all settings. With catheters on both faces of the septum, the field between them produced a lethal zone at each face; septa up to 8 mm were transmurally lethal at 1000 V, but in thicker septa the zones were separated by an acutely blocked but surviving mid-septal layer (5.6 mm at 1000 V in a 12-mm septum; 6.6 mm at 1500 V and 1.8 mm at 2000 V in a 15-mm septum), and a lateral margin of 2.1–3.6 mm (1.0–1.8 mm with repeated applications) surrounded every septal lesion. With the circular bipolar catheter, lesions were shallower than with unipolar delivery and a 1.6–2.0-mm margin persisted across the line at all voltages (0.6–0.8 mm with repeated applications); in a 3-mm wall, 1000–1500 V left a 0.6–1.0-mm acutely blocked but surviving layer beneath the electrodes. title: Exchange in Transient Carboxylic Anhydrides
description: Data archive for "Exchange in Transient Carboxylic Anhydrides" The hydration of carbodiimides is commonly used to drive nonequilibrium chemical systems, often by converting carboxylic acids into transient aqueous anhydrides. This fuel reaction has found broad applicability in functional systems, from single-molecule motors to responsive bulk materials. The reaction cycle is usually presented in terms of activation (anhydride formation) and deactivation (hydrolysis) steps. Here, we investigate the additional role of exchange within the activated state. Slowly hydrolyzing anhydride dimers and polymers were generated using carbodiimide and then treated with distinct carboxylic acids. The formation of new anhydrides was monitored using 13 C NMR spectroscopy, allowing rate constants to be determined. The anhydrides exchange at an intermediate rate, with on the order of 10 exchange events per hydrolysis reaction under typical conditions. This process yields unique behavior. At long reaction times, the ratios of different anhydride assemblies do not trend toward the equilibrium distribution (fast exchange limit), nor are they determined solely by activation/deactivation rates (slow exchange limit). Instead, it is possible to favor distinct species because of the balance between exchange and deactivation. The implications of this result for the assembly of nonequilibrium species with transient covalent bonds is discussed.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23403819

title: Experimental Plasma Discharge Dataset from the TCABR Tokamak
description: Description This dataset comprises 2,173 experimental plasma discharges from the TCABR (Tokamak à Chauffage Alfvén Brésilien) tokamak, operated by the Institute of Physics of the University of São Paulo (IFUSP). The database includes 1,684 non-disruptive and 489 disruptive discharges. All discharges are labeled for machine learning applications. The data features high-resolution (1 μs) magnetic diagnostics, including: Plasma current (Iₚ) – measured by Rogowski coils Loop voltage (Vₗₒₒₚ) – measured by toroidal loops Magnetic fluctuations – measured by an array of Mirnov coils distributed poloidally TCABR operates in a pure Ohmic L-mode regime with a circular cross-section, providing a highly reproducible environment (∼ 5% variation) free from confounding variables associated with auxiliary heating. This characteristic makes the dataset particularly valuable for studying MHD instabilities and disruption precursors, as well as for developing and validating machine learning-based disruption prediction algorithms.  Classification Methodology Disruptive discharges were identified through the temporal evolution of the plasma current, focusing on its rapid terminal decay. An automated procedure detected candidate current-quench events by determining the times at which the plasma current crossed 80% and 20% of a local reference current, respectively, and calculating the corresponding decay interval, Δt80−20. When available, loop voltage, Mirnov coil signals, and Hα emission were used as complementary indicators. title: FROM AQUEDUCTS TO SMART WATER NETWORKS: THE EVOLUTION OF HYDRAULIC ENGINEERING
description: Abstract: Water management is one of the oldest and most persistent engineering challenges. Societies have always needed to collect, transport, lift, store, and distribute water while controlling losses and adapting infrastructure to local terrain and climate. This paper examines the historical development of hydraulic engineering from ancient irrigation and gravity-fed water systems to mechanized pumping and contemporary smart water networks. Using a qualitative historical-comparative method, selected technologies are evaluated according to four criteria: source of hydraulic energy, method of flow control, infrastructure function, and relevance to modern water engineering. The analysis shows that the history of hydraulic engineering is characterized by a gradual shift from passive use of gravity and landscape toward active control through mechanical devices, pressurized systems, powered pumps, measurement, and digital monitoring. Ancient canals and aqueducts established principles of gradient control and durable infrastructure; Greek and Roman technologies advanced lifting and distribution; engineers of the Islamic Golden Age developed sophisticated pumps and water-raising machines; industrialization made large-scale pressurized supply possible; and modern systems increasingly combine sensors, data analytics, leak detection, and automated control. The study argues that contemporary smart water infrastructure should be viewed as the latest stage in a long engineering process aimed at increasing reliability, efficiency, controllability, and resilience in the movement of water. description: Climate gradients and habitat discontinuity structure genetic variation in a spring-specialist plant Dataset DOI: 10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdtj Description of the data and file structure We collected tissue from plants from 17 populations of crimson monkeyflower from the Southwestern United States. Samples for each of these populations were collected from distinct sampling sites represented by a large spring or seep.  These sampling sites are identified by unique two letter codes throughout this manuscript with exact location information recorded for all sites.   Crimson monkeyflower populations are limited to landscape features that support perennial water sources, such as mountain ranges and riparian corridors. Our populations were collected from eight geographically distinct landscape features, including two mountain ranges (Huachuca Mountains and Black Mountains) and six riparian corridors (Gila River, Aravaipa Creek, Verde River, Oak Creek, Colorado River and Virgin River). For each population, leaf tissue from four to ten individuals was sampled for genetic analysis. We obtained 19 additional tissue samples from herbarium specimens from unique sampling locations allowing us to sample the southern portion of the range, resulting in a total of 189 samples. Tissue collections consisted of 2-3 leaves, which we dried in paper envelopes using silica gel.  We ground tissue using a FastPrep-24 homogenizer (MP Biomedicals) and extracted DNA from samples using a modified CTAB protocol (Doyle and Doyle 1987) with quality control performed using nanodrop and gel electrophoresis. We digested genomic DNA samples using EcoRI and MspI before ligating to adapters and indices as part of a reduced representation protocol (ddRADseq; Peterson et al., 2012) . We performed size selection using a Pippin Prep (Sage Science, Beverly, Massachusetts, USA) to select fragments between 400 and 600 bp. Samples were then pooled into a single library and sequenced at the Genomics and Cell Characterization Core Facility at the University of Oregon using a single lane of an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, SP 100 cycle run. Alignment and Genotyping We demultiplexed sequences using fastq-multx (Aronesty 2013) and completed sequence assembly and genotype calling using ipyrad (Eaton and Overcast 2020) . Raw reads were quality filtered to allow a maximum of 5 low-quality bases per read (Q < 20) and require a minimum read length of 35 bp after adapter trimming. Adapter sequences were removed, and reads were mapped to the Mimulus verbenaceus genome (MvBLg_v2.0; LaFountain et al. 2022) using a clustering threshold of 85% similarity. Consensus base calls required a minimum depth of 6 reads (both for statistical and majority-rule calling), with clusters exceeding 10,000 reads excluded. The datatype for assembly was specified as ‘ddrad’ for this assembly, with two restriction overhangs specified (AATTC, CGG). Initial variant calling produced a dataset of 150,710 loci across 189 individuals. We used VCFtools to filter this dataset to remove non-biallelic loci. Loci were further filtered to remove those with a minor allele frequency (MAF) ≤ 0.02 and those with ≥ 60% missing data. After filtering out low quality loci, missing loci per individual were calculated and used to filter out individuals missing > 60% of their data, in order to avoid bias in downstream analyses. High levels of missing data per individual can bias downstream estimates of heterozygosity and population structure (O’Leary et al. 2018) . Lastly, loci were thinned to one SNP per tag to reduce linkage among markers. Python scripts for descriptive statistics, regression verification, diagnostic analyses, and selected robustness assessments. Tabulated results, including correlations, descriptive statistics, model diagnostics, sensitivity analyses, and data used to construct figures. Documentation of the computational environment, data provenance, and execution procedures. A README describing each file and instructions for reconstructing the analytical workflow. The underlying data were compiled from publicly available sources, including the World Bank, FAOSTAT, MapBiomas, and the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE). Reproducibility and limitations The repository is a partial reproducibility archive. Certain statistical results were retained from previous calculations, and some original procedures, including the complete stationarity-testing workflow, underlying annual MapBiomas spatial proxies, and original Monte Carlo CUSUMSQ implementation, are not included. Forest management simulations across Europe under climate change scenarios using the 3D-CMCC-FEM v5.7
description: This dataset was produced within the Horizon Europe project OptFor-EU – OPTimising FORest management decisions for a low-carbon, climate-resilient future in Europe (2023–2027). It contains outputs from forest ecosystem simulations performed with the 3D-CMCC-FEM model, aimed at assessing the impacts of alternative forest management practices (FMP) under present and future climate scenarios across Europe. Model description All simulations in this dataset were conducted using 3D-CMCC-FEM, a process-based forest ecosystem model that simulates eco-physiological and biogeochemical processes at daily resolution and hectare scale. The model explicitly represents species composition, age structure, stand density, and tree dimensions. It can simulates carbon and water cycles under different climate and forest management scenarios. 3D-CMCC-FEM has been widely applied across European forest ecosystems and constitutes a core modelling component of OptFor-EU (Collalti et al., 2014, 2018, 2024; Dalmonech et al., 2022). Simulations description Simulations were conducted across Case Study Areas (CSA), combining European Forest Types (EFT), 20-year age classes (AC), and multiple forest management practices (FMP). For each CSA, up to 14 EFT, 8 AC, and 9 FMP were implemented, depending on regional applicability. From the EURO-CORDEX generation CMIP5 downscaling experiments, high-resolution climate input data is available from the regional climate models (RCM) HIRHAM5-HADGEM2ES and RACMO22E-HADGEM2ES, for the Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 2.6, 4.5 and 8.5 (Jacob et al., 2020). Further details on the simulation protocol are documented in OptFor-EU Deliverable D2.2. title: Forest management simulations across Europe under observational climate data (CERRA) using 3D-CMCC-FEM v5.7
description: This dataset was produced within the Horizon Europe project OptFor-EU – OPTimising FORest management decisions for a low-carbon, climate-resilient future in Europe (2023–2027). It contains outputs from forest ecosystem simulations performed with the 3D-CMCC-FEM model, aimed at assessing the impacts of alternative forest management practices (FMP) under present and future climate scenarios across Europe. Model description All simulations in this dataset were conducted using 3D-CMCC-FEM, a process-based forest ecosystem model that simulates eco-physiological and biogeochemical processes at daily resolution and hectare scale. The model explicitly represents species composition, age structure, stand density, and tree dimensions. It can simulates carbon and water cycles under different climate and forest management scenarios. 3D-CMCC-FEM has been widely applied across European forest ecosystems and constitutes a core modelling component of OptFor-EU (Collalti et al., 2014, 2018, 2024; Dalmonech et al., 2022). Simulations description Simulations were conducted across Case Study Areas (CSA), combining European Forest Types (EFT), 20-year age classes (AC), and multiple forest management practices (FMP). For each CSA, up to 14 EFT, 8 AC, and 9 FMP were implemented, depending on regional applicability. Using the Copernicus European Regional ReAnalysis (CERRA) dataset, high-resolution observational climate input data were used to drive the simulations across Europe, providing meteorological forcing at approximately 5.5 km spatial resolution for the historical period (Ridal et al., 2024). Further details on the simulation protocol are documented in OptFor-EU Deliverable D2.2. title: G-IDSS - Dataset for a Decentralised Data Storage Service for Energy Communities
description: Measurement data, access control policies and analysis scripts for the paper "Decentralised Peer-to-Peer Data Management for Energy Communities". The deposit contains the results of eight experiments run on two clusters at the Technical University of Denmark, at community sizes from 2 to 1,600 peers: query scaling, the effect of the time budget under cluster and emulated residential networks, the saving from in-network aggregation over horizons of one day to one year, governance and consent decisions, an end-to-end trading cycle, community-scoped settlement with signed totals, behaviour with peers offline, and a comparison against a single store holding the same data. Also included are the data contract defining the community data model, the default and consent access policies, and the Python scripts that generate every figure and table in the paper. The data are synthetic: each peer holds quarter-hourly measurements for ten customers, generated locally from a seed derived from the peer identifier. Most runs use a thirty-day horizon from 1 September 2026; the aggregation experiment additionally sweeps one day and one year at fifty peers. No measurements from real households are included. See the accompanying software deposit for the implementation. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23479520

title: GIS-Based Dataset for Floating Photovoltaic Assessment of Hydropower Reservoirs in Türkiye
description: Description This dataset accompanies the research article entitled “GIS-Based Techno-Economic Assessment and Prioritization of Floating Photovoltaics on Hydropower Reservoirs in Türkiye: Energy Generation and Water Conservation.” The study presents a nationwide geographic information system (GIS)-based assessment of floating photovoltaic (FPV) deployment potential across 108 hydropower reservoirs in Türkiye. It integrates reservoir characteristics, spatial solar energy resources, evaporation estimates, techno-economic parameters, and multi-criteria decision-making to evaluate the potential contribution of FPV systems to renewable electricity generation and water conservation. The analysis considers four reservoir surface-coverage scenarios ranging from 5% to 20%. At 5% coverage, the estimated nationwide FPV capacity reaches 16.29 GWp, with an annual electricity generation potential of 25.76 TWh. Estimated annual water savings range from 71.34 to 144.48 hm³, depending on the floating system configuration. The techno-economic assessment incorporates investment and operating costs, levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), net present value (NPV), and electricity selling-price scenarios. Economic and infrastructure-scale screening identifies 51 candidate reservoirs, representing 4.24 GWp of FPV capacity and 6.84 TWh of annual electricity generation. Multi-criteria prioritization identifies Karakaya, Ilısu, and Ermenek among the leading candidates. The associated research materials are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further investigations into the integration of floating solar photovoltaics with existing hydropower infrastructure. Keywords: Floating photovoltaics; Hydropower reservoirs; Geographic information systems; Renewable energy; Water conservation; Techno-economic assessment; Türkiye. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23471460

title: GLOBAL SUCCESSES IN COMBATING CLIMATE CHANGE, PROTECTING BIODIVERSITY AND PUBLIC HEALTH.
description: This study examines the critical operational gap between macroscopic climate science and localized public health infrastructure through the implementation of the unified healthcare paradigm. Despite the abundance of ecological data at the macro level, translating these ideas into practical clinical interventions at the local level remains a persistent challenge. Using an integrated research project with mixed methods, designed for the period from 2020 to 2026, we are implementing a predictive machine learning system using random forests (RF) and gradient boosting machines (LightGBM). Worldwide, thanks to the implementation of this predictive architecture, an algorithmic accuracy of 88% in predicting boundaries has been achieved, which has given municipal medical facilities a 6‑day operational period for the proactive deployment of medical resources. The analytical work, combined with climate monitoring and medical management, provides a scalable empirical foundation for the global sustainability of the environment and health. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23531441

These are labelled by their latitude of injection and season ('ANN' for annually constant; 'MAM' for constant innjection over only northern hemipshere spring, March-April-May; 'SON' for southern hemisphere spring, September-October-November; see Zhang et al., 2024 ) The G6-1.5K-SAI, -HiLLA and single latitude injeciton scenarios were run by Walker Lee, NCAR. The termination scenario, G6-1.5K-SAI-End was run by Claire Zarakas at Carbon Plan. Each scenario has three associated output netCDF files stored here. These are (for the G6-1.5K-SAI scenario): geomip_WACCM_G6-1p5K-SAI_to_NorESM2-LM_earth.nc : monthly zonal-mean extinction, single-scattering albedo and asymmetry factor on the 14 short-wave NorESM2-LM radiation bands;   geomip_WACCM_G6-1p5K-SAI_to_NorESM2-LM_earth.nc : monthly zonal-mean extinction, single-scattering albedo and asymmetry factor on the 16 long-wave NorESM2-LM radiation bands;  geomip_WACCM_G6-1p5K-SAI_to_NorESM2-LM_p.nc : pressure, surface area density and mean radius. title: GeoShift: a four-survey geochemical benchmark for cross-survey evaluation under detection-limit censoring (data)
description: GeoShift is a benchmark for evaluating machine-learning models across geochemical surveys under detection-limit censoring. This record archives its data. Observational arm: harmonised concentrations (mg/kg), left-censoring indicators and per-cell detection limits for 39 primary-core elements in NGSA (Australia, 1,315 samples) and NASGL (conterminous USA, 4,857 samples), with sample identifiers, coordinates, Köppen climate group and GLiM lithology for all 8,285 observational samples. GEMAS (Europe, 2,113 samples) is represented by identifiers, coordinates and fold assignments only; its values are not redistributed and are fetched from the Geological Survey Ireland publication on data.gov.ie by the code record. Controlled arm: Tellus (Ireland and Northern Ireland, 5,643 topsoil samples), with published X-ray fluorescence (XRFS) and aqua-regia ICP values for 47 elements measured by both routes, a left-censoring indicator per route, and limit provenance (38 elements accredited on both routes). Also included: frozen fold assignments (random, spatially blocked, environmentally blocked, leave-one-survey-out, pairwise and predictor-space protocols), element crosswalk, detection-limit tables, censoring audits and SHA-256 checksums. Derived from NGSA (Geoscience Australia, CC BY 4.0), NASGL (U.S. Geological Survey, public domain) and Tellus (Geological Survey Ireland and Geological Survey of Northern Ireland, CC BY 4.0). title: Ghana Climate Finance and Macrofiscal Context: OECD Commitments (2000-2024) with World Bank, IMF, Ghana Debt and GCF Records.
description: This dataset provides a curated compilation of Ghana’s climate-related development finance and macroeconomic context, designed to support research on financing instruments, creditor composition, concessional lending and sovereign debt. The climate-finance component contains 2,719 OECD recipient-perspective commitment records covering 2000–2024. A cleaned version excludes one flagged exact duplicate, leaving 2,718 records across the full period and 2,587 records within the principal analytical window of 2010–2024. Records retain provider names, financial instruments, flow classifications, climate objectives, activity descriptions, amounts and source references. The compilation also includes 19 World Development Indicators series, with coverage extending back to 1983 where available; IMF financing-arrangement history from a snapshot dated 31 August 2024; Ghana Ministry of Finance public-debt observations preserved by report vintage; selected Green Climate Fund project approvals, instruments and disbursement events; and a documentary register, pilot evidence notes and qualitative coding protocol. Selected project and documentary material extends beyond 2024 and is identified as contextual evidence. It includes the original research workbook, CSV snapshots of all 18 worksheets, eight derived data tables, a data dictionary, methodological documentation, source-specific rights statements and file checksums. A Python reproduction script regenerates the cleaned records, annual and subperiod summaries, provider-coverage tables, concentration measures and robustness comparisons without external dependencies. All eight derived CSV files reproduce byte for byte. Climate-finance amounts represent reported commitments rather than national receipts, expenditure or sovereign liabilities. Provider coverage and climate-attribution methods vary across years. Missing values are preserved, overlapping public-debt vintages remain separate, and regional project totals are not assigned wholly to Ghana. Documentary pilot findings are preliminary secondary interpretations rather than a completed qualitative analysis. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23269848

title: GloUTCI-M: A Global Monthly 1 km Universal Thermal Climate Index Dataset from 2000 to 2025 (2022–2025 Extension)

title: Global 0.1° Monthly Anthropogenic CO₂ Emissions Dataset with Near-Real-Time Updates
description: This dataset provides global monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates at a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°, with the latest update extending through September 2026. The dataset is designed to provide a valuable resource for assessing the global carbon budget and the effectiveness of climate mitigation efforts. The estimates are generated using a deep learning–based framework that employs a convolutional neural network as its backbone and incorporates a mask fusion module to address spatially missing input data. The framework integrates satellite observations, meteorological reanalysis data, and temporal and spatial encoding features to estimate anthropogenic CO₂ emissions at a global scale. The data are provided in NetCDF format on a global 0.1° × 0.1° grid (1800 × 3600 cells) using the WGS84 geographic coordinate system. Each file contains monthly anthropogenic CO₂ emission estimates for all 12 months of a given year, expressed in tonnes month⁻¹ cell⁻¹. Files follow the naming convention ACO2_01deg_YYYY.nc , where YYYY denotes the corresponding year. The dataset is also updated regularly at doi: 10.12237/casearth.6a01788fe8a21d1686165027 A manuscript describing the methodology and dataset is in preparation. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23794545

description: Overview This repository is part of the Global Forest Carbon Sequestration Potential under Future Climate Change data collection accompanying the manuscript: The effects of global climate change on forest carbon sequestration potential in vegetation. The data collection quantifies the spatially explicit potential for global forests to accumulate vegetation carbon through 2100 and evaluates how this potential is affected by future climate change, atmospheric CO₂ concentration, and disturbance . The complete data collection includes: Carbon Sequestration Potential Gap (CSPG2100) — the primary summary product representing the net change in live vegetation biomass carbon between 2020 and 2100. Annual Biomass Projections — annual live vegetation biomass projections from 2021 through 2100 used to derive CSPG2100. In these simulations, climate, atmospheric CO₂ concentration, and disturbance all vary according to SSP126 . This experimental design represents the combined effects of the three future forcing components on forest biomass. title: Global map of Local Climate Zones
description: A global 100 m spatial resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) map, derived from multiple earth observation datasets and expert LCZ class labels. The LCZ map is based on the LCZ typology (Stewart and Oke, 2012) that distinguish urban surfaces accounting for their typical combination of micro-scale land-covers and associated physical properties. The LCZ scheme is distinguished from other land use / land cover schemes by its focus on urban and rural landscape types, which can be described by any of the 17 classes in the LCZ scheme. Out of the 17 LCZ classes, 10 reflect the 'built' environment, and each LCZ type is associated with generic numerical descriptions of key urban canopy parameters critical to model atmospheric responses to urbanisation. In addition, since LCZs were originally designed as a new framework for urban heat island studies (Stewart and Oke, 2012), they also contain a limited set (7) of 'natural' land-cover classes that can be used as 'control' or 'natural reference' areas. As these seven natural classes in the LCZ scheme can not capture the heterogeneity of the world’s existing natural ecosystems, we advise users - if required - to combine the built LCZ classes with any other land-cover product that provides a wider range of natural land-cover classes. title: Global organic soil disturbance and greenhouse gas emissions, 2001 to 2024: model outputs
description: Organic soils, including peatlands, contain large amounts of organic matter and can release greenhouse gases when drained or burned. This dataset maps organic soil extent and disturbance and estimates the associated emissions for 2001 to 2024 at 30 meter resolution. The maps and tables can help users examine where modeled emissions are concentrated and compare the contributions of drainage and fire. The downloads below include: A global map showing organic soil cover as a percentage of each 1 km cell. Separate maps of average annual drainage and fire emissions for each reporting period, also at 1 km resolution. Country and global summary tables, plus detailed results by country, climate, land use, drainage, and fire category. The maps are GeoTIFFs that can be opened in GIS software. Emissions maps report metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per cell per year. Summary tables are supplied as CSV files, and the detailed results are available in both CSV and Parquet formats. Results cover five reporting periods: 2001 to 2005, 2006 to 2010, 2011 to 2015, 2016 to 2020, and 2021 to 2024. Emissions are annual averages within each period. The final period spans four years. The model builds on the organic soil probability estimates developed by Isik and Hengl (2026) . We apply probability thresholds that vary by climate domain to define organic soil extent, then combine this map with land use, drainage indicators, and burned area data to estimate disturbance and emissions. The same probability layer and thresholds are used for all five periods. Emissions are calculated primarily using Tier 1 methods and default factors from the 2013 IPCC Wetlands Supplement. Please cite the Isik and Hengl source dataset separately when using the probability inputs. To request the 30 m model outputs as GeoTIFF tiles or a Zarr dataset, contact Erin Glen at the World Resources Institute's Land and Carbon Lab: erin.glen@wri.org . Open access downloads for these files are being prepared, subject to institutional approval. Links will be added here when ready. Results depend on the source maps and emission factors and do not replace national greenhouse gas inventories. Blank or missing results should not be interpreted as modeled zeros. See readme_data.md for units, file descriptions, and guidance on using the data. This dataset accompanies Mapping global organic soil disturbance and associated greenhouse gas emissions, 2001–2024 (in press), in Frontiers in Environmental Science . title: Guest molecule diffusion in the chitosan–ZnCl2 complex crystal: A molecular dynamics simulation study
description: We present combined molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using adaptive steered MD and umbrella sampling MD methods. The simulations can be used to evaluate the potential of mean force (PMF), i.e., the free energy change, for the diffusion of a ZnCl₂ molecule in the pathway introduced in the chitosan–ZnCl₂ complex crystal models. With some exceptions, most of the PMF plots showed a moderate increase in endothermic free energy of approximately 10 kcal/mol up to a ZnCl₂ moving distance of 1.5 times the fiber repeat distance, accompanied by exothermic peaks in free energy. During its movement, the ZnCl₂ molecule made more frequent contact with the O6 hydroxyl groups than with the N2 primary amino groups, whereas these contacts disappeared in the gap crystal models with the expanded pathway. These results suggest that ZnCl₂ molecules prefer to interact with O6 hydroxyl groups rather than N2 amino groups in the confined space inside the crystal. The O6 hydroxyl group, which is connected to a freely rotatable C5-C6 bond, can adopt oriented positions of wider range. This is consistent with the fact that the chitosan–ZnCl₂ complex crystal was obtained by in situ solid-state conversion of the original chitosan crystal. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18332365

The dataset includes 2780 events characterized by at least one impact statistic: area inundated, fatalities, persons affected or economic loss. Economic losses are presented both in the original currencies and price levels as well as inflation and exchange-rate adjusted to 2025 value of the euro. The spatial footprint of affected areas is consistently recorded using more than 1400 subnational units corresponding, with minor exceptions, to the European Union’s Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics (NUTS), level 3, or International Territorial Levels (ITL), level 3 for the UK. Daily start and end dates, information on causes of the event, notes on data quality issues or associated non-flood impacts, and full bibliography of each record supplement the dataset. Apart from the possibility to download the data, the database can be viewed, filtered and visualized online: https://naturalhazards.eu . title: Harmonised satellite, meteorological and ground-observation database for 128 cities, with surface NO₂ estimates for 100 cities
description: Air quality estimation failure in scarcest monitoring networks: a climate-dependent limit on satellite-to-surface NO₂ inversion   Satellite spectrometers measure tropospheric NO₂ columns, whereas exposure assessment requires surface concentrations. Machine-learning inversion is widely used to bridge this gap and often reports high predictive skill; however, validation is typically conducted within the monitoring network used to train the model. The extent to which these models transfer to the data-scarce regions where they are most needed remains unquantified. We assembled a harmonised database covering 128 cities from 2019 to 2025, combining Sentinel-5P TROPOMI NO₂ columns, MERRA-2 meteorology, Global Human Settlement Layer urban morphology, and surface observations from four national monitoring networks in the United States, China, India, and the Arabian Gulf. We fitted gradient-boosted trees using a validation protocol specified before modelling. Under leave-one-city-out validation across 35 temperate and subtropical cities, the inversion achieved an R² of 0.570 ± 0.004, outperforming climatology (0.437) and persistence (0.347). The same model and data achieved an R² of 0.840 under temporal hold-out, indicating that the gap between reported and deployable skill reflects validation design rather than model choice. When applied to five hot, arid cities withheld from all model development, the inversion performed poorly (R² = −0.83; bias = −7.4 ppb). Across all 54 cities with ground observations, the within-city correlation between column and surface concentrations declined systematically with mean air temperature (r = −0.707, p = 2.3 × 10⁻⁹), suggesting that expected performance can be predicted from climate. A climate-gated, two-stage model substantially reduced the arid-region bias to −0.23 ppb but recovered little variance (R² = 0.15); performance also did not improve as arid training cities were added. These results indicate that transferability is constrained primarily by column-to-surface physics, rather than model capacity or training-set size. We provide surface NO₂ estimates for 100 cities, each accompanied by two independent confidence measures that diverge in the cities of greatest interest.   These are the derived datasets for this study. The maps form part of the STECCI Interactive Digital Climate Atlas, developed under Work Package 2 (WP2). The Atlas employs a high-resolution spatial framework of 600 × 600 m, representing a substantial improvement in spatial detail compared with the 10 × 10 km resolution originally envisaged in the project's Grant Agreement. The cartographic outputs provide a spatial overview of projected seasonal temperature and precipitation patterns across Europe, supporting the identification of regional climatic differences and potential environmental pressures affecting cultural heritage. title: High-resolution (100 m) daily temperature and relative humidity dataset for Belgium for 2020 from UrbNet
description: This dataset provides high-resolution (100 m) meteorological information covering Belgium for the year 2020, generated using the UrbNet machine-learning framework (Souverijns et al., 2026). It includes daily minimum, mean and maximum near-surface (2 m) air temperature and relative humidity. UrbNet is a convolutional neural network trained to reproduce high-resolution simulations from the UrbClim urban climate model. By combining large-scale meteorological forcing from ERA5 reanalysis with detailed land-surface characteristics, including land use, vegetation cover, building density and topography, UrbNet generates spatially consistent meteorological fields at 100 m resolution across regional and national domains. The dataset captures fine-scale spatial variations in meteorological conditions, including urban heat island effects, temperature differences between built-up and vegetated areas, coastal influences and topographic variations. It thereby provides substantially more spatial detail than conventional meteorological reanalysis products. title: Historical Observations Data Platform Weather Stations
description: The Historical Data Platform (HDP) is a cloud-based, historical weather observations data platform focusing on near-real time to enable California’s energy sector access to high-quality, open climate and weather data in the formats that energy practitioners require. HDP applies best-in-class standards to historical weather observations to increase the number of reliable, accurate, long-standing observational records available to energy sector planners, including 8 variables identified as critical by energy industry engagement. HDP’s QA/QC pipeline included variable expansion (e.g., solar radiation, winds, precipitation) and careful handling for the kinds of extreme events facing western North America. The QC protocol is comprehensive, scientific, open, and transparent. Care was taken to address extreme events and ensure that the quality control process did not remove real extreme events while fixing issues such as sensor malfunctions. Inaccurate observations can cause serious problems for energy practitioners, leading to consequences such as incorrect maintenance decisions, missed safety thresholds, or over- or under-investment in grid hardening. This dataset supports ongoing efforts in electricity demand planning, asset placement, resiliency, and estimating renewable energy generation capacity needs, and serves as a critical localized dataset for future downscaling efforts of global climate models in the variables and resolution (hourly, sub 3km) needed in energy sector applications. The HDP dataset includes 15,064 standardized stations sourced from 27 open-access networks and covers 1980-2022, increasing the number of high-quality weather observing stations available to data users from ~500 to 15,000.   Dataset Format Note : Each station is stored as an independent .zarr in AWS S3 cloud storage. title: Historical and Projected Hydroclimatic Data for Four European Case Studies
description: This dataset contains historical and projected hydroclimatic data developed within Task 1.1 of the Horizon Europe RECREATE project. The dataset covers four European case studies: North Holland (Netherlands), Kalundborg (Denmark), Syros (Greece), and Costa Brava (Spain). The data are derived from CMIP5/EURO-CORDEX climate projections obtained through the Copernicus Climate Data Store. They include a historical reference period (1971–2005) and future projections (2006–2095) under three Representative Concentration Pathway scenarios: RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5. Seven combinations of Global Climate Models (GCMs) and Regional Climate Models (RCMs) were selected for the analysis. River discharge and runoff-related data were additionally obtained using two hydrological models: E-HYPEgrid and VIC-WUR. The main hydroclimatic variables are air temperature, precipitation, evaporation, and discharge. The data support the analysis of climate change impacts on water availability, the development of water supply and demand scenarios, and the assessment of climate adaptation strategies across the RECREATE case studies. The methodology and results are described in RECREATE Deliverable D1.1, "Future water supply availability and demand based on different RCP scenarios" (2025). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23763056
