title: Hotel Electricity Consumption Dataset for CNN-Based Forecasting and Gravitational Search Optimization (2023–2025)
description: This dataset contains electricity consumption records from a five-star hotel in Jakarta, Indonesia, enriched with calendar-related features to support electricity demand forecasting, energy consumption analysis, and cost optimization. The dataset consists of 910 daily observations collected between January 2023 and June 2025, where each record represents one day of electricity consumption. It was prepared to support the research entitled “Optimization of Hotel Electricity Energy Consumption Using Hybrid CNN and Gravitational Search Optimization to Support SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy.” The dataset includes electricity consumption during off-peak (LWBP) and peak (WBP) tariff periods, reactive energy measurements, and electricity consumption from three commercial tenant zones, anonymized as Zone A, Zone B, and Zone C. Dataset Attributes Each daily observation includes the following attributes: DATE: Date of electricity consumption record. DAY_OF_WEEK: Day of the week. IS_WEEKEND: Binary indicator identifying weekends. IS_HOLIDAY: Binary indicator identifying public holidays. WEEK_OF_MONTH: Week number within the month. MONTH: Month of the year (1–12). LWBP_USED: Electricity consumption during off-peak tariff periods. LWBP_PRICE: Electricity cost associated with off-peak consumption. WBP_USED: Electricity consumption during peak tariff periods. WBP_PRICE: Electricity cost associated with peak consumption. KVARH_USED: Reactive energy consumption. TOTAL_PRICE: Total recorded electricity cost. TOTAL_BUILDING_ELECTRICITY: Total building electricity consumption, used as the forecasting target. A_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone A. A_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone A. B_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone B. B_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone B. C_ELECTRICITY_USED: Electricity consumption of anonymized Zone C. C_ELECTRICITY_PRICE: Electricity cost of Zone C. Research Applications This dataset supports: Daily electricity consumption forecasting using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN). Temporal analysis of electricity demand based on calendar features and historical consumption. Electricity cost optimization using the Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSO). Analysis of electricity consumption under peak (WBP) and off-peak (LWBP) tariff structures. Evaluation of energy allocation strategies across building and commercial tenant zones. Research supporting Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7): Affordable and Clean Energy. In the associated study, a CNN model was developed using an input window of 14 consecutive days to predict daily building electricity consumption. The forecasting framework was combined with a Gravitational Search Algorithm to explore electricity allocation alternatives and potential cost savings under predefined operational boundaries. Data Confidentiality The hotel name and commercial tenant identities have been removed from the dataset. Commercial tenants are represented using anonymized identifiers (Zone A, Zone B, and Zone C). The dataset is shared for academic research purposes, subject to applicable data-sharing permissions. This dataset is intended for researchers working in energy forecasting, building energy management, machine learning, time-series analysis, and electricity cost optimization. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23490920

title: Hourly dispatch model of the European 2050 power system under climate change: input data and results
description: Input data and model results for the article "Stress-Testing Europe's Planned 2050 Electricity System Under Climate Change: Price Impacts, Regional Vulnerability, and Transmission Constraints". The model simulates the European power system hour by hour for one year in 2050. Each of 30 countries (EU-27 plus Switzerland, Norway and the UK) is one node, connected to its neighbours by interconnectors. Generation, storage and interconnector capacities follow the ENTSO-E TYNDP 2050 National Trends scenario and are the same in every scenario. Electricity demand, solar and wind capacity factors, hydro inflows and thermal plant availability change with the climate. There are 10 scenarios: a baseline (weather year 2013) and three climate pathways (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP7.0), each with low, medium and high demand-side adaptation. Each scenario is solved as a single linear problem with linearized unit commitment in PyPSA. Files: - accreu_inputs.zip: everything the model needs to run (demand, capacity factors, hydro inflows, plant availability, capacities, costs, starting network). - accreu_results.zip: solved networks (PyPSA NetCDF), hourly prices, generation, curtailment and load shedding for each scenario, plus summary tables and the stress-event analysis. See README.md for a full description of the files. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23535332

title: Hourly hurricane wind fields for North Carolina: Florence (2018), Dorian (2019) and Isaias (2020)
description: Hourly fields of the 10 m wind speed and direction over North Carolina and the surrounding coast for three hurricanes that struck the state: Florence (2018), Dorian (2019) and Isaias (2020). They were produced for the Atlantic Marine Energy Center (AMEC) to estimate wind damage to power lines, and they give the wind at any site within the area of each storm, such as the location of a tower, pole or substation. The fields follow the blending approach of Wang and Bocchini (2025), with a parametric vortex near the storm center and the ERA5 reanalysis away from it. The record includes the three fields in HDF5 format, the IBTrACS best tracks, a comparison with 38 weather stations and a short description. Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information (2026). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23399993

title: Hourly wind and solar generation profiles for U.S. EIA-860 plants (2020–2024) driven by TGW meteorology (1980–2024)
description: Dataset overview This dataset provides hourly capacity-factor time series for every wind and solar generator in the contiguous United States listed in the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) Form 860 surveys for 2020 through 2024. Generation is computed by running NREL’s reV  with  PySAM  ( windpower  and  pvwattsv5  modules) on plant inventories derived from EIA-860, with each generator forced by the IM3  Thermodynamic Global Warming (TGW)  downscaled climate dataset for weather years 1980 through 2024. For each EIA-860 plant year (the inventory of operating generators in a given vintage of EIA-860), 45 annual CSVs provide the hourly capacity factor of every generator under each historical weather year from 1980 to 2024. The data is intended to be aggregated at flexible scales — for example, to balancing authority (BA) level, or to nodes within a production cost model — supporting reliability assessments, long-horizon resource adequacy studies, and analyses of inter-annual variability, seasonality, and extreme weather events. title: HydroMap labels and protein structures for FastHydroMap
description: HydroMap simulation-derived residue labels for a frozen cohort of 1,000 protein chains, each with three independently seeded restrained explicit-water production replicas. Includes original and completed heavy-atom structures, production configurations, per-replica measurements, and three-replica mean, sample standard deviation and standard error. Targets include dewetting free energy (Fdewet) and water-structure components PC1, PC2 and PC3. These are HydroMap-derived labels, not FastHydroMap neural-network predictions. The final model uses an 800/100/100 train/validation/test split. A separate archive supplies the exact precomputed inputs for the 800-protein refit. No full simulation trajectories are included. The original labels and metadata are CC BY 4.0; source PDB data retain CC0 terms and third-party notices remain applicable. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23543197

title: Hygrothermal Aging Dataset and Performance of Thermoset Barrier Coatings for Infrastructure Longevity
description: Processed and derived data from an accelerated hygrothermal aging study of an epoxy barrier coating used for the rehabilitation of infrastructure. Coupons of a toughened epoxy composite were aged by dry-heat and by water immersion at four temperatures (20, 40, 60 and 80°C), for exposure periods ranging from an initial ~2-week sorption window to fourteen months of long-term gravimetric monitoring, and characterised by tensile testing (n = 5 specimens per condition), dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA; tan delta peak, ASTM D7028; n = 3 replicates) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; first heating scan; n = 3 replicates), together with gravimetric water-uptake measurements. This dataset contains the derived/processed results reported in the associated manuscript: tensile modulus, strength and elongation at break across four aging conditions — dry-heat aging for two months; water immersion for two months, tested wet; water immersion for two months followed by drying, to assess the reversibility of property loss; and water immersion for four months, tested wet — each reported across the four aging temperatures. Glass transition temperature (Tg) by DMA and DSC after two months of water exposure showed a comparatively narrow range (DMA ≈ 30–36°C; DSC ≈ 31–36°C) despite close to a two-order-of-magnitude change in tensile modulus over the same temperature range, indicating that Tg alone does not capture the extent of hygrothermal degradation in this system. Initial sorption rate constants at each temperature, together with an Arrhenius fit of the rate constant (apparent activation energy ≈ 10.1 kJ/mol, R² = 0.98, over 20–80°C), and the long-term (to fourteen months) 60°C weight-change curve are also included; the latter shows weight gain continuing for approximately eight months (peaking near 35%) before a subsequent decrease, consistent with a transition from diffusion-controlled moisture uptake to degradation-associated water transport (swelling, leaching, or partial network dissolution) at prolonged exposure. The raw, coupon-by-coupon water-uptake, mechanical and thermal data are openly available in DiVA and are not duplicated here; see Related works and References for the full set of underlying and related records. title: ICES-XPS Macro-fiscal Implications of Climate Change and Adaptation Dataset
description: This dataset presents the macroeconomic and fiscal implications of climate change and adaptation in Europe, assessed with ICES-XPS (ICES-eXtended Public Sector), a multi-regional, multi-sectoral, recursive-dynamic computable general equilibrium (CGE) model of the global economy developed at the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC). The analysis considers seven climate impacts: sea-level rise, riverine floods, agriculture, pollination, wildfires, heat-related health and heat-related labor productivity and supply. Adaptation includes planned public adaptation, with implications for public budgets and investment, and private adaptation, such as energy use for cooling and heating. Results are reported for three adaptation levels. The dataset provides estimates of changes in gross domestic product (GDP), government income, government investment and public debt. Results are expressed as percentage changes relative to the no climate change scenario (NO_CC). Results are expressed as percentage changes relative to a baseline scenario.   Dataset documentation (README):   https://iiasa.github.io/ACCREU_datasets/ices/ICES-XPS_README For a detailed description please refer to the Technical documentation of ICES-XPS model extensions within the ACCREU project Data access and file listing: https://iiasa.github.io/ACCREU_datasets/ices/ices-xps-file_access DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23769839

title: IGM viewer: Ice loss in the European Alps until 2050, Cook et al. (2023)
description: Outputs of the paper Ice loss in the European Alps until 2050 using a fully assimilated, deep-learning-aided 3D ice-flow model (Cook et al., 2023, Geophysical Research Letters, doi:10.1029/2023GL105029 ), prepared for the IGM map viewer: igm-model.org/latest/viewer/#study=2023-Cook-GRL . Derived from the data record of the paper ( doi:10.5281/zenodo.8037001 ): the runs of the 12 glacier clusters are merged into one map of the European Alps on the 100 m model grid (EPSG:32632), every 5 years from 2020 to 2050. Three scenarios: present : present-day surface mass balance (SMB) (runs Prog2050SMB20yC1 to C12); feedback : present-day SMB with SMB-elevation feedback (Prog2050SMB20yC1SMBF to C12SMBF); trend : SMB extrapolated from its trend since 2000 (Prog2050SMB20yIDC1 to IDC12). Layers: ice thickness (thk, m), surface speed (velsurf_mag, m/yr), SMB (smb, m ice/yr), ice surface elevation (usurf, m) and bed elevation (topg, m). Ice fields are masked where the ice is thinner than 1 m, the bed elevation is given where there is ice at any time step, and placeholder SMB values below -50 m/yr are set to nodata. Format: data.bin holds Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs placed one after the other (int16, value = stored / scale, nodata -32768, time steps as bands); igm_viewer.json describes the study and gives the position and scale of each GeoTIFF in data.bin. The initial states, other runs, area and volume series and the code of IGM v1.0 are in the original record. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24021640

title: IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE ON SANITARY–HYGIENIC INDICATORS AND ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS IN UZBEKISTAN
description: climate change has emerged as one of the most significant global challenges of the 21st century, exerting profound effects on environmental quality, public health, water security, infectious disease dynamics, and sanitary–hygienic stability, particularly in climate-sensitive regions such as Central Asia. Uzbekistan, characterized by arid and semi-arid climate zones, limited freshwater resources, high evapotranspiration, and rapid socio-economic transformations, is increasingly vulnerable to climate-driven shifts in sanitary–hygienic indicators that shape population health and environmental safety. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of how rising temperatures, intensified droughts, extreme weather events, atmospheric pollution, desertification, and water scarcity interact to alter water quality parameters, microbiological contamination patterns, food hygiene risks, air sanitation levels, and vector-borne disease propagation in Uzbekistan. Utilizing an integrated methodological approach that encompasses environmental sampling, spatiotemporal trend analysis, climate modeling, microbial risk assessment, and adaptive-system design, the study evaluates the current and projected impacts of climate change on sanitary–hygienic conditions and formulates evidence-based adaptive management frameworks suitable for national implementation. Findings reveal strong correlations between climatic variables and sanitary deviations, including increased microbial loads in surface waters during heatwaves, elevated particulate-matter concentrations facilitating bioaerosol spread, reduced water-treatment efficiency under high temperatures, and accelerated spoilage rates of perishable foods due to thermal shifts. Additionally, long-term projections suggest that without adaptive interventions, Uzbekistan could experience a 20–40% rise in climate-driven hygienic risks by 2050. The study proposes a multidimensional adaptive management system incorporating early-warning surveillance, climate-informed risk forecasting, sustainable water-resource governance, improved heat-resilient sanitation infrastructure, hygiene-oriented public-health education, and digital monitoring platforms capable of real-time hazard detection. The research contributes a novel conceptual and operational framework for integrating climate resilience into national sanitary–hygienic policy and underscores the need for cross-sectoral collaboration to safeguard public health in a warming climate. title: IMPROVING MECHANISMS FOR ATTRACTING INTERNATIONAL INVESTMENT DURING THE TRANSITION TO A GREEN ECONOMY
description: The transition to a green economy requires investment mechanisms that combine environmental objectives with commercially viable projects and credible institutions. This study examines how competitive procurement, payment guarantees, long-term contracts, and development finance can support international investment, using Uzbekistan’s solar energy sector as an empirical case. The research applies comparative project analysis to three solar projects, examines the disclosed financing structure of the Samarkand–Jizzakh investment package, and conducts an illustrative sensitivity analysis of financing costs. Calculations show that the average awarded electricity tariff for the two subsequent projects was 32.55% below the Navoi benchmark. The Samarkand–Jizzakh package combined USD 193 million in sponsor equity and USD 216 million in development-bank debt, alongside payment guarantees of up to USD 12 million. These findings document the coexistence of competitive tariffs, foreign participation, and coordinated risk mitigation; they do not establish a causal effect of guarantees or procurement reform. The article proposes an integrated investment mechanism linking project preparation, transparent procurement, targeted financial support, grid readiness, and environmental verification. Its principal contribution is a practical framework for evaluating investment attraction through financial closure, fiscal exposure, and verified environmental performance. title: INTEGRATED DESIGN, OPTIMIZATION AND MECHATRONIC CONTROL OF A FOUR-SECTION ULTRASONIC AEROSOL HUMIDIFICATION SYSTEM FOR COTTON LINT BEFORE BALING
description: This study integrates the theoretical design, operating-regime optimization, mechatronic control and energy assessment of a four-section ultrasonic aerosol humidifier for cotton lint before baling. Fine mist is produced by piezoelectric atomization and carried in conditioned air through a moving lint layer, with flow direction alternating between consecutive sections. A sorption–transport model is linked to a three-factor Box–Behnken response analysis, while feedforward and feedback control are evaluated using a delay-based simulation. The source-reported factor–response pairs show close agreement between calculated and experimentally labelled values, and the modeled chamber substantially improves moisture uniformity relative to one-sided treatment. Air recirculation is predicted to reduce the required mist output and heating duty. The study differentiates direct source-reported observations from mathematical predictions, controller simulations and engineering estimates. The integrated findings provide a design basis for prototype validation and industrial implementation. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24015543

title: INVESTIGATION OF THE EFFICIENCY OF AN ELECTRIC GENERATOR WITH COUNTER-ROTATING ROTOR AND STATOR DESIGNED FOR OPERATION IN LOW-SPEED WATER AND WIND FLOWS
description: This article examines the design of a multi-pole electric generator featuring a counter-rotating rotor and stator, intended to enhance the efficiency of electricity generation from low-head water flows and low-speed wind currents. Utilizing conventional high-speed generators for low-speed energy flows necessitates the use of gearboxes or other mechanical transmission systems; this increases the structural complexity of the unit, leads to energy losses, and raises operational costs. To address this issue, a design utilizing the counter-rotation of the rotor and stator is proposed. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23834767

title: IPCC AR6 Sea Level Projections
description: Description This data set contains the sea-level projections associated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report. It contains the full set of samples for the global projections (under ar6.zip), as well as summary relative sea level projections (under ar6-regional-confidence.zip and, without the AR6 estimate of background sea level process rates, ar6-regional_novlm-confidence.zip). Most users will want to focus on the confidence_output_files, which correspond most directly to the figures and tables in the report. For the global projections, samples from the individual probability distributions described in AR6 WG1 9.6.3 are in the full_sample* directories. Regional projections can also be accessed through the NASA/IPCC Sea Level Projections Tool at https://sealevel.nasa.gov/ipcc-ar6-sea-level-projection-tool . title: IRONMAN personal race data: Hawaii 2022 World Championship and Barcelona 2019 - v2.2 including code
description: Verion 2.2 including code Version 2.1, including energy_hydration_reconstruction_v2.pdf + AndreasWillBarcelonaRun061019.gpx + AndreasWillBarcelonaBike061019.gpx Personal race data from the IRONMAN World Championship, Kailua-Kona, 8 October 2022 plus IRONMAN Barcelona 2019, 6 October 2019, (Hawaii 2022: bike Garmin Edge 520 Plus with Garmin Vector, run Apple Watch Series 7; Barcelona 2019: bike Garmin Edge 520 Plus with Garmin Vector 3, run Garmin Forerunner 935), together with exports from Garmin Connect and Strava, cardiopulmonary exercise testing with lactate diagnostics from May 2022, and two race photographs. Background: I qualified at IRONMAN Barcelona 2019 in 10:02 h; the Hawaii slot was deferred to 2022 because of COVID-19. Achilles tendinopathy prevented run training for the six weeks before the race, and my plan was to run conservatively from the first step. title: ISK-EASIN database: invasion risk screening records and taxon-specific risk assessment area maps
description: This dataset brings together published invasion risk screening evidence generated with the Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) family of decision-support tools and links it to taxon concepts in the European Alien Species Information Network (EASIN). It provides a structured, taxon-centred resource for discovering, comparing and reusing screening evidence while preserving the geographical, methodological, numerical, bibliographic and taxonomic context of individual records. The compilation covers eligible applications published from 2005 through July 2026 and contains 3,221 screening records for 862 taxa across 269 risk assessment areas. Seven screening tools are represented: FISK, FI-ISK, MFISK, MI-ISK, AS-ISK, TAS-ISK and TPS-ISK. The deposit comprises: An Excel database containing 862 taxon-specific screening tables, an EASIN taxon index, 214 bibliographic entries, 269 risk assessment areas and a 123-entry country-code legend. A ZIP archive (513.11 MB) containing 862 taxon-specific assessment-area maps in TIFF format. A README documenting the files, field definitions, geographical conventions, interpretation and citation requirements. Each screening record retains all 13 fields: EU Status; Risk assessment area; Toolkit; Threshold; BRA score; BRA risk level; BRA+CCA score; BRA+CCA risk level; Reference; Taxon name (Vilizzi 2026: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-07629-x ); Pooled taxon designation; Unaccepted taxon name; and Misspelt taxon name. Source-reference hyperlinks and links to the underlying taxonomic dataset are preserved. Records from different applications, assessment areas and toolkits remain separate. EASIN taxon information was retrieved on 22 May 2026, as documented in the associated manuscript and the worksheet “EASIN 2026-05-22”. The full EASIN taxonomic snapshot comprised 15,688 taxon names; this deposit contains the subset of 862 taxa represented by screening records. The retrieval date is distinct from the literature-search cutoff and the workbook release date of 26 October 2026. The dataset supports evidence synthesis, methodological comparisons, identification of geographical and taxonomic screening gaps, and prioritisation of further assessment. Users can establish whether a taxon has already been screened, retrieve the relevant thresholds and outcomes, compare evidence across assessment areas and toolkit generations, identify applications requiring updates, and locate candidates for climate-sensitive reassessment. Retaining historical names, pooled designations and misspellings strengthens traceability to the original studies. The maps depict the geographical coverage of screening evidence, using country-level coverage and approximate assessment-area locations or centroids classified as EU, Partly EU or Non-EU. They are not species-occurrence or species-distribution maps. Screening outcomes are conditional on the assessment area, toolkit, threshold and source evidence; they should not be interpreted as globally transferable species-level classifications. ISK screening supports initial risk identification and prioritisation and does not replace comprehensive risk assessment. This deposit makes the research data available independently of their implementation in EASIN species factsheets. It accompanies the manuscript  Integrating published invasion-risk screening evidence into the European Alien Species Information Network (EASIN)  by Lorenzo Vilizzi, Ana Cristina Cardoso, Chiara Magliozzi and Stelios Katsanevakis, currently in preparation for submission. Publication details will be added when available. This study was supported by the European Union’s Horizon Europe project GuardIAS (Guarding European Waters from IAS, grant agreement 101181413). title: Ice Anatomy: A Benchmark Dataset and Methodology for Automatic Ice Boundary Extraction from Radio-Echo Sounding Data
description: The measurement of ice thickness is of great importance for the accurate estimation of glacier volume and the delineation of their bedrock topography. In particular, this is a crucial factor in forecasting the future evolution of glaciers in the context of a changing climate. In order to derive the ice thickness, the travel time of electromagnetic waves in radargrams acquired by radio-echo sounding (RES) systems is analyzed. This can only be achieved by identifying the ice surface and underlying ice bottom in corresponding radargrams. Manually identifying these two reflection horizons in RES data is a laborious and time-consuming process. Consequently, scientists are attempting to automate this task through the use of techniques such as deep learning. Such automation can significantly reduce the time between a field campaign and the calculation of the glacier's ice thickness distribution. In this paper, we present the first benchmark dataset for delineating the ice surface and bottom boundaries in RES data, to facilitate straightforward comparisons of deep learning models in the future. The ``IceAnatomy'' dataset comprises radargrams and the corresponding manual picks, amounting to a total of over 45,000km of observations. The RES data originates from three sources: FAU, CReSIS, and AWI. The dataset comprises different RES systems as well as different pre-processing methods. In addition, the data was acquired over a large range of geographical and glaciological settings, featuring different thermal regimes present in Antarctica and the Southern Patagonian Icefield. This diversity ensures that the models' behaviors can be analyzed in different scenarios. We define a standardized train-test split for each source in the dataset. This allows us to introduce not only a baseline model trained on the entire training set (the ``omni'' model), but also three source-specific baseline models. The source-specific models are trained exclusively on the subset of the training data acquired by the specified source. The baseline models provide an initial benchmark against which subsequent models can be compared. The source-specific models demonstrate more accurate results than the omni model. For the FAU, CReSIS, and AWI test sets, the source-specific models achieve  Mean Meter Errors of 2.1m, 23.1m, and 4.9m for the ice surface and 9.1m, 78.2m, and 29.3m for the ice bottom. In relation to the mean measured ice thickness, these errors equate to 1.2%, 3.1%, and 0.3% for the ice surface and  4.9%, 10.4%, and 1.5% for the ice bottom.    For more information, please read the following paper: https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/19/5337/2025/ Please also cite this paper if you plan on using the dataset.   For the implementation of a baseline model please visit: https://github.com/ki7077/IceAnatomy   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23368993

title: Implementation and Performance Evaluation of a Solar-Powered Closed-Loop Recirculating Hydro-Gravitational Energy Storage System with Reinforcement Learning Control
description: This repository contains dataset files, mathematical model implementations, and code artifacts for a Solar-Powered Closed-Loop Recirculating Water Gravity Battery System . The system integrates a differentiable digital twin framework for microgrid energy management, deep reinforcement learning algorithms (including Proximal Policy Optimization) for dynamic dispatch and battery energy storage system scheduling, and integrated cyber-physical security monitoring protocols for smart grid optimization. Key Features: Hydro-Gravitational Energy Storage Modeling: Formulations and numerical simulations for closed-loop, solar-rechargeable water gravity battery systems. Reinforcement Learning Dispatch Control: Implementation of PPO-based adaptive control and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) optimization models for dynamic load management and energy storage scheduling. Cyber-Physical Power System Security: Algorithms for false data injection attack (FDIA) detection, Extended Kalman Filtering (EKF), and Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) verification protocols for resilient microgrid operation. title: InCUBE Dataset: 3D Surveying Data, Point Clouds and BIM Models of the Santa Chiara Building, Trento, Italy
description: The InCUBE dataset provides raw and processed 3D surveying data acquired at the Santa Chiara district in Trento, Italy, within the activities of the European Union-funded InCUBE project (Grant Agreement No. 101069610). The dataset is intended to support research and development in 3D data processing, Building Information Modelling (BIM), Historical Building Information Modelling (HBIM), interoperability between software tools, and Building Energy Modelling (BEM). The dataset includes: - 359 individual terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) scans acquired with a Leica RTC360 scanner, comprising approximately 800 million points at a 2 mm resolution. - 359 panoramic images acquired by the laser scanner. - Two mobile mapping scans acquired with a Leica BLK2GO device. - Two point-cloud datasets derived from aerial images, reported in the project repository as containing approximately 186 million points at a 1 mm resolution. - The final aligned and merged point cloud of the building, containing approximately 388 million points at an average resolution of 5 mm. - The BIM model of the entire building, provided in IFC and RVT formats. The different data types enable investigations into 3D surveying, point-cloud processing, BIM/HBIM generation, data interoperability, and building energy-efficiency analysis. title: Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles
description: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively. title: Input Parameter Dataset for Stochastic Multi-Carrier SSCEE Scheduling with Electric-Drone Mobility
description: Input Parameter Dataset for Stochastic Multi-Carrier SSCEE Scheduling with Electric-Drone Mobility This dataset provides a structured numerical input specification for a stochastic multi-carrier energy scheduling benchmark incorporating carbon-emission trading (CET), renewable portfolio standards (RPS), peer-to-peer (P2P) electricity trading, hydrogen conversion, and electric-drone mobility. title: Interaction between burial depth and N source in drip-fertigated maize: Agronomic performance and correlation with spectral indices.
description: Increasing drought severity and evaporative demand in Mediterranean areas makes it necessary to implement irrigation systems with high water and nutrient supply efficiency. The combined management of drip irrigation burial depth and different nitrogen (N) sources, thus far unexplored, predicting these effects using proximal and spectral vegetation indices. A 2-year field experiment was conducted comparing maize yield and N uptake from four N fertilization treatments: ammonium sulfate (AS), AS with the nitrification inhibitor DMPP (AS+INH), calcium nitrate (CN) and a control without N fertilization combined with surface or subsurface (30 cm depth) drip fertigation. Multispectral data were collected to calculate various vegetation indices, while the chlorophyll content was measured with a soil plant analysis development (SPAD) sensor in the second year. Subsurface drip and AS+INH increased maize grain yields compared to surface drip and AS-only (by 12 % and 18 %, respectively, P < 0.05). However, this was observed only in the second season, as were increases in grain N content. The  results show that the use of CN performed better in surface drip, while the use of NH4+-N-based fertilizers were recommended for subsurface irrigation. Regarding the spectral data, at the flowering-milky kernel and dent kernel phenological stages Normalized Difference Red Edge (NDRE) and the canopy chlorophyll content index (CCCI) were the two vegetation indices that best estimated agronomical parameters and were able to discriminate the phenological differences between irrigation systems. This study highlights the potential for (i) predicting yield and N uptake using proximal and multispectral sensors in drip-fertigated maize and (ii) optimizing crop performance by combining drip burial depth and N source (DMPP combined with subsurface irrigation), with relevant implications for climate change adaptation (i.e., potential improvements in crop phenology and water saving). description: This dataset contains the processed data and the Python scripts supporting the figures and tables of Benmahi et al., "Hemispheric asymmetry and up/down anisotropy of Jupiter's auroral electron precipitation: Juno/JEDI statistics", submitted to JGR: Space Physics. The data are derived from the Juno/JEDI level-3 electron differential intensities archived in the NASA Planetary Data System (Mauk et al., 2026), for perijoves PJ3 to PJ66 and Juno planetocentric distances below 200000 km. Two corrections were applied before analysis, a power-law replacement of the small-pixel data below about 50 keV from PJ20 onward and the removal of the Minimum Ionizing Bump near 160 keV. The Juno magnetic footprint was computed with the JRM33 internal field model combined with the CON2020 current sheet model, at a reference altitude of 400 km. Footprints were sampled on a 0.33 deg x 0.33 deg grid in System III latitude and west longitude, and one average spectrum was computed in each grid cell crossed during each perijove. Each cell was assigned to the polar emission (PE), main emission (ME) or outer emission (OE) region using the Juno/UVS main emission masks of Groulard et al. (2024) and the mean Io magnetic footprint. Downward (planetward) and upward (anti-planetward) fluxes were obtained by averaging the directional intensity over the corresponding loss cone and multiplying by pi, then integrating between 30 keV and 1 MeV. Files jedi_gridcell_fluxes.dat gives, for each grid cell, perijove, hemisphere and flux direction, the energy flux in mW m-2, the mean electron energy in keV and the electron number flux in cm-2 s-1. It reproduces Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2. jedi_gridcell_spectra.dat gives the corresponding grid-cell averaged differential flux spectra, in the same row order, and jedi_energy_axis.dat gives their energy axis in keV. jedi_up_down_ratio_map.dat gives the ratio of the upward to downward energy flux per grid cell, all perijoves combined. It reproduces Figure 2 and Table 3. juno_footprint_tracks.dat gives the Juno magnetic footprint trajectories shown in Figure 2. auroral_boundaries.dat gives the mean ME boundaries and the mean Io footprint contour shown in Figure 2. auroral_boundaries_per_perijove.dat gives, for each perijove and hemisphere, the inner and outer ME boundaries used to assign the grid cells to the PE, ME and OE regions. They are the Juno/UVS masks of Groulard et al. (2024) up to PJ39, and the mean of the PJ1 to PJ39 masks from PJ40 onward. All .dat files are plain text, with header lines starting with # followed by one line of column names and space-separated values. They can be read in Python with pandas.read_csv(file, comment="#", sep=r"\s+"). The Python scripts used to read the processed data, assign the grid cells to the auroral sub-regions, compute the statistics and produce the figures are included, together with the script used to export these files. title: KET Ultrarelativistic Electron Event Data
description: This data repository provides 6-hourly time profiles for the 13 ultrarelativistic solar energetic electron events identified in Ulysses/KET observations from 1990–2008. The event selection follows the methodology described in the accompanying paper by Jöhnk et.al. : "Ultrarelativistic SEP electron events measured by the Ulysses Kiel Electron Telescope" Candidate solar energetic electron events were detected from significant count-rate increases in multiple KET electron sub-channels, screened against Jovian electron enhancements using proton channels, and assigned onset times using higher time-resolution HET electron data. For each event, the repository contains fluxes sampled at 6-hour intervals for the E12 channel in discrete C2 PHA bins, starting three days before and ending 10 days after the reported event period. The C2 PHA data bins are: [20, 40, 60, 80, 90, 100, 110, 120, 130, 140, 150, 160, 170, 185, 200] For each bin, the effective energy in [MeV] as derived by the iterative Bow-Tie method as well as the flux and error of flux in [1/(cm^2 sr MeV s)] are provided. Time intervals that did not allow to apply the Bow-Tie method e.g. due to low statistics and thus yielding no effective energys of PHA bins and fluxes are set to -999   These time profiles are intended to support reproducible analysis of the temporal evolution of the events and provide the observational basis for deriving background-corrected count rates, energy spectra, and maximum electron energies using the GEANT4 response functions and iterative Bow Tie method described in the paper. The dataset therefore complements the publication by making the event-resolved time series available in a uniform format for comparison, reanalysis, and future SEP electron studies.   *Note that depending on the event strength, different time intervals may improve the accuracy of the calculated effective energys and fluxes. To enable the interested user to follow the methodolgy and apply it to his needs, the PHA resolved response functions for the C2 detector in the E12 channel are provided in addition. title: Key Projects and Design Strategies in Energy-Efficient Contemporary Architecture
description: The built environment accounts for approximately 39% of global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions and over 36% of final energy consumption worldwide. In response to pressing climate imperatives, contemporary architecture has undergone a paradigm shift from conventional resource-intensive design toward ultra-low-energy, net-zero, and energy-positive building standards. This paper conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of iconic energy-efficient architectural projects utilizing the standardized IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) research framework. By evaluating landmark international case studies—including The Edge (Amsterdam), Powerhouse Brattørkaia (Trondheim), Bullitt Center (Seattle), Pearl River Tower (Guangzhou), and the Bahrain World Trade Center (Manama)—this study synthesizes the core mechanisms bridging passive architectural strategies (building orientation, high-performance thermal envelopes, natural ventilation) and active technological innovations (Building-Integrated Photovoltaics [BIPV], geothermal energy loops, and IoT-driven smart automation). Quantitative metrics demonstrate that the synergistic implementation of these approaches can achieve operational energy reductions exceeding 70% relative to regional baseline standards, while generating substantial surplus energy. Finally, the study evaluates technical, financial, and policy barriers and proposes actionable frameworks for adapting green building methodologies to hot, arid continental climates such as Central Asia. title: MEDALUS-R: European Desertification Susceptibility Maps at 1 km Resolution (1996–2025)
description: Dataset overview This dataset provides harmonized, spatially explicit maps of desertification susceptibility across 37 European countries at a spatial resolution of 1 km, covering three consecutive decadal periods: 1996–2005, 2006–2015, and 2016–2025. The maps were produced using MEDALUS-R , a revised, data-driven framework for the large-scale spatiotemporal assessment of climate-conditioned desertification susceptibility, developed by Borrelli et al. (2026). Building on the original Mediterranean Desertification and Land Use (MEDALUS) framework, MEDALUS-R incorporates methodological advances in indicator normalization, objective weighting, parameter optimization, and the explicit representation of anthropogenic pressure and mitigation potential. The framework integrates four principal components: (i) Climate Quality Index (CQI), representing climatic stress and moisture constraints; (ii) Natural Land Susceptibility (NLS), representing intrinsic soil and vegetation sensitivity and exposure to natural stress processes; (iii) Human Pressure (HP), representing anthropogenic disturbances and land-use pressures; and (iv) Mitigation Potential (MP), representing the capacity of land management and conservation measures to moderate susceptibility. The resulting Desertification Susceptibility Index (SDI) is calculated using a multiplicative formulation, with consistent normalization and parameterization across the three decades to support temporal comparability. Dataset contents The repository includes three georeferenced raster datasets in GeoTIFF format: MEDALUS-R_Desertification_Susceptibility_Europe_1996-2005_1km.tif — Desertification susceptibility classification for 1996–2005. MEDALUS-R_Desertification_Susceptibility_Europe_2006-2015_1km.tif — Desertification susceptibility classification for 2006–2015. MEDALUS-R_Desertification_Susceptibility_Europe_2016-2025_1km.tif — Desertification susceptibility classification for 2016–2025. Each raster represents the spatial distribution of desertification susceptibility according to eight MEDALUS-consistent ordinal classes: 1 — Non-affected (N) 2 — Potentially affected (P) 3 — Fragile 1 (F1) 4 — Fragile 2 (F2) 5 — Fragile 3 (F3) 6 — Critical 1 (C1) 7 — Critical 2 (C2) 8 — Critical 3 (C3) Increasing class values indicate progressively greater desertification susceptibility. The classification is derived from the continuous SDI using data-driven thresholds and provides a consistent basis for spatial comparison and the analysis of decadal transitions. Technical specifications Geographical coverage: 37 European countries Temporal coverage: 1996–2025 Temporal aggregation: Three decadal periods Spatial resolution: 1,000 m × 1,000 m Coordinate reference system: ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035) File format: GeoTIFF (.tif) Data type: Unsigned 8-bit integer Raster dimensions: 3,922 columns × 4,060 rows Valid pixel values: 1–8 NoData value: 15 The three rasters share a common spatial extent, grid alignment, coordinate reference system, and classification scheme, enabling direct pixel-wise comparisons between periods. Scientific interpretation and potential applications The dataset supports the assessment of continental-scale spatial patterns and long-term changes in desertification susceptibility. It can be used to identify areas characterized by increasing susceptibility, examine geographical differences across climatic and biogeographical regions, quantify transitions between susceptibility classes, and support spatial prioritization for soil protection, sustainable land management, and land degradation neutrality strategies. The maps are intended for scientific research, geospatial analysis, environmental monitoring, and policy-support applications, including assessments relevant to European soil protection and climate adaptation initiatives. title: Machine Learning-Based Predictive and Prescriptive Maintenance for Induced Draft Fan in Steam Power Plant
description: The Induced Draft (ID) Fan at the case-study unit has no installed redundancy. If it fails, the unit is derated by up to 50% or tripped by a Master Fuel Trip. Route-based monitoring finds damage late, because early vibration amplitudes sit below the ISO 10816 threshold. We treated this as a DMAIC problem, fishbone analysis and a Cost-Benefit screen ranked an explainable autodetection layer above analyst training and material fixes. The detector is a 135,750-parameter one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) whose layers follow a Digital Signal Processing (DSP) equivalence (convolution as FIR filtering, max-pooling as envelope demodulation, stacked layers as Zoom-FFT), so an engineer can check its decisions against physics. SHAP attributions are mapped to the frequency and cyclic-spectral domains (CS-SHAP). Run-to-failure data could not be obtained from the plant, and MAFAULDA (50 kHz, 97,550 segments) was used as a surrogate for ID Fan fault modes. With a leakage-safe file-level split (1,560 training, 391 test files), accuracy reached 99% and macro-F1 0.99 over six machine conditions, above the 90% Critical-to-Quality target. CS-SHAP energy clustered on the resonance carrier near f ~ 2 kHz around the BPFO and BPFI markers, as DSP theory predicts. The improvement becomes a condition-based SOP with three-tier early warning and a model-drift control plan. By converting the single annual unplanned event into scheduled work, it targets an MTTR reduction from 120 to 72 hours or 40%,against an estimated IDR 5.70 billion per unplanned event and is projected to reduce ID Fan EFOR from 0.29% toward 0%. Measurement campaign on light-off performance and thermal response of Pd-based oxidation catalysts on cordierite and additively manufactured stainless steel monoliths: Experimental dataset
description: This dataset contains measurements from 10 light-off experiments conducted on a synthetic gas test bench (SGB) at the Chair of Thermodynamics of Mobile Energy Conversion Systems (TME), RWTH Aachen University. The experiments compare two oxidation catalysts with similar palladium (Pd)-based formulations applied to different monolithic carriers: a conventional series-production cordierite substrate and a 316L stainless steel substrate manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM). The measurement campaign investigates the influence of the carrier material and its thermal properties on pollutant conversion and catalyst heating behavior. It aims to assess the feasibility of additively manufactured metallic carriers for automotive exhaust aftertreatment and to establish a test procedure for comparing their thermal response with that of conventional cordierite carriers. Carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH₄) were used as model exhaust gas species and oxidized in oxygen-containing gas mixtures, with nitrogen (N₂) as the balance gas. The experiments cover three gas compositions and three heating protocols. These comprise a quasi-static reference ramp of 5 K/min and two transient heating protocols intended to represent aspects of automotive cold-start heating. For the transient protocols, the test bench temperature setpoint was increased in a step to 450 °C, using either limited or maximum heater power to obtain slower or faster heating, respectively. The dataset includes temperature measurements, mass flow controller data, and gas analyzer readings, with a focus on the light-off phase. Temperature measurements within the catalyst samples provide insight into their thermal response and the temperature rise associated with exothermic oxidation reactions. Together, these measurements support the comparison of pollutant conversion, light-off behavior, and heat release for the two carrier types. The 10 experiments cover selected combinations of the following gas compositions and heating protocols. Gas compositions All concentrations are given as volume fractions. CO: 1,000 ppm; O₂: 3,000 ppm; N₂ balance. CO: 10,000 ppm; O₂: 30,000 ppm; N₂ balance. CH₄: 100 ppm; O₂: 3,000 ppm; N₂ balance. Heating protocols Quasi-static: nominal temperature ramp of 5 K/min. Slow transient: step change in the test bench temperature setpoint to 450 °C with limited heater power. Fast transient: step change in the test bench temperature setpoint to 450 °C with maximum heater power. The datasets follow this nomenclature: “CarrierMaterial_Concentation_Species_RampGradient_InternalIdentifier.csv” , where: the internal identifier is used for referencing into the internal database. description: MeteoEurope1km is a daily gridded meteorological dataset for Europe at a 1-km spatial resolution for the 1961–2020 period. It holds five daily variables: TMAX , TMIN and TMEAN (maximum, minimum and mean air temperature), SLP (mean sea level pressure) and PRCP (total precipitation). This record is the entry point to the collection and holds no data itself. The daily data are published in separate records, one per variable and decade, each with one uncompressed ZIP archive per year of daily Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs. Monthly and annual aggregates and climate normals for 1961–1990 and 1991–2020 are published in one record per variable for TMAX, TMIN, TMEAN and PRCP; for SLP only daily data are available. The records and their DOIs are listed below and in catalog.csv . Methods Daily gridded temperature data were interpolated using the Regression Kriging, with digital elevation model (DEM) and topographic wetness index (TWI) as covariates. Daily gridded sea level pressure data were interpolated using Ordinary Kriging. Daily gridded precipitation data were interpolated using Indicator and Ordinary Kriging methodology in two steps: Indicator Kriging for the prediction of precipitation occurrence, then Ordinary Kriging for the prediction of total daily precipitation at the locations where precipitation occurs. Grid and values Coordinate reference system EPSG:27704 (WGS 84 / Equi7 Europe), the azimuthal equidistant projection of the Europe zone of the Equi7Grid. Pixel size 1000 m, grid dimensions 8229 x 5588 pixels. Values are stored as integers (Int16) and must be divided by 10 to obtain degrees Celsius, millibars or millimetres. The NoData value is -9999. title: Meteorological and Bioclimatic Data from Urban Measurement Sites in Bydgoszcz (Poland), 2024
description: This dataset contains meteorological and bioclimatic data collected in 2024 at five measurement sites in Bydgoszcz, Poland, representing different urban and rural environments: City River Area (CRA), City Urban Area (CUA), Upland Urban Area (UUA), Suburban Area (SA), and Rural Area (RA). The dataset includes meteorological variables such as air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, cloud cover, and solar radiation, as well as selected bioclimatic and thermophysiological indicators: PST, heart rate (HR), hyperthermia risk (Oh_H), and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) and others.  The data support research on urban climate, spatial variations in human thermal comfort, and the influence of local meteorological conditions on human bioclimatic conditions. They can be used for comparative analyses of urban and rural environments and for investigating the relationships between meteorological conditions and human thermal stress. This research was supported by the Regional Initiative of Excellence grant (RID/SP/0048/2024/01), entitled Extreme Weather Events Caused by Contemporary Climate Change and Their Impact on Humans and Their Functioning in the Natural Environment. title: Minimal effects of short-term novel bait consumption and restricted rations on the physiology and thermal tolerance of the American lobster (Homarus americanus)
description: Diet is known to modulate ectotherm thermal performance, making its impacts crucial to consider in the face of climate change. Recent shifts in bait usage in the Maine lobster fishery have exposed lobsters to new food sources, including terrestrial – based foods, the physiological impacts of which are largely unknown. Here, we acclimated juvenile female Homarus americanus to three diets: frozen menhaden ( Brevoortia tyrannus ) , fresh mussel ( Mytilus edulis ), or salted pig hide ( Sus domesticus ). Lobsters offered pig hide consumed minimal amounts; this treatment may be regarded as a starvation treatment. After three weeks we measured their aerobic scope, acute cardiac thermal tolerance, and pre – and post–trial hemolymph protein concentration. Results suggest lobster metabolism and acute cardiac thermal tolerance are robust to short – term nutritional variation, including starvation – like conditions and changes in hemolymph protein levels. This study highlights the need for a more detailed understanding of bait usage and consumption in the lobster fishery to elucidate potential impacts of fisheries management on lobsters coping with climate change.   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23224354

title: Mirror of "North American Boreal and Arctic Pyrogenic Carbon Mid-Infrared Soil Spectra and Sample Collections 2010-2020", archived on EDI Data Portal
description: This mirrors a dataset archived on the EDI Data Portal, shown here to help list SS4GG contributions. Please refer to the definitive, official archive: https://doi.org/10.6073/pasta/7742240be8eb320d3ae4bff01fb93b45 Description: 1120 soil samples from North American boreal and Arctic sites were sourced from studies focusing on fire history and associated impacts on carbon cycle dynamics. Data providers supplied measurements of various physicochemical soil properties, including organic carbon content (%) and bulk density (g cm-3), with some studies reporting total nitrogen (%). We do not have explicit information on the methods each study used to measure organic carbon, bulk density, and total nitrogen. After collecting samples from various projects, the Woodwell Climate Research Center provided mid-infrared scans and James Cook University measured pyrogenic carbon content using hydrogen pyrolysis on a subset of 100 samples. The mid-infrared measurements were completed on all 1120 samples using a Bruker Vertex 70 Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometer with a Pike Autodiff diffuse reflectance accessory. The mid-infrared data was pivoted to long form for data submission. To get this in a traditional wide soil spectroscopy format, pivot the wavenumber column to occupy column names, with a different wavenumber name for every column, and pivot the absorbance column to contain absorbance values for each wavenumber per sample, with a unique sample ID per row. Samples also have associated metadata, including location information, the depth of the sample taken, and time since last burn. The latitude and longitude information uses datum NAD83 and has varying precision per project. The time since last burn column has a collection of character entries stating if the time since last burn is unknown or if the area is unburned, while the numeric entries specify how many years prior the area was burned. title: Modelled flood extents for Los Santos (Grand Theft Auto V) under IPCC AR5 and AR6 sea level rise scenarios
description: Modelled flood extents for the fictional city of Los Santos, the setting of Grand Theft Auto V, under IPCC AR5 and AR6 sea level rise scenarios combined with the historical maximum storm surge at the Los Angeles tide gauge. Supporting dataset for Nörenberg, P. and Lantuit, H.: Sea level rise in Los Santos and Los Angeles: a comparative flood analysis using Grand Theft Auto V, Geoscience Communication, 2026. Contents.  Flood masks for all 25 scenarios as GeoTIFF rasters and as polygons with areas attached; the scenario table giving sea level rise, storm surge, total still-water level, flooded area and percentage of land area; a response curve of flooded area against still-water level from 0 to 10 m in 0.05 m steps, so any revised projection can be read off without re-running the model; the 31 shoreline points that fix the sea level datum; and the script that applies the calibration. What is deliberately not here.  The terrain this study is built on is a community reproduction of a proprietary Rockstar Games asset, and the satellite-style basemap is a capture of the same game world. Neither is ours to redistribute, and neither is the calibrated elevation model derived from them. They are therefore excluded. The calibration constants in the README are sufficient to reproduce the elevation model from the source mesh. Calibration.  Elevations in the rasterised mesh are in arbitrary units; elevation_m = (raw_pixel_value + 333.2486218064515) × 1.13414841. Cell size 1.0524 m. Land above mean sea level 44.4000 km². Storm surge 1.591 m. Two cautions.  The grid has no coordinate reference system and cannot have one, because the coordinates are a video game; every layer shares one grid and overlays exactly, and GIS software will correctly report an undefined spatial reference. Do not assign a real-world CRS. Units are metres. Separately, the plane outside the rasterised mesh is stored as exactly 0.0, which after calibration reads as a spurious +377.95 m plateau over 37.7 % of the extent, and must be excluded explicitly. On the numbers. These are static, or "bath-tub", inundation areas: land lying below a given still-water level, assuming hydraulic connectivity to the ocean. They are not predictions of where water would reach during a particular event, and they overestimate extent relative to a hydrodynamic model. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23932368

title: Molecular Dynamics Dataset of NaCl-Containing Ice Ih Using GROMACS: Temperature-Dependent Structural Properties and Ion-Specific Tetrahedral Order (240–273 K)
description: This dataset contains molecular dynamics simulation inputs, trajectories, and structural-analysis data for sodium chloride (NaCl)-containing hexagonal ice (ice Ih) at nominal temperatures of 240, 250, 260, and 273 K. The simulations were performed using GROMACS 2023.3 and the TIP4P/Ice water model. The simulated system contains 2,284 water molecules, 10 Na⁺ ions, and 10 Cl⁻ ions, corresponding to 10 NaCl ion pairs. The final configuration was subjected to steepest-descent energy minimization and NVT equilibration before production simulations of 1 ns at each nominal temperature. The dataset includes simulation structures, topology and ion-parameter files, molecular dynamics input files, production trajectories, energy and log files, and processed structural-analysis results. The analyses cover oxygen–oxygen and ion–oxygen radial distribution functions, ion–oxygen coordination numbers, hydrogen-bond connectivity, molecular tetrahedral-order parameters, mean-square displacement, and spatially resolved tetrahedral order as a function of distance from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Associated analysis scripts are included where available. The dataset supports examination of temperature-dependent structural changes in NaCl-containing ice Ih and comparison of the local structural perturbations associated with Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The results indicate a modest reduction in global structural ordering with increasing temperature, nearly unchanged average hydrogen-bond connectivity, and pronounced ion-specific spatial heterogeneity in tetrahedral order. The simulations represent a fixed-composition, fixed-volume model over 1 ns trajectories. title: Monte Carlo gamma energy deposition data for polystyrene scintillator geometries
description: This record contains Monte Carlo simulation data for studying gamma energy deposition in generalised-taper polystyrene scintillator geometries. The Geant4 isotropic-source dataset (G4-01) contains simulations for 2,208 geometries at seven gamma energies from 59.5 to 1,332 keV. It comprises 61,824 runs, each with one million primary gamma histories. The Geant4 parallel-beam dataset (G4-02) contains simulations for 1,024 geometries exposed to a uniform parallel gamma beam at the same seven energies. It comprises 50,176 runs, each with one million primary gamma histories. The FLUKA parallel-beam dataset (FL-01) contains simulations for 1,024 geometries exposed to a uniform parallel gamma beam at the same seven energies. It comprises 14,336 runs, each with one million primary gamma histories. Its geometries and source configuration are matched with those of G4-02, although the numbers of independent simulation replicates differ. The FLUKA isotropic-source dataset (FL-02) contains simulations for 2,048 geometries at the same seven energies. It comprises 14,336 runs, each with one million primary gamma histories. G4-01 and FL-02 use isotropic-source configurations, but their geometry counts and numbers of replicates differ. Together, the four datasets comprise 140,672 simulation runs and 140.672 billion primary gamma histories . The simulation tables are provided in HDF5 format within TAR archives. The record also includes archive containing supporting scripts. These datasets describe radiation-transport quantities. Optical photon transport, photosensor response, electronics, and experimental detector efficiency are outside their scope. When comparing results between codes, the source configuration and the definitions of the reported quantities should be checked carefully: the FLUKA histogram-based probability is a finite-bin proxy and is not identical to the Geant4 event-wise probability of positive energy deposition.   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23878640

title: National contributions to climate change due to historical emissions of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide
description: A complete description of the dataset is given by Jones et al. (2023) . Key information is provided below. Background A dataset describing the global warming response to national emissions CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O from fossil and land use sources during 1851-2024. National CO 2  emissions data are collated from the Global Carbon Project (Andrew and Peters, 2025; Friedlingstein et al., 2025).  National CH 4  and N 2 O emissions data are collated from PRIMAP-hist (HISTTP) (Gütschow et al., 2024). We construct a time series of cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions for each country, gas, and emissions source (fossil or land use). Emissions of CH 4  and N 2 O emissions are related to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions using the Global Warming Potential (GWP*) approach, with best-estimates of the coefficients taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021). Warming in response to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions is estimated using the transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions (TCRE) approach, with best-estimate value of TCRE taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021, Canadell et al., 2021). 'Warming' is specifically the change in global mean surface temperature (GMST). The data files provide emissions, cumulative emissions and the GMST response by country, gas (CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or 3-GHG total) and source (fossil emissions, land use emissions or the total). Data records: overview The data records include three comma separated values (.csv) files as described below. All files are in ‘long’ format with one value provided in the Data column for each combination of the categorical variables Year, Country Name, Country ISO3 code, Gas, and Component columns. Component  specifies fossil emissions, LULUCF emissions or total emissions of the gas. Gas specifies CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or the three-gas total (labelled 3-GHG). Country ISO3 codes are specifically the unique ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes of each country. Data records: specifics Data are provided relative to 2 reference years (denoted ref_year below): 1850 and 1991. 1850 is a mutual first year of data spanning all input datasets. 1991 is relevant because the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was operationalised in 1992. EMISSIONS_ANNUAL_{ref_year-20}-2024.csv: Data includes annual emissions of CO 2 (Pg CO 2 year -1 ), CH 4 (Tg CH 4 year -1 ) and N 2 O (Tg N 2 O year -1 ) during the period ref_year-20 to 2024. The  Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables. Data are provided from ref_year-20 because these data are required to calculate GWP* for CH 4 . EMISSIONS_CUMULATIVE_CO2e100_{ref_year+1}-2024.csv: Data includes the cumulative CO 2 equivalent emissions in units Pg CO 2 -e 100 during the period ref_year+1 to 2024 (i.e. since the reference year). The Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables.  GMST_response_{ref_year+1}-2024.csv: Data includes the change in global mean surface temperature (GMST) due to emissions of the three gases in units °C during the period ref_year+1 to 2024 (i.e. since the reference year). The Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables.  Accompanying Code Code is available at:  https://github.com/jonesmattw/National_Warming_Contributions . title: Norway spruce shows stronger growth sensitivity and weaker intrinsic water-use efficiency response than Scots pine under increasing water limitation in southern Finland
description: The data supporting this study consist of tree-ring growth, stable carbon isotope, forest inventory, and climate records collected across southern Finland for the period 1990-2022. Tree-ring samples were obtained from six forest sites, including three Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris L.) stands located on mineral soils and three Norway spruce ( Picea abies (L.) Karst) stands located on organic soils representing contrasting local moisture conditions. Annual basal area increment (BAI) was derived from dendrochronological measurements and used as an indicator of radial growth. Carbon isotope discrimination (Δ¹³C) was estimated and measured from d13c from annual tree rings and used to estimate intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE). To place site-level observations within a broader regional context, the tree-ring records were combined with species-specific growth indices (GIs) obtained from the Finnish National Forest Inventory (NFI). The NFI data represent regional growth dynamics across a wider range of sites and soil conditions than those included in the tree-ring network. Climatic drivers of growth and physiological responses were characterized using annual and seasonal climate variables, including vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and summer water balance. These variables were used to quantify atmospheric moisture demand and water availability and to assess their influence on interannual variability in BAI and iWUE. Site-level analyses incorporated local moisture conditions, whereas regional analyses focused on species-specific responses across southern Finland. The final dataset therefore includes annual observations of (i) tree growth expressed as basal area increment and NFI growth indices, (ii) carbon isotope discrimination and derived intrinsic water-use efficiency, (iii) climate variables describing atmospheric demand and water availability, and (iv) site descriptors including species, soil type, and relative moisture conditions. The dataset was designed to evaluate changes in growth and water-use efficiency under increasing water limitation and to compare species-specific responses across spatial scales ranging from individual forest stands to the regional forest inventory network. title: On a critical acceleration scale of dark matter in ΛCDM and dynamical dark energy: data and manuscript
description: Manuscript and CSV data behind the figures and tables of Xu (2025), On a critical acceleration scale of dark matter in ΛCDM and dynamical dark energy , ApJ 981, 40, doi: 10.3847/1538-4357/adaeb3 , arXiv: 2203.05606 . Contents: the manuscript (PDF) and csv/ (19 CSV files: the plotted data of the 18 data figures and the values of Table 1). Companion datasets of the same Virgo simulation: 10.5281/zenodo.6541231 (halo-based statistics) and 10.5281/zenodo.6757654 (correlation-based statistics). The earlier data record of this work is zenodo.org/records/15128034 . Major findings: In the Virgo N-body simulation the acceleration fluctuation of halo particles about their halo's mean has an RMS of a c = 1.2×10 -10 m/s² at z = 0, the value of the empirical acceleration a 0 of the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation and MOND. The velocity fluctuation of halo particles is u c = 496 km/s at z = 0, and the energy cascade between haloes proceeds at ε u ≈ −3×10 -7 m²/s³ (plateau 2.8–3.3×10 -7 m²/s³ for z ≤ 1). The three are linked by ε u ≈ −a c u c /[2(3π)²], with the factor 3π from the angle at which a merging halo enters; the simulation gives −a c u c /ε u = 189 at z = 0, against 2(3π)² = 178. The relation predicts a c ∝ (1+z) 3/4 (∝ t −1/2 in the matter era); the simulation gives a c ∝ a −0.69 , the EAGLE simulation a 0 ∝ a −0.75 , the Magneticum simulation a 0 ∝ a −0.98 ; MOND with a 0 ∝ cH would give a −3/2 . Fitting log M b = α log v f − γ log(1+z) + β 0 to 253 galaxies (118 at z = 0, 135 at 0.6 < z < 2.5) gives γ = 0.89 for α = 4 (95 per cent range 0.69–1.10), consistent with 3/4 and below the MOND value 3/2; the positive γ comes from the offset between the local and the high-redshift samples. The deep-MOND force law F = m a²/a c follows for baryons that share the cascade rate of dark matter and whose effective kinetic energy grows linearly with speed, as in the maximum-entropy velocity distribution of dark matter. The energy density a c ²/G ≈ 2×10 -10 J/m³ is of the order of the dark-energy density (5×10 -10 J/m³); a dark-energy model built on the acceleration fluctuation of all particles. title: Opportunity losses of green hydrogen production globally, benchmarked against the global green hydrogen project pipeline
description: Green hydrogen has been proposed by some as a solution for hard-to-abate emissions. Here, we quantify the opportunity loss (tCO2/MWh) of using RE for green hydrogen globally using a global geospatial model to assess i) the available renewable electricity, ii) the annual green hydrogen production and iii) emissions effects from a range of end-uses, including direct use of RE, industrial electrification, supporting electric vehicles, powering heat pumps and a range of green hydrogen end-uses. Results are assessed globally using i) the International Financial Institution Technical Working Group's mitigation factors for grid-connected renewables, ii) mitigation potentials for green hydrogen end-uses taken from Terlouw, T., Moretti, C., Harpprecht, C.  et al.  Global greenhouse gas emissions mitigation potential of existing and planned hydrogen projects.  Nat Energy   10 , 1503–1515 (2025) and ii) bespoke models for electrified end-use emissions savings.  Global estimates of the renewable electricity availability and green hydrogen production potential under the cost-optimal electrolyser ratio and wind:solar hybridisation are included in Global_Results_H2.csv. , with details of the optimal electrolyser sizing and wind:solar hybridisation for a 1 MW project at each gridcell. Estimates of the mitigation effects and opportunity losses are benchmarked to the global planned green hydrogen project pipeline in IEA_Project_Benchmarking_Full.csv , with data taken from the International Energy Agency's Hydrogen Project Tracker. title: Optimal Persistence in the p=2 Spherical Spin Glass: System-Size and Temperature Dependence of the Inter-Basin Crossing Rate — revised manuscript, code, and data

The archive contains the LaTeX source of the article (red-marked and clean versions), the point-to-point response to the referee, all six figure PDFs, and the simulation and analysis code together with the underlying data. The study concerns a persistent random walker (mass m, friction gamma, persistence time tau_p = m/gamma) on the GOE quadratic landscape H(x) = -1/2 x^T J x of the p=2 spherical spin glass, and measures the inter-basin crossing rate Gamma(tau_p) between the two minima. Both fixed-temperature canonical Langevin dynamics and microcanonical dynamics pinned to a level set H = E_H are included; the latter locates the topological transition at the saddle energy e_c and supplies an upper bound on the crossing rate above e_c. GOE top-gap statistics from 500 disorder realisations per system size support the N^{-2/3} soft-edge scaling. Each figure is regenerated from the bundled JSON data by the corresponding generate_fig*.py script. All paths are relative; the only dependencies are numpy and matplotlib. ORRC v1.0 provides hourly surface and near-surface meteorological fields at 0.09° (~10 km) resolution on a rotated regular latitude–longitude grid covering North America, Central America, and nearly all of Greenland, from 2015 to present. It supports near-real-time climate monitoring and is intended for operational climate services, event monitoring, and the routine update of climate indicators without waiting for future CaSR releases. ORRC-a v1.0 is adjusted relative to CaSR v3.2 using the 2020–2024 overlap period. Day-of-year mean corrections are calculated using a 31-day moving window. title: PALM-BIO 2.0: Modernised and extended biometeorology module for the PALM model system
description: General info This archive contains supporting data for GMD manuscript PALM-BIO 2.0: Modernised and extended biometeorology module for the PALM model system . Abstract The first version of the biometeorological module (BIO) contained three widely used indices: Perceived Temperature (PT), Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), and Physiologically Equivalent Temperature (PET). Supported indices were calculated directly in PALM and used as user-defined outputs. However, the implementation had several limitations. The most critical shortcoming was the need to rerun the entire simulation whenever any index parameters were changed. To solve these issues, we developed a new version of the BIO module, PALM-BIO 2.0 (or just BIO 2.0). The most essential updates are as follows: internal temporal averaging to ensure consistent results; correction of meteorological variable calculations at human body height; rewriting of the PET; multiple parameterisations for calculating the mean radiant temperature (MRT). We evaluated both module versions on the same high-resolution summer-day simulation. The domain-averaged differences are modest for MRT, which is higher in BIO 2.0; UTCI is slightly lower in almost every hour, and PT in every hour. PET differs the most, both in magnitude and in the part of the domain affected. Finally, BIO 2.0 is designed for straightforward extension, and two new indices have been implemented: Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT; indoor and outdoor versions) and humidity index (HUMIDEX). The organisation of directories is as follows model -   - code_bio1.0 - source code of the version of the PALM model with the original BIO module used in this study  - code_bio2.0 - source code of the version of the PALM model with the BIO 2.0 module used in this study  - revisions.txt - git revision numbers validation -   - diff_palm-ref - differences between the modelled and the reference outputs (MRT, UTCI, WBGT, PET)  - ref_bio_mrt_BIO2.0 - reference MRT with corrected errors  - ref_bio_pet_VDI-3787 - reference PET outputs  - ref_bio_utci_f90-code - reference UTCI outputs  - ref_bio_wbgt_Liljegren - reference WBGT outputs new_holesovice_bio_av_xy_N02 - processed GeoTiff files for all analysed variables from BIO 2.0 module new_holesovice_bio_bio_N02 - processed GeoTiff files for all variables from the optional BIO 2.0 module output old_holesovice_bio_av_xy_N02 - processed GeoTiff files for all analysed variables from original BIO module Structure and naming convention The output archives include the folder output-gis .
