title: PHYSIOLOGICAL MECHANISMS OF HORMONAL REGULATION OF GLUCOSE METABOLISM AND ENERGY HOMEOSTASIS
description: Glucose metabolism and energy homeostasis are fundamental physiological processes that ensure the continuous supply of energy to cells and maintain metabolic stability. These processes are regulated by complex interactions between the endocrine system, nervous system, and peripheral metabolic tissues. Insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone, and incretin hormones play essential roles in maintaining glucose concentrations and coordinating energy utilization. This article examines the physiological mechanisms underlying hormonal regulation of glucose metabolism, emphasizing pancreatic endocrine function, hepatic glucose production, peripheral glucose uptake, and neuroendocrine control. The study is based on a theoretical analysis of established physiological and endocrinological literature. The analysis demonstrates that glucose homeostasis depends on the coordinated regulation of insulin secretion, counterregulatory hormonal responses, and tissue-specific metabolic activity. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for explaining the pathophysiology of insulin resistance, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and diabetes mellitus. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23960449

title: PV–Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) Under Supply Constraints: A Scenario-Based Decision-Support Dashboard
description: Standalone residential photovoltaic systems with battery energy storage (PV–BESS) face variable solar generation, changing household electricity demand, and equipment constraints. Aggregate energy indicators, however, do not reveal which household loads can be supplied at particular times. This study designs and preliminarily evaluates an offline, scenario-based decision-support dashboard for assessing hourly household load fulfillment. Guided by Design Science Research Methodology, the artifact integrates sequential energy accounting, researcher-defined load priorities, battery operating constraints, and interactive scenario visualization. A hypothetical cross-context experiment pairs 4,415 hourly records derived from Germany's 2025 DARCK household electricity dataset with NASA POWER solar-resource estimates for an Indonesian location. Seven scenarios are simulated using a reference configuration comprising a 3.08-kWp PV array, a 5-kW inverter, and a 9.6-kWh battery. Across the experiment containing a synthetic 72-hour zero-PV intervention, allowing battery discharge for all loads produces 2.513 kWh of unmet priority-load demand across 44 hours, whereas restricting discharge to priority loads produces no modeled priority-load shortfall. Extending the interruption to 168 hours results in 2.943 kWh of unmet priority-load demand under the priority-load-only policy. Energy-accounting checks and dashboard comparisons support internal computational consistency and traceability of reported outcomes within the defined modeling assumptions, not physical-system reliability or improved user decision-making. title: Pilot-scale integrated LCA and C-LCC analysis for sustainable active material selection in sodium-ion batteries
description: The sustainability of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) is strongly influenced by the environmental and economic performance of their active materials, particularly at early development stages. However, comparative assess- ments of multiple synthesis pathways under harmonized pilot-scale conditions remain limited. In this study, three Na0.7MnO2 cathode synthesis routes (solid-state, sol–gel, and hydrothermal) and three biomass-derived hard carbon anode production pathways (walnut shell via thermal treatment, corn straw via hydrothermal processing, and pomelo peel via chemical activation and carbonization) were assessed within a cradle-to-gate framework. Laboratory-scale data were upscaled to a pilot-scale production scenario (100 kg day 1) using a process-based scaling approach. Environmental impacts were quantified using the ReCiPe 2016 midpoint (H) method, while economic performance was evaluated through Commodity Life Cycle Costing (C-LCC) coupled with Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis.,The results reveal that process configuration and energy intensity dominate sustainability performance, outweighing the influence of raw material origin. Among cathode pro- duction routes, the solid-state method showed the lowest global warming potential (7.3 kg CO2 -eq kg 1) and median C-LCC (3.5 € kg 1), whereas the hydrothermal route exhibited significantly higher burdens (211.5 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 124.2 € kg 1). For anode materials, pomelo peel–derived hard carbon presented the most favorable environmental and economic profile (57.6 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 11.2 € kg 1), while corn straw–based production was strongly driven by electricity demand.,These findings identify energy and auxiliary material intensity as key drivers of sustainability and provide guidance for material and process selection in emerging sodium-ion battery technologies. title: Postbiotics and Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) in the Pathophysiology of Digestion: A New Therapeutic Concept
description: This article examines the role of postbiotics and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in the physiology and pathophysiology of the digestive system and their cellular and molecular mechanisms of action. Particular attention is paid to how microbiota-derived metabolites regulate the intestinal epithelial barrier, local immunity, inflammation, energy metabolism and metabolic homeostasis. The mechanisms through which the major SCFAs—acetate, propionate and butyrate—support colonocyte energy supply, tight-junction function, G-protein-coupled receptor signalling and the modulation of histone deacetylase activity are discussed, together with the effects of postbiotics (inactivated microorganisms and/or their components) on epithelial protection, immune reactivity and intestinal microecology. The pathogenetic links between dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction are analysed in relation to inflammatory bowel diseases, irritable bowel syndrome, antibiotic-associated microbiota changes, obesity and insulin resistance. Drawing on research published in 2025–2026, the article considers the therapeutic prospects of postbiotics and SCFAs, criteria for assessing their efficacy and safety, and the limitations of translating experimental findings into clinical practice, including individual microbiota variability, the need to standardise preparations and the demand for high-quality clinical trials. title: Predicting Band Gap of Perovskite Materials for Solar Cell Application Using Machine Learning Regression Trees and Ensemble Models
description: The urgent global demand for clean energy has accelerated the research into perovskite materials, which are highly praised for their exceptional light-absorbing abilities and ease of large-scale fabrication in next-generation solar cells. A perovskite’s ultimate efficiency is decided by its band gap, which controls the wavelengths of light it harvests. Traditional methods for identifying the ideal perovskite combination, such as trial-and-error lab experiments or intensive computational simulations, are incredibly slow and expensive, creating a significant obstacle to materials discovery. To develop a fast, reliable machine learning framework that accurately predicts band gaps for various perovskite compositions without requiring slow, manual testing. To accomplish the work, we collected a comprehensive dataset of known perovskite materials and extracted their core properties to use as features. These features were then used to train and compare several machine learning algorithms, including Fine Tree (FT), Medium Tree (MT), Coarse Tree (CT), and Bagged Trees (BGT) . Among the implemented models, the BGT model outperforms the others, achieving the highest predictive accuracy (R²) of 94.50% and 98.02% on the validation and test sets for bandgap prediction of perovskite solar cell materials, respectively. This research successfully demonstrates that machine learning acts as a powerful screening tool. By bypassing the traditional trial-and-error approach, this framework provides an accelerated, data-driven path to discovering cheaper, more efficient materials for solar energy. title: Present and future daily air temperature records and indicator maps for 54 African cities at 300 m resolution
description: This dataset provides daily minimum and maximum 2 m air temperature (Tmin and Tmax) and 31 climate and heat-stress indicator maps for 54 African cities at 300 m resolution, covering present-day conditions and four future climate and urban-development scenarios. The dataset combines high-resolution urban climate simulations with projected climate change and urban expansion. It covers multiple aspects of urban heat, including extreme temperatures, warm nights, urban heat island intensity, heatwaves, thermal stress and potential impacts on outdoor working conditions. Spatial resolution is 300 m for 51 cities and 600 m for Cairo, Johannesburg and Luanda. Cities covered Abeche, Abuja, Ali Sabieh, Antananarivo, Asmara, Bamako, Bata, Bo, Bouake, Brazzaville, Cairo, Carnot, Casablanca, Darou Mousty, Dodoma, Franceville, Gaborone, Gabu, Galkayo, Gbarnga, Gitega, Harare, Johannesburg, Juba, Kankan, Khartoum, Kigali, Kinshasa, Kumasi, Luanda, Lusaka, Maseru, Mbabane, Mbale City, Moroni, Nairobi, Naqamte, Niamey, Nouakchott, Ouahigouya, Parakou, Port Louis, Praia, Sao Tome, Serrekunda, Sokode, Tete, Tiaret, Tripoli, Tunis, Victoria, Windhoek, Yaounde and Zomba. Climate periods and scenarios Scenario Climate period Urban land-use conditions Present 2001–2020 Present-day SSP2-4.5 2021–2040 Around 2030 SSP2-4.5 2041–2060 Around 2050 SSP2-4.5 2081–2098 Around 2090 SSP3-7.0 2066–2085 Around 2075 Present-day conditions are simulated using the UrbClim urban climate model (De Ridder et al., 2015), driven by ERA5 reanalysis. Future conditions combine UrbClim simulations with projected urban land use from GeoDynamiX (White et al., 2012) and CMIP6-based temperature adjustments using a delta quantile-mapping approach (Souverijns et al., 2023). Future daily records represent climate-adjusted historical weather sequences. The methodology and temporal conventions are described in README.txt. Dataset variables Each city contains daily minimum ( tmin ) and maximum ( tmax ) 2 m air temperature in °C, together with the following 31 spatial indicators for each climate and urban-development configuration. title: Probabilistic dispersal chains for 292 Iberian vertebrates: data, scripts and results
description: Data, scripts and results of a study of probabilistic dispersal chains for the 292 terrestrial vertebrates of mainland Spain and Portugal, anonymised for double-anonymous peer review. The archive holds the 5,899 planning units of the UTM 10 km grid (land areas, land-acquisition costs, protection shares), the species layers on the planning units (atlas records; baseline and 2050/2070 RCP 8.5 projections constrained by species-specific dispersal, as presence/absence, full and filtered probability), the dispersal values of every species with their sources, all scripts (input construction, dispersal coding, analysis, figures) and every result (persistence units, minimum-set and area-budget networks, evaluation). Start with README.md. The chainplan R package is archived separately (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23643673) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23645171

title: Processed CMIP6 Earth System Model Carbon–Nitrogen Cycle Data
description: Overview This repository documents the processing workflow used to derive global annual carbon–nitrogen cycle data from original CMIP6 Earth system model (ESM) monthly output. The development of this dataset was motivated by the development of CNit (Carbon–Nitrogen Interactions in Terrestrial ecosystems; see  CNit documentation ;  Tang et al., 2025a ,  2026a ,  2026b ,  2026c ), the coupled carbon–nitrogen cycle model for MAGICC (Model for the Assessment of Greenhouse Gas Induced Climate Change; see  MAGICC repository ;  Meinshausen et al., 2011 ). During the processing and analysis of ESM output, we identified notable mass-conservation issues that prevented the direct calibration of CNit, which strictly conserves carbon and nitrogen mass. Through investigations involving ESM teams and analysis of the model output, we found that these issues are related to the way carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes are reported in ESM output. Based on these findings, we have provided recommendations for future data providers, data users, and different MIPs. Further details are provided in  Tang et al., (2025b)  and the accompanying  community technical report . The processed dataset ( 17 ESMs across the 1pctCO2 series, historical, and SSP scenarios ) can support a range of applications, including calibration and evaluation of simple climate models (SCMs) at both spatially resolved and global-integrated scales, intercomparison of terrestrial carbon–nitrogen cycle states and fluxes across ESMs, analysis of carbon–nitrogen cycle responses across experiments and scenarios, and evaluation of model consistency and mass conservation. The dataset also provides a standardized annual-resolution basis for analysing the variation and temporal evolution of terrestrial carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes across CMIP6 ESMs.   Changelog 2026-10-08 — Initial upload Added README.ipynb : A notebook documenting the background, data processing and correction procedures, and data distribution. Added notebooks.tar.gz and  environment.yml : Source code and the environment file for reproducing the data processing workflow. Added land_area_related.tar.gz : Multiple .pkl files containing ESM-specific grid area, land fraction, and land area data . Added global_annual_data.tar.gz : A single NetCDF file,  CMIP6_ESM_carbon_nitrogen_cycle_outputs_global_annual_processed_by_Gang_Tang.nc , containing global land-integrated annual data for all ESMs and experiments .    Added annual_data.tar.gz : Multiple NetCDF files containing gridded annual data for each model–experiment combination . This file is not provided here because of difficulties uploading the large global gridded annual data to Zenodo. Instead, it is available from Figshare (link: https://doi.org/10.26188/34089963 ). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23114183

title: Processed data for coastal flood vulnerability assessment in Xiamen, China, under climate change and socioeconomic development
description: This dataset contains processed data supporting an assessment of coastal flood vulnerability in Xiamen, China, under climate change and socioeconomic development. It includes maximum inundation depth, inundation duration, economic and societal loss estimates, vulnerability indicators, and population exposure statistics. The assessment considers tropical cyclone intensities associated with 10-, 100-, and 1000-year return periods for a 2020 baseline and future conditions in 2100 under SSP5-8.5, with population and GDP projections under SSP5. Additional attribution experiments examine the separate and combined effects of climate change and socioeconomic change. The vulnerability outputs include a dynamic vulnerability index incorporating inundation duration and a comparison vulnerability index. The files are primarily provided in XLSX format as static values without active formulas. The accompanying README and Dataset_Guide.xlsx document the directory structure, scenario codes, field units, data sources, population-input variants, and processing notes. A consolidated Regional Data worksheet provides district-level statistics in a consistent tabular structure. This deposit contains processed research outputs. Original FVCOM netCDF files, bathymetry, and mesh connectivity are not included. Geographic coordinates and derived inundation depths are retained. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23434824

title: PubChemQC wB97X-D/def2-SVPD//wB97X-D/def2-SVP dataset, release 1.0.0: per-molecule CSV tables
description: CSV tables of a quantum chemical dataset of 11,398,933 neutral, closed-shell molecules from PubChem (downloaded on 6 November 2020), with one row per molecule. Calculations: Conformer search with CREST and the semiempirical method GFN2-xTB; the lowest-energy conformer was passed to density functional theory (DFT). Geometry optimization and harmonic vibrational analysis (frequencies, infrared intensities and Raman activities) at the wB97X-D/def2-SVP level. Up to ten singlet and ten triplet excited states (time-dependent DFT, TD-DFT) at the wB97X-D/def2-SVPD level at the optimized geometry. Cation and anion single-point calculations (vertical ionization energy and electron affinity) at the wB97X-D/def2-SVPD level at the optimized geometry. Not included in this record: Vibrational spectra (all harmonic frequencies, infrared intensities and Raman activities). The CSV tables give only the lowest frequency and the number of imaginary frequencies; the spectra are in the per-molecule JSON and MessagePack records (see Related resources). Atomic-orbital (AO) and molecular-orbital (MO) data at the wB97X-D/def2-SVPD level, which are in the per-molecule MessagePack records (see Related resources). This record consists of five XZ-compressed CSV files with the same 98 columns. Each file name contains the release version and the MD5 checksum of the file. title: Public Utility Data Liberation Project (PUDL) Data Release
description: v2026.10.0 (2026-10-14) This is a regular monthly PUDL data release, primarily motivated by updating the EIA-860M monthly data through August 2026. It also brings in final release 2025 data for the EIA-860, EIA-861, and EIA-923, plus straggler FERC Form 1 filings from 2025. We made several important improvements for reproducibility in this release. These changes make all outputs fully deterministic, which will make it possible to detect specific changes between builds. We've also added the new table core_epamats__hourly_emissions brings hourly mercury and hydrogen chloride emissions into PUDL. Thanks to @bsousa22 for this contribution! Finally, we fixed a longstanding bug in the net generation and fuel allocation that silently dropped legitimate data for generators transitioning between proposed / existing / retired status across a multi-year ETL run. Enhancements Added county_id_fips and state_id_fips to the core_eia__entity_plants , out_eia__monthly_generators and out_eia__yearly_generators tables. See PR #5688 . out_eia__yearly_generators_by_ownership now identifies each generator's operator as well as its owners, via new operator_utility_id_eia , operator_utility_id_pudl and operator_utility_name_eia columns, with foreign key checks on the IDs. See issue #5550 and PR #5585 . New Data EPA MATS Created the core_epamats__hourly_emissions table, bringing hourly mercury and hydrogen chloride emissions data from the EPA into PUDL. See issue #5357 and PR #5572 . Thanks to contributor @bsousa22 for bringing in this data! Expanded Data Coverage EIA-860 Added final release data from 2025 for EIA-860 . See issue #5589 and PR #5591 . EIA-860M Added EIA-860m data through August 2026. See issue #5677 and PR #5680 . EIA-861 Added EIA-861 final release 2025 data. See issue #5701 and PR #5702 . EIA-923 Added final release data from 2025 for EIA-923 , and monthly release from June 2026. See issue #5594 and PR #5599 . FERC Form 1 Integrated any updates or straggler filings from 2025 for FERC Form 1 . See PR #5668 . Documentation Fixed dbt macro argument documentation in dbt/macros/schema.yml and dbt/tests/data_tests/generic_tests/schema.yml to match dbt 1.12's stricter validation of macro arguments: blocks against their jinja signatures, clearing a long list of spurious dbt parse warnings. Also standardized on the long-form string type name (rather than str ) throughout, since both are accepted by dbt but were used inconsistently. See PR #5593 . New Data Tests & Validations Added unit tests for the ID assignment process that builds core_epa__assn_eia_epacamd_subplant_ids . Fixed several bugs that those tests exposed, including one that could split a physically connected group of generators into separate subplants. Simplified the underlying ID assignment logic to be entirely graph-based. See issue #5675 and PR #5543 . Part of an effort to harmonize the Open Grid Emissions initiative and PUDL. See epic #5439 which is tracking that effort. Added minimum and maximum constraints for plant and Census latitudes and longitudes, to catch impossible locations. EIA-860M coordinates are not cleaned up (about 0.04% of its records are obviously wrong), so core_eia860m__changelog_generators is exempt, and new dbt tests cap the number of known bad records in it instead. See PR #5697 . Bug Fixes & Data Cleaning Made the EIA-930 and FERC-714 hourly demand imputation deterministic. The underlying tensor-completion algorithm previously relied on a unseeded random subsampling mechanism which meant demand_imputed_pudl_mwh values could shift slightly from one build to the next. For our hourly annual (8760) imputation blocks, the subsampling wasn't any faster than using all the data points, so we removed it. Added a guard against the algorithm stopping prematurely on a transient dip in its convergence metric. This was never observed happening, but seemed uncomfortably close to the set tolerance. Also stopped replacing values that were not flagged for imputa

title: Public disclosure record of the US Section 45Q carbon storage subsidy: subpart RR filings census and IRS aggregate series, and the credit visibility gradient
description: What the United States publishes about the physical performance behind its energy tax credits, and which instrument outside the tax system does the publishing. Two parts. The section 45Q record: reported sequestration by reporting year and well class, 2016 to 2023; a facility level census of every annual monitoring report filed under subpart RR and published in the EPA archive, nineteen facilities and sixty one facility years, the complete population rather than a sample; the national aggregate as published in the IRS inflation adjustment notices, 2013 to 2021, with the end of the series documented; and counts at each stage of the disclosure chain. The credit visibility gradient: seven credits on one table, holding the claiming authority and the tax confidentiality regime constant and varying the instrument outside the tax system that records the quantity. For each credit it records the claiming form and its confidentiality basis, the determining quantity, the independent record and the purpose it is produced for, what the public can see, whether identity, dollars and physical quantity are public, the instrument type and its legal authority, how easily that instrument could be removed, and the projected five year cost. A precedents table records regimes that publish claimant identity or subsidy amounts, at home and abroad. The tax return is never the public record. Where a performance quantity is visible at all, another institution is publishing it for its own reasons, and a record counts as independent only where the quantity would be generated by the same process if the credit did not exist. Compiled from primary United States government documents. Series verified 4 August 2026, refreshed 23 August; the gradient compiled and verified at the issuing sources 25 to 27 August 2026. No value is estimated; sources and access dates are recorded per item in the provenance sheets. Supports the author's studies of measurement, verification and disclosure in carbon storage.  Version 4 adds two short articles drawing on this record: “The carbon credit for oil now pays on tons nobody can see” (op-ed, November 2026) and “Norway publishes the tonnes. America files them away.” (article, November 2026). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24011776

title: QM/MM free energy simulation data for "Tuning the ZIKV NS3 Helicase Motor Activity through Magnesium Coordination and RNA-Driven Allostery"
description: This repository contains the input files and results of the hybrid QM/MM free energy calculations of ATP hydrolysis in the Zika virus NS3 helicase (ZIKV NS3h) reported in García-Martínez, Ruiz-Pernía and Tuñón, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2026, 148, 37154–37166 (https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.6c11584). The minimum free energy paths were obtained with the Adaptive String Method (ASM) at the B3LYP-D3/6-31G(d)/MM level, using Amber24 interfaced with Gaussian16, followed by umbrella sampling along the path collective variable and WHAM integration. Two datasets are provided, each as a zip file: - asm_calculation_ssRNAfree_open.zip: ATP hydrolysis in the ssRNA-free ZIKV NS3h, "open-A" active-site conformation. - asm_calculation_ssRNAbound_closed.zip: ATP hydrolysis in the ssRNA-bound ZIKV NS3h, "closed" active-site conformation.  Each folder contains: - the topology file - the initial structures of every node - the Amber input template, the collective variable definitions, the restraints file, the initial guess string and the group file - a results folder with the converged string, the PMF and the umbrella sampling trajectory of the node corresponding to the rate limiting transition state. A README in each folder explains how to generate the inputs and how to display the QM region in VMD. The classical MD trajectories, the DFTB3/MM path explorations and the classical (MM) ASM calculation of the Mg²⁺ coordination change are available from the authors upon reasonable request. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20323439

description: This dataset contains Table 3.7 of the PhD (Candidate of Sciences) thesis of L. M. description: This dataset is the coded database behind the RESILIAGE policy recommendations. It describes 984 policy documents on disaster risk reduction, climate change adaptation and cultural and natural heritage, from international organisations, the European Union, national governments and local authorities, so that policymakers, practitioners and researchers can find and compare the policies relevant to heritage-based community resilience. It belongs to the Global database (Task 6.2) in Work Package 6 and is documented in deliverable D6.2 – Policy recommendations. Politecnico di Torino collected the documents and coded each one against a common template. For each document the table gives the title, issuing authority, geographical level (global, European and 94 countries, with a focus on the CORE Lab countries), hazards addressed, intended audience, a 100–130 word summary, the resilience (SYRI) dimensions and thematic tags, document type, language, publication date, a link to the source and automatically extracted key terms. The archive contains the table as a UTF-8 CSV and as XLSX, and a README with the data dictionary and value lists. Four internal processing fields of the working database were removed; the content is otherwise unchanged. Annex 1 of deliverable D6.2 is included as a separate PDF (6 pages): the overview of the Comparative Policy Survey criteria and input methods, that is, the coding template that gives each field's definition, allowed values and filling rules. title: RFF-SP scenarios with FaIR v2.1
description: This dataset contains output from the 10,000 Resources for the Future Socioeconomic Projections , run with the FaIR reduced complexity climate model (v2.1.1) using an IPCC Sixth Assessment Report consistent calibration of 1,001 probabilistic ensemble members  (v1.0). A total of 10,010,000 climate projections are produced. Climate projections are produced for 1750 to 2301. FaIR is run using stochastically generated internal variability. The RFF-SPs contain CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions. The scenarios have been infilled using the Silicone package ( Lamboll et al. 2020 ) to decompose the total CO2 into fossil and land-use components, and to infill emissions of other greenhouse gases and short-lived climate forcers, following the same strategy used to infill scenarios in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report Working Group 3 from a large database of integrated assessment model pathways  (see Kikstra et al. 2022 ). To extend scenarios beyond 2100 - the time horizon of IAM pathways - the approach consistent with extending the SSPs for CMIP6 is used ( Meinshausen et al. 2020 , sec. 2.3). Code and instructions to reproduce the results is available at  https://github.com/chrisroadmap/rff-fair2.1 . Dataset contents: output[0-9].zip : RFF-SP projections, in batches of 1,000 individual netCDF files (data_output/stochastic/run?????.nc) where ????? is in the range 00001 to 10000). Each file contains: Global mean near-surface air temperature, rebased to 1850-1900 mean Ocean heat content change since 1750 Effective radiative forcing with respect to pre-industrial (IPCC Sixth Assessment Report Working Group 1 convention of anthropogenic components using a 1750 baseline and natural components using a long pre-1750 mean) CO2 concentrations (ppm) CH4 concentrations (ppb) N2O concentrations (ppb) infilled_extended.zip : These are the infilled emissions used to run FaIR, containing 53 emissions species (data_processed/infilled_extended/emissions?????.csv). Time period covered is 2015 to 2300. Pre-2015 emissions can be obtained from the Reduced Complexity Model Intercomparison Project , using the CMIP6 historical emissions from 1750 to 2014. Bridging from 2015 to 2020 was performed using SSP2-4.5, as in the original RFF-SPs for CO2, CH4 and N2O. ssp.zip : For completeness and comparison, the eight main SSP scenarios (ssp119, ssp126, ssp245, ssp370, ssp434, ssp460, ssp534-over, ssp585) are run with the same emissions scenarios and calibration dataset. rcp.zip : For extra completeness, the four RCP scenarios (rcp26, rcp45, rcp60 and rcp85) have been provided. These are run with the same calibration dataset and  therefore are not entirely consistent with IPCC AR6 assessed ranges of climate change . They are provided for comparison only. Notes about the data All variables in each file have dimension (timebounds, ensemble member) except for N2O which is unaffected by climate in this calibration of FaIR, having dimensions of (timebounds). Scenario 00001 runs from 1750 to 2301. Other scenarios run from 2020 to 2301, as the historical period is the same for every scenario. This approximately halves the size of the data output. RCPs run from 1765 to 2301. Note that all variables in the output files are on timebounds . 2020 corresponds to 2020-01-01, 2021 to 2021-01-01, and so on. To approximate midyear values, take the mean of consecutive years. Infilled emissions are on timepoints , i.e. are representative of midyear values. See here for an explanation . Update in v2.0 `output5.zip` was accidentally omitted from previous versions of the data, which is now fixed As `fair-2.1.0` breaks in modern enviroments, depending on a legacy version of `xarray`, `fair-2.1.1` is used here. Results do not bit compare to previous versions (hence a breaking change update to v2.0), but verified with AI that they are close (differences order 1e-6). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23465844

title: RSE-AS: Processed Causal Microgrid Dataset and Out-of-Distribution Scenarios (2017–2023)
description: This dataset accompanies the research study entitled “Causality-Aware Risk-Sensitive Economic Action Selection for Battery-Constrained Deep Reinforcement Learning in Renewable Microgrid Energy Management.” The dataset provides processed, hourly renewable microgrid data for developing and evaluating a causality-aware, risk-sensitive economic action-selection method (RSE-AS) applied to battery energy storage management with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) reinforcement learning. Dataset contents Training (2017–2020): 35,064 hourly observations. Validation (2021): 8,760 hourly observations. Testing (2022): 8,760 hourly observations. Additional testing (2023): 8,753 hourly observations, ending December 31, 2023, at 16:00 UTC. Out-of-distribution evaluation (2022): Four controlled scenarios comprising a 20% increase in demand, a 30% reduction in photovoltaic generation, a 50% increase in electricity tariffs, and a combined perturbation scenario. The processed files include electricity demand, photovoltaic generation, electricity tariffs, forecast information, uncertainty estimates, and temporal features. To support causal decision-making, the evaluation workflow constructs decision-time observations using lagged load, photovoltaic generation, one-hour-ahead net-load forecasts, and uncertainty estimates. Temporal alignment and forecast-target timestamps were checked during dataset validation. title: Raw DFT data, analysis scripts, SHA-256-hashed pre-registrations and deviation logs for a series of pre-registered studies on how elastic constants change between exchange-correlation (XC) functionals.
description: Bulk modulus (version 1.0, studies III to III-f; companion article submitted to Physical Review B). For 28 solids and the functionals LDA, PBE, PBEsol, revPBE, WC and r2SCAN, computed with Quantum ESPRESSO/pslibrary and GPAW, the logarithmic shift of the bulk modulus relative to PBE follows the volume change only partly (ρ ≈ 0.6). The fraction ρ obeys a first-order law, ρ = 1 + m/B′, set by the volume scaling of the non-self-consistent XC energy difference, confirmed on 16 new solids. Cubic shear constants C′ and C44 (version 2.0, studies IV to VI; second article in preparation). For 22 cubic solids (70 converged pairs, PBE as reference, LDA and PBEsol as targets), the PBE constant at the target volume plus a non-self-consistent strain correction reproduces the self-consistent shear constants with a median error of 0.36 %. The volume fraction of the shear shift depends on the convention used for the compressed PBE cell (median 0.78 with stress–strain coefficients, 0.50 with Lagrangian constants) and varies between solids; a first-order relation reproduces it. The version also includes an exchange/correlation split, robustness controls (k-point and smearing convergence, fit order, bootstrap intervals), a cross-check with Quantum ESPRESSO and functional-specific PAW datasets, and the analyses of the revised second article with the independent review report and point-by-point response. title: Raw data for the project 'Upcycling Waste Aromatic Polymers as Adsorbents for Atmospheric Water Harvesting'
description: Plastic pollution and water scarcity are two of the most pressing global challenges of the 21 st century. Conventional recycling approaches such as mechanical reprocessing, pyrolysis, and depolymerisation often lead to material degradation, high energy demands, or low-value outputs. Waste aromatic plastics are crosslinked and sulfonated to yield hydrophilic hypercrosslinked polymers that exhibit excellent water sorption capacity, reaching 0.19 g×g -1 at 30% and 0.57 g×g -1 at 90% relative humidity and 25 °C. This work outlines a potential second service life for waste polymers as robust materials for sustainable water production, bridging the dual challenges of plastic waste management and water scarcity. title: ReBASE – 20CRv3 Storyline Dataset Submission to WCRP EPESC CEAA: 2021 Pacific Northwest Heatwave
description: This store contains the ReBASE ( https://ed-hawkins.github.io/ReBASE ) submission from the University of Reading and the University of Edinburgh to WCRP EPESC CEAA. It provides an 80-member ensemble factual and counterfactual event data from the 20CRv3 storyline simulations for the June 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave. Factual and counterfactual members are not paired. Experiments: Factual simulations use observed SST and sea ice. Counterfactual simulations are based on a 1950s climate: these include spatially and seasonally varying perturbations to the SSTs, a 1950s climatology sea ice field, and 1950s CO 2 levels. The factual–counterfactual global warming level difference is 1K. Event definition: Maximum daily-maximum 2m temperature averaged over 45–52°N, 119–123°W during 25–30 June 2021, using cosine-latitude weighting. Data tiers Tier 1 ( ReBASE_20CRv3_tier1.nc ): Ensemble mean change in event intensity, dI (factual minus counterfactual), in K. Tier 2 ( ReBASE_20CRv3_tier2.nc ): Factual ( mx2t_f ) and counterfactual ( mx2t_cf ) raw event-intensity samples,  (K), with 80 ensembles. Tier 3 ( ReBASE_20CRv3_tier3.nc ): Daily fields for the five days preceding the event for each ensemble over 30–70°N, 60–180°W. Variables: 2t_f , 2t_cf (2m temperature, K);  gh_f , gh_cf (500 hPa geopotential height, m);  msl_f , msl_cf (mean sea-level pressure, Pa); tcc_f , tcc_cf (total cloud cover, %); soilw_f , soilw_cf (top-layer soil water fraction); pwat_f , pwat_cf (precipitable water, kg m⁻²). title: Reconstructed Relative Humidity at Daily Temperature Extremes in GFDL SPEAR_MED Historical and Future Climate Simulations (1961–2100), 65°F M3, 30 Members
description: We reconstructed relative humidity at the time of daily maximum temperature (RH_Tmax) and daily minimum temperature (RH_Tmin) for 30 members of GFDL SPEAR_MED from 1961 to 2100. The simulations include the historical period through 2014 and SSP5-8.5 from 2015 to 2100. Separate local XGBoost models for RH_Tmax and RH_Tmin were trained using ERA5 data from 1961–2000 and evaluated with ERA5 data from 2001–2025. The models use daily Tmax, Tmin, Tmean, RHmean, and three temperature-difference predictors. For SPEAR application, we use the 1961–1990 ensemble-mean climatology and M3 low-frequency trend adjustment, while retaining daily variations from the individual ensemble members. We then restore the SPEAR ensemble-mean RHmean M3 trend. The reconstructed values are provided over eligible land grid cells when the adjusted/detrended Tmax is at least 65°F (291.48 K), with the required predictors and models available. RH_Tmax and RH_Tmin represent relative humidity concurrent with Tmax and Tmin, respectively. They are not the daily minimum and maximum RH. The release contains 4,200 annual NetCDF4 files on the 360 × 576 SPEAR grid, arranged in 30 member ZIP archives. It also includes the trained 65°F XGBoost models, shared preprocessing resources, production code, a Conda environment file, and documentation. The original SPEAR Julian calendar is preserved. Local source and ZIP SHA-256 checks and the final Zenodo upload MD5 comparisons completed successfully on 8 November 2026. See the README for the variable definitions, coverage, use, and limitations. title: Regional Differences in Agricultural Climate Sensitivity: A SADC-Africa Comparative Analysis (2000–2022)
description: This repository contains the dataset and R code supporting the study “Regional Differences in Agricultural Climate Sensitivity: SADC Compared with the Rest of Africa, 2000–2022.” The study examines associations between rainfall and temperature anomalies and agricultural performance, tests differences between SADC and non-SADC countries, and assesses whether irrigation coverage moderates these relationships. The assembled panel contains 1,242 country–year records covering 54 African countries from 2000 to 2022 . Its country–year structure is balanced, but missing values produce outcome-specific estimation samples. The principal outcomes are the natural logarithms of cereal yield and agricultural, forestry and fishing value added per worker. Climate measures include standardized rainfall and temperature anomalies, squared rainfall anomalies, and alternative climate indicators. Structural variables include irrigation coverage and agricultural land share. Rainfall measures were derived from CHIRPS version 2.0 , and temperature measures from ERA5-based country series obtained through the World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal . Standardized anomalies use the 1981–2010 reference period . The broader dataset incorporates agricultural, food-security and macroeconomic indicators compiled from FAOSTAT, the World Development Indicators and International Financial Statistics. The R code implements country and year fixed-effects models, regional climate interactions, structural adjustment and irrigation moderation. It calculates predicted contrasts and joint hypothesis tests, uses country-clustered inference, and provides Driscoll–Kraay sensitivity estimates. Robustness checks examine alternative climate measures, country-specific trends, exclusion of 2020–2022, historical SADC membership and leave-one-country-out estimates. The principal regional classification applies end-of-study SADC membership throughout the observation period. The materials support replication and further comparative research on agricultural climate sensitivity and adaptation. Estimates represent conditional associations, not causal effects of regional membership, irrigation investment or anthropogenic climate change. Significant moderation does not necessarily establish protection against adverse climatic conditions. Users should cite this repository and the original data providers. Third-party data remain subject to their respective licences and terms of use. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23695620

title: Relational Graph Learning for Urban Heat Archetyping and Cross-City Transfer
description: Data, code and simulation outputs supporting the article on graph-based urban heat archetypes in two Mediterranean historic cores: downtown Amman, Jordan, and the Casco Antiguo of Seville, Spain. Building and street archetypes are derived from spatial form alone using a graph convolutional autoencoder, with every thermal and energy variable withheld from training. The fixed partitions are then scored against four independent held-out outcomes: daytime and night-time land surface temperature, simulated pedestrian radiant exposure (mean radiant temperature and UTCI from SOLWEIG), and rooftop photovoltaic yield. Contents. Building and street attribute tables for both cities with archetype assignments; SOLWEIG diurnal simulation output under own and harmonised meteorological forcing, including a canopy-removed Seville counterfactual; rooftop photovoltaic yield and heritage-constrained scenarios; a footprint-typology benchmark; and the revision analyses - a four-classifier comparison, bootstrap and input-perturbation uncertainty, and a check of the modelled shadow geometry against satellite land surface temperature. Verification. Run python docs/verify_results.py from the deposit root. It reproduces the published partition sizes exactly and the published effect sizes to within 0.001, and confirms the documented convention for the modelled sun-exposure field. OpenStreetMap. Building footprints and street centrelines derive from OpenStreetMap, which is licensed ODbL 1.0. No OpenStreetMap geometry or tags are redistributed here, so that this deposit can be released under CC BY 4.0. description: This dataset contains the data and R code supporting the article “Remote Sensing of Leaf Area Index as an Indicator of Ecosystem Resilience to El Niño-Driven Climate Variability in the UK”. title: Replication package for "Decarbonisation in OECD Economies: A Hybrid LOPCOW–IT2F-CoCoSo and CS-ARDL Framework for Strategic Energy Transformation"
description: This chapter develops and applies an integrated hybrid analytical framework that combines uncertainty-aware fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making with cross-sectionally augmented panel econometrics to evaluate decarbonisation performance and the effectiveness of carbon pricing and green finance instruments in OECD economies over 2007–2023. In the strategic ranking stage, the Logarithmic Percentage Change-driven Objective Weighting (LOPCOW) procedure is combined with the Interval Type-2 Fuzzy Combined Compromise Solution (IT2F-CoCoSo) method to produce a composite decarbonisation performance score across six criteria: CO 2 emissions per capita, primary energy intensity, the renewable energy share, the effective carbon price, green bond issuance relative to GDP, and the OECD Environmental Policy Stringency Index. In the econometric stage, a CS-ARDL panel model is estimated for the long-run elasticity of CO 2 emissions intensity with respect to these drivers, with cross-sectional dependence handled through Common Correlated Effects augmentation; because the short time dimension does not allow country-specific estimation, long-run coefficients are pooled across countries and cross-checked with the cross-sectionally augmented distributed lag (CS-DL) estimator. Three principal findings emerge. First, the country ranking is led by the Scandinavian–Alpine cluster and closed by Iceland, Australia and the United States, with Türkiye in a transitional twenty-fifth position. Second, the renewable energy share is the most robust policy-relevant driver of lower emissions intensity (−0.090, p < 0.001), whereas the effective carbon price has a small, negative and marginally significant long-run effect (−0.009, p = 0.067) that remains negative across five robustness specifications; green bond issuance has no detectable effect, consistent with the additionality debate in the green finance literature. Third, carbon-pricing exposure declines steeply down the ranking, and its joint reading with the ranking identifies three decarbonisation profiles—pricing-intensive leaders, established-pricing intermediate performers and structural laggards with weak or absent pricing—each implying a distinct optimal policy mix. The framework constitutes a diagnostic instrument for differentiated national decarbonisation strategies, with direct relevance to the Turkish emissions trading system established under the 2025 Climate Law. title: Reproduction package and derived data for "Rooftop photovoltaic potential and carbon offsets for building-stock carbon peaking: A building-by-building assessment of Qingdao, China"
description: Overview. This deposit contains the documentation, supplementary tables and reproduction package supporting the manuscript "Rooftop photovoltaic potential and carbon offsets for building-stock carbon peaking: A building-by-building assessment of Qingdao, China" (submitted to Renewable Energy). The study assesses rooftop photovoltaic (PV) potential for 2,229,005 height-attributed buildings in Qingdao (534.3 km² of roof footprint) and couples the resulting hourly generation to a building-stock turnover carbon-peaking model. Contents (104 files, 5.6 MB). The archive is organised in seven numbered groups. – Root (7 files) — SI1_Supplementary_Documentation.pdf and 00_Supplementary_Material_Index.md give the packaging map, the recomputation specification for the 168-row hourly absorption matrix (SI-B), the data dictionary, host-model input notes and script notes; also included are the SI label mapping, the package README, an upload note and restore_script_inputs.py. – 01_Supplementary_A_Methods (1 file) — SI-A: model equations and parameterisation. – 02_Supplementary_B_Hourly_Matrix (3 files) — the 168-row SI-B absorption and avoided-emission matrix (3 scenarios × 7 load shapes × 8 absorption settings), its recomputation specification and stage35_si_b_168.py. – 03_Supplementary_C_Coupling_Scenarios (5 files) — SI-C1 coupling sensitivity grid (216 rows), SI-C4 annual trajectories 2015–2050 and peaking summaries, SI-C5 carbon-factor and host-baseline sensitivity. – 04_Supplementary_D_Code_and_Data (68 files) — Code_and_Metadata/ (24 files: citywide summary, historical distributed-PV capacity model, host-model inputs, hourly NASA POWER inputs for three representative points, the citywide hourly generation series 2023–2025, the machine-readable manifest, the OpenStreetMap ingestion path and a requirements lock); Reproduction_Package/ (39 files: 24 script files under scripts/, of which 22 are numbered stage scripts covering the chain from building footprints to available roof area, installed capacity, hourly generation, integration correction and carbon-peaking coupling, plus the OSM deviation pathway, reference_pipeline.py, the verification scripts, data dictionaries, a de-identified per-building scalar table for the Shibei District pilot (42,259 buildings) and a 200-building synthetic validation set); SI-D1 district-level capacity and shaded generation; SI-D5 OSM-vs-AI footprint deviation. – 05_Supplementary_E_Validation (6 files) — SI-E1 stratified footprint-match sample, SI-E2 match summary, SI-E3 Sobol indices with convergence series (D = 10) and the 216-row structural scenarios, SI-E4 output distribution from N = 1024 Saltelli sampling (12,288 evaluations), and the validation note. – 07_Figure_S1_Block_Shading_Validation (3 files) — Figure S1, the block-scale validation of the 12-sector solar-trajectory shading method against a 300 m raster DSM, with its per-building and summary tables. – 08_Raw_Data_and_Sensitivity_Tests (11 files) — height-error propagation (7 tables), load-shape sensitivity, LCOE screening and storage/weather-year sensitivity. Reproducibility. The scripts read only the bundled inputs; no proprietary geometry and no environment variables are required. Verification entry points: verify_bundled_inputs.py (7 checks), verify_si_b.py (11 checks) and reference_pipeline.py --validate (13 checks). Recomputation of the 168-row SI-B matrix from the shipped inputs reproduces the shipped curtailment rates to within 0.1 percentage point on average (162 of 168 rows identical cell by cell; maximum deviation of deliverable energy 10.9 GWh, ≤ 0.03%). Restrictions. The complete building geometry (2,229,005 footprints with heights) is not included: it originates from a licensed commercial remote-sensing product that permits publication of aggregate results but prohibits redistribution of the raw geometry.

title: Research Dataset and Bibliometric Analysis Outputs for Digital Technologies and Climate Change Education (2006–2026)
description: Overview This repository contains the research dataset, bibliometric analysis outputs, and visualization files supporting the study entitled “Digital Technologies for Climate Change Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of Emerging Trends and Research Directions.” The study maps the development of research on digital technologies and climate change education using publications retrieved from the Scopus database. Data Collection and Selection The bibliographic records were retrieved from Scopus on 18 August 2026 using a search strategy combining terms related to climate change education, climate literacy, and digital technologies. The search covered publications from 2006 to 2026. Following the screening and eligibility assessment, 323 documents were retained for the bibliometric analysis. Repository Contents The repository includes the following research materials: Scopus bibliographic metadata: Exported publication records used as the primary dataset for bibliometric analysis, including available titles, authors, abstracts, publication years, source titles, keywords, affiliations, citation information, and references. Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny outputs: Results supporting the analysis of annual scientific production, leading publication sources, influential contributors, thematic structure, thematic maps, and research trends. VOSviewer outputs: Network visualizations used to examine author co-authorship and keyword co-occurrence patterns. Figures and visualization files: Image files corresponding to the figures presented in the manuscript, including the study selection flowchart, publication growth, leading sources, author collaboration network, keyword co-occurrence network, thematic map, and trend topics. Supporting documentation: Available search strategies, data-processing notes, and analysis settings to facilitate transparency and reproducibility. Analytical Approach Bibliometric performance analysis and science-mapping techniques were used to investigate publication growth, influential authors, institutions, countries, and publication sources; scientific collaboration networks; keyword co-occurrence; thematic structure; and temporal research trends. The results were interpreted to identify relationships among digital technologies, pedagogical approaches, and educational objectives in climate change education. Research Purpose and Reproducibility These materials are provided to support research transparency, verification of reported findings, and further investigation of digital technologies in climate change education. Researchers may use the metadata and analysis outputs to explore publication patterns, collaboration structures, thematic relationships, and potential research directions, subject to the applicable data license and the terms of the original data sources. Data Limitations The dataset reflects the Scopus search strategy, indexing coverage, eligibility criteria, and retrieval date. It should not be interpreted as a complete representation of all research on digital technologies and climate change education. Because the search was conducted on 18 August 2026, coverage of publications from 2026 is incomplete. The original Scopus export and analysis settings should be consulted when reproducing the results. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23540960

title: Research data and computational models for Particle delivery and contact-induced interlayer damage in confined graphite processing
description: This dataset supports “Particle delivery and contact-induced interlayer damage in confined graphite processing” by Wenli Zhu, Jiann-Wen Woody Ju and Aihua Zhang. It contains processed experimental input tables, thermal-control data, gas–particle transport event arrays and selected histories, contact-initiation exports, model configurations, executable analysis code and numerical plotting sources. The first-arrival arrays permit independent recomputation of arrival mass, kinetic energy, energy per arriving mass, and the contributions of shared and condition-specific particle identities. The contact data resolve initiation mode under the specified support geometry and interface parameters. These are conditional transport and damage-initiation calculations, rather than predictions of exfoliation yield or complete product distributions. Start with README_PUBLIC.md and the R11 figure/data map. Model definitions, compact solved-array projections and processed exports are identified separately; build-only COMSOL files do not contain saved solutions. Complete large evolution histories are not included in this compact release. Commercial COMSOL and MATLAB licences are required separately to execute the corresponding native models; event-array analysis can be performed with the supplied Python workflow. title: Research dataset for creating impact factors for the biodiversity and climate impact assessment method BIOVALENT
description: This repository provides a research dataset for creating impact factors for the biodiversity and climate impact assessment method BIOVALENT (EL Geneidy et al., 2026) by applying LC-IMPACT (Verones et al., 2020; Verones 2021) and ecoinvent (ecoinvent 2016). BIOVALENT method applies established life cycle assessment (LCA) methods and can be used to assess biodiversity and carbon footprint of human activities, such as consumption.  The BIOVALENT method is described in detail in El Geneidy, S., Peura, M., Aumanen, VM. et al. Value-transforming financial, carbon and biodiversity footprint accounting. J. Ind. Ecol. 30, 2803–2817 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s44498-026-00151-8. Please, also cite the published journal article when using this dataset. Here we used LC-IMPACT version 1.3 (Verones 2021) and ecoinvent version 3.10.1 (ecoinvent 2016).  The data is not at the moment peer-reviewed.  Units The code included in this repository generates impact factors expressed as global potentially disappeared fraction of species (global PDF) per biodiversity loss driver in terrestrial, marine and freshwater ecosystems per unit of activity. It also produces biodiversity footprint measured as Biodiversity equivalent (BDe) per activity (El Geneidy et al., 2026). BDe represents the spatially explicit potential global loss of species across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems. Its values range from 0 to 1, where 0 indicates no risk of extinction and 1 indicates that the share of global species in the risk of extinction is 100 %. Climate impact of activities is measured in carbon dioxide equivalent.   Contents of the dataset R-code used for creating the impact factors for biodiversity and climate impact assessement: 20260629_Creating_impact_factors.R The dataset that provides an Excel file containing regionalised characterization factors from LC-IMPACT, expressed in global PDF per unit of biodiversity loss driver (Verones 2021), which are used by the accompanying R-code: 20260629_LC_for_Ecoinvent_v.3.10.1.xlsx Notes To fully utilise this dataset, an ecoinvent licence is required.       DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23808080

title: Residual reinforcement learning cuts modelled stack wear in a fuel-cell mini-excavator: Co-simulation benchmark against tuned energy managers data and code
description: This record contains the data and code of a simulation study on energy management and storage sizing for a 5-t fuel-cell hybrid mini-excavator. The companion article has been submitted to Automation in Construction. **Study in brief.** The machine has a proton-exchange-membrane fuel cell, a 9.9 kWh LFP battery and a 20.5 F supercapacitor on a 650 V DC bus; its boom, arm and bucket are driven by electric planetary-roller-screw cylinders. The plant is a Simcenter Amesim 2504 model exported as FMI 2.0 co-simulation units (FMUs). A residual reinforcement-learning energy manager (MMEG-TD3), which corrects six parameters of a charge-sustaining expert controller, is compared with six tuned rule- and optimisation-based managers (including adaptive ECMS and MPC) and three direct deep-RL learners. The comparison uses three training seeds, a protocol fixed before training and a single evaluation on frozen test records. The cost combines equivalent hydrogen with modelled fuel-cell degradation and battery wear. A 3×3 battery–supercapacitor sizing map is included. **Files** - `1_code_models_data.zip` (317 MB): analysis code that regenerates every table and figure of the article (`code_v15/`); simulation, training and evaluation code; FMUs of all plants; load records with construction manifests and operating-phase labels; the phase classifier and all learner checkpoints with their selection files; training logs; the protocol and freeze lists (SHA-256); and the scores of every tuning, validation, test and sizing-map run. - `2_trajectories_test_part1.zip` to `2_trajectories_test_part6.zip` (2.2 GB in total): 10-ms trajectories of the single test evaluation (24 records) for every controller and seed, split into six parts for upload; unpack all parts into the same folder. - `README.md`: folder layout and step-by-step reproduction. - `SHA256SUMS.txt`: checksums of every archive and of every file inside them. - `LICENSE_code_MIT.txt`: licence of the code. **Reproduction.** Unpack all archives into one folder. The statistics, tables and figures of the article are regenerated from `1_code_models_data.zip` alone in a few minutes (Python 3.8+, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib); the generated tables are identical to those of the article. The test scores can be recomputed from the trajectories in the six `2_trajectories_test_part*.zip` archives, and any trajectory can be re-simulated with the included FMUs and checkpoints (Python, PyTorch, FMPy; Windows 64-bit). Trajectories of tuning, validation and sizing-map runs are not included; their scores are, and they can be regenerated with the same code. **Load records.** Simulated with the Simcenter Amesim demonstration model Hydraulic_Excavator_LS (a full-size hydraulic excavator) and scaled to the drives of the mini-excavator; they are not measured duty cycles. **Licences.** Data: CC BY 4.0. Code (.py, .ps1): MIT. **Funding.** Basic Science Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), funded by the Ministry of Science and ICT (NRF-RS-2026-25619102); ANCHOR program through the Ulsan ANCHOR Center, funded by the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the Ulsan Metropolitan City, Republic of Korea (2026-ANCHOR-07-001). **Contact.** Kyoung Kwan Ahn, University of Ulsan (kkahn@ulsan.ac.kr). description: This dataset contains interview records and a data-evaluation workbook from a field investigation of AI-assisted digital textile printing at three commercial facilities in Mumbai, India, coded DP-F1, DP-F2 and DP-F3. Supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions programme, RhECAST focuses on agroforestry, a time-honored practice in European countries known for its rural benefits and potential for carbon sequestration. The project specifically targets the Po-Venetian Plain in Italy, a region facing significant atmospheric pollution, and combines landscape archaeology, computer-based modelling, and archaeological soil geochemistry to explore the long-term CO2 sequestration of historical agroforestry practices. RhECAST's innovative approach offers insights into sustainable landscape management and climate change mitigation, with the potential for replication in similar European regions such as Germany, Spain, and Portugal. Through this repository, we provide the data, publications, methods, and models used in RhECAST, fostering further research and application in the field of sustainable land use and carbon sequestration.  Overview This dataset is part of the RhECAST project, focusing on sustainable land use strategies, agroforestry, and computer-based modelling to tackle climate change. title: Safety and sustainability assessment in the development of new EDLC supercapacitors for energy storage
description: Next-generation energy storage solutions rely on advanced materials (AM) intentionally designed for enhanced physicochemical properties or improved functional performance. However, the development and use of AM in different applications may present challenges including human health safety and potential unintended environmental impacts. This study presents the practical application of the Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework to the development of environmentally friendly supercapacitors in a Horizon Europe project. Safety assessments identified material hazards and occupational exposure risks, while environmental sustainability was evaluated via cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) and material criticality and circularity assessment. Results indicated that most polar aprotic electrode inks like dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) lack mutagenicity or carcinogenicity. In contrast, Triton X-100 raised ecotoxicity concerns. Binders like polyvinylidene fluoride and styrene-butadiene rubber may trigger long-term inhalation concerns during electrode printing process without proper local exhaust ventilation. The LCA results showed that encapsulation accounts for more than 30% of the climate-change impact of supercapacitor production, primarily because of metal use. Owing to the higher specific capacitance, the flexible supercapacitor developed in the current project is estimated to reduce environmental burdens per farad by at most 30%. Material recycling could provide a further reduction of 15–25%.  DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23876453

title: Sea surface Dimethylsulfide Concentration and Emission Flux over the North Atlantic Ocean
description: The dataset represents gridded monthly time series of seawater dimethylsulfide (DMS) concentration and total cumulative sea-to-air emission fluxes over the North Atlantic at a spatial resolution of 0.25°×0.25°. The seawater DMS data were generated using a Gaussian process regression (GPR) model to predict daily concentrations across the North Atlantic Ocean. The predictors used are: CHL, MLD, NO₃, PAR, SSS, Si and SST. The daily sea-to-air DMS flux was calculated using gas transfer velocity (Blomquist et al., 2017) and DMS derived from GPR predictions. The monthly total cumulative emission fluxes (EDMS) were computed by integrating the daily sea-to-air DMS flux over the area of each pixel within the domain and over the days of the month. title: Social Cognitive and Planned Behaviour Model of Indonesian and Indian Pre-Service Science Teachers' Intentions to Teach Climate Change Education: A PLS-SEM Analysis
description: This study examined the factors associated with Indonesian and Indian pre-service science teachers’ (PSTs’) intentions to teach climate change education (CCE) using an integrated model informed by Social Cognitive Theory and the Theory of Planned Behaviour. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 302 PSTs from Indonesia (n = 208) and India (n = 94). Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) to evaluate direct and indirect relationships. Seven of the nine hypothesised direct relationships were statistically significant. Knowledge was positively associated with self-efficacy and attitude, while emotions were positively associated with attitude but not significantly associated with self-efficacy. University support was positively associated with self-efficacy but not significantly associated with attitude. Both self-efficacy and attitude were positively associated with intention to teach CCE. Indirect effects further indicated that university support was associated with teaching intention through self-efficacy, while emotions were indirectly associated with intention through attitude. These findings suggest that teacher education programmes should complement climate change knowledge with opportunities to strengthen PSTs’ teaching self-efficacy and foster positive attitudes towards CCE. Universities could support these efforts through relevant coursework, practical teaching experiences, and access to instructional resources that prepare future science teachers to integrate climate change into their teaching. title: Source-based and full-scale anthropogenic nitrous oxide emissions from China's 339 cities for 2010-2024
description: Nitrous oxide ( N 2 O ), a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 273 times greater than CO 2 , has risen steadily in atmospheric concentration, posing a growing threat to climate targets under the Paris Agreement. China, as the world’s largest emitter of anthropogenic N 2 O , has declared that the new round of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) climate commitments and announced the action plan of N 2 O emission control in the industrial sector . However, existing N 2 O inventories remain fragmented—limited in scope, spatial resolution, and timeliness—due to reliance on aggregated data and inconsistent accounting boundaries. Here, we present a source-based, full-scale, and monthly N 2 O emission inventory for China’s all 339 cities from 2010 to 2024, building on the China High Resolution Emission Database (CHRED 3.0). This inventory integrates source-level data from over 1.5 million industrial facilities, spanning major emission sources including energy use, industrial production, agriculture, and waste. Our approach ensures methodological consistency and captures monthly, city-level dynamics of N 2 O emissions. Compared with existing inventories, the dataset improves spatial and temporal resolution and provides a more detailed representation of emission patterns. This dataset offers a valuable resource for understanding N₂O emission dynamics and supporting mitigation policy design. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23684644

title: Souveraineté énergétique et transition écologique : une analyse comparée des stratégies de décarbonation du Maroc et de l'Afrique du Sud
description: Le continent africain conjugue un potentiel renouvelable considérable et un déficit d'accès à l'électricité qui touche près de 600 millions de personnes (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2022). Cet article propose une analyse qualitative, documentaire et comparative des stratégies de décarbonation du Maroc et de l'Afrique du Sud, deux cas retenus pour leurs héritages énergétiques contrastés : diversification tournée vers le gaz et les renouvelables au Maroc, dépendance historique au charbon en Afrique du Sud. Le cadre théorique croise la courbe environnementale de Kuznets, l'identité de Kaya et le Trilemme énergétique, articulés au sein d'une grille comparative à quatre dimensions souveraineté, décarbonation, gouvernance, justice sociale construite à partir d'un corpus de sources institutionnelles et académiques publiées entre 2013 et 2024. Les résultats montrent que les deux trajectoires, bien que difficilement comparables terme à terme, se heurtent à des obstacles structurels proches : financement vert, gouvernance locale, capital humain. Ils confirment aussi que la souveraineté énergétique ne constitue pas, en soi, un frein à la transition écologique. L'article propose enfin, à titre prospectif, un modèle de décarbonation souveraine appuyé sur l'intégration énergétique régionale via la Zone de libre-échange continentale africaine (ZLECAF). The resulting spatial prioritizations are intended to support climate-informed land stewardship and protected-area planning. title: Spatially structured genetic variation and contrasting climatic associations of calcareous and siliceous populations of Dianthus gratianopolitanus in Central Europe: implications for conservation
description: Rocky outcrop plants outside the alpine system are often highly threatened in Central Europe because habitat loss and fragmentation act on already scattered populations. Dianthus gratianopolitanus (Cheddar Pink) is not itself listed under the EU Habitats Directive, but it is a characteristic and diagnostic species of several rare habitat types as listed in its Annex I. We analysed 13 metapopulations (68 sites, 582 individuals) from calcareous (8 metapopulations) and siliceous (5 metapopulations) bedrock types from across its distribution range for genetic structure and differentiation using nuclear AFLP markers, complemented by plastid haplotype analysis (280 individuals). We modelled habitat suitability under current and future climate. Genetic variation was strongly spatially structured (AMOVA: Φ ST = 0.238; 76.1% within sites, 16.1% among sites within metapopulations, 7.8% of variance among metapopulations). Calcareous metapopulations tended to harbour higher AFLP diversity, with significantly higher down-weighted marker values (DW = 12.11 vs. 8.33, p = 0.005), whereas siliceous metapopulations showed lower diversity and lower within-metapopulation differentiation (F ST = 0.22 vs. 0.11). Total and polymorphic fragment numbers did not differ significantly. Differentiation between bedrock groups was low (1.17% of molecular variance, F CT = 0.012) and confounded with geography; plastid haplotypes were geographically structured and mostly local. Habitat suitability models (AUC 0.93–0.98) indicated contrasting climatic associations: precipitation of the warmest quarter was the most important predictor for calcareous occurrences (41.4%) and minimum temperature of the coldest month was for siliceous occurrences (28.1%). Projections suggest a substantial contraction of climatically suitable area by the end of the twenty-first century, with drought stress affecting southern calcareous populations and cold limitation affecting northern siliceous populations. Our results support conserving as many sites as possible within metapopulation networks and combining site protection with carefully evaluated, local-first ex situ and assisted-recruitment measures.   This account contains supplementary material to the study comprising the following information: Supplementary Material 1: Accession table Supplementary Material 2: Figures A.1 to A.13, Genetic analysis of metapopulations and spatial documentation. title: Stakeholder perceptions and AHP pairwise comparisons for sustainable floating photovoltaic deployment on lakes
description: This dataset contains anonymised stakeholder survey responses collected to investigate perceptions of floating photovoltaic (FPV) deployment and to derive criterion weights for an integrated multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) of sustainable FPV lake coverage. The questionnaire combined two components: Stakeholder perception assessment: Questions addressing the perceived contribution of FPV to the energy transition and climate change mitigation, as well as potential conflicts with existing lake uses and landscape aesthetics. Scenario-based questions were used to identify individual acceptance thresholds for FPV deployment. Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP): Fifteen pairwise comparisons among six sustainability criteria using Saaty's 1–9 scale. The criteria covered three ecological aspects (water quality, water balance and thermal lake characteristics), one economic aspect (electricity yield and economic performance) and two social aspects (usage competition and landscape impact). The dataset comprises 183 anonymised survey responses from experts, students and non-experts. Of these, 182 contain complete AHP pairwise comparison matrices. The dataset retains the incomplete response for transparency. The data are provided as a UTF-8 encoded CSV file with 37 variables. An accompanying metadata dictionary documents the variable definitions, response coding, pairwise comparison structure and handling of missing values. Research context The survey data support the study Sustainable Floating Solar Deployment on Lakes: Linking Public Perception and Site Suitability through Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis . The study integrates stakeholder-derived criterion weights with site-specific ecological, economic and social sustainable surface coverage (SSC) optima for three European water bodies: Lake Leimersheim (Germany), Lake Sekdoorn (Netherlands) and Lake Toules (Switzerland). The present dataset contains the questionnaire responses rather than the underlying lake monitoring measurements or complete model outputs. title: Stress2Twin: Hardware-Software Profiling and Autoscaling Traces for a Heterogeneous Edge Cluster
description: Stress2Twin is a reproducibility dataset and reference implementation for a profile-driven Network Digital Twin that generates guarded autoscaling and weighted-routing policies for heterogeneous edge-computing nodes. The package contains 16 independent hardware-software profiling experiments covering different worker and replica-count combinations, and 10 real cluster policy deployments. The evaluated policies include fixed-RPS round-robin and sequential activation baselines, a latency-aware autoscaler, a steady-state profile optimizer, and one-step and two-step guarded optimizers. The measurements expose offered load, successful throughput, request loss, P95 request latency, queue time and depth, per-worker power measurements, replica assignments, routing weights, and active-pod observations. The profiling grid uses 50-request/s increments. The cluster traces cover offered loads from 50 to 2,000 requests/s; 1,650 requests/s is the validated supported region used by the main comparisons, while higher loads are retained to show saturation behavior. The included Python implementation reconstructs a measured lookup oracle from the individual worker profiles, derives operating-zone boundaries, generates scaling and routing policies, simulates those policies, and compares predicted behavior with the real deployments. Three executable notebooks regenerate the policy workbooks, figures, KPI tables, and real-versus-simulated comparisons. Major findings: A superheavy dark matter particle of mass m X ≈ 10 12 GeV, with size r X = 4ħ²/(Gm X 3 ) ≈ 10 -13 m, is found by three routes: the free-streaming scale, an "X miracle" analogous to the WIMP miracle, and the scaling laws of dark matter haloes. title: Supporting information for "Global and regional Pleistocene benthic δ18O stacks on age models with and without astronomical tuning"
description: Note: The BIGSTACKs are in the file "Zhou et al_Supplementary_data_files.xlsx". Constructing accurate age models for Pleistocene marine sediments is crucial for our understanding of glacial-interglacial cycles and other climatic processes. Benthic foraminiferal δ 18 O stacks, a proxy for ice sheet and climate evolution, are often used for stratigraphic alignment and chronology development in deep-sea sedimentary records, in combination with biostratigraphy, paleomagnetism, and radioisotopic constraints. Selection of an appropriate benthic δ 18 O alignment target influences the derived chronology at a given site, and divergent regional trends in benthic δ 18 O highlight the need for ocean-specific benthic δ 18 O stacks. The specific scientific question to be addressed by a study may also influence whether the alignment target should include astronomical tuning. Here, we introduce three benthic δ 18 O stacks – Atlantic, Pacific, and global – with three distinct chronologies for the global stack that incorporate astronomical forcing constraints to various degrees. The new global stack utilizes data from 224 cores and includes 50% more data than the previous “ProbStack” (Ahn et al., 2017). Hand-tuned regional and global stacks, intended as updates to the “LR04” stack (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005), incorporate chronologies transferred from absolutely dated archives during 0-654 thousand years ago (ka) and an astronomically forced ice sheet model during 654-2700 ka. Due to the heterogeneous nature of the age constraints used for these stacks, we call them BIGSTACK mixed , BIGSTACK mixedA , and BIGSTACK mixedP . For applications where astronomical tuning should be minimized, we present a global stack primarily constrained by geomagnetic reversal age estimates, BIGSTACK magrev . We also develop a third age model, BIGSTACK auto , which uses an automated optimization algorithm to “minimally tune” the stack to the pervasive ~41 kyr obliquity cycle, while avoiding assumptions about astronomical phase relationships. This suite of stacks offers flexibility in choosing δ 18 O stratigraphic alignment targets, to allow a wide range of applications in paleoceanographic hypothesis testing. Feb. 10th, 2026 update : the gap of NaN values in BIGSTACK mixed should be 645-650 ka, but in the previous version was 10 kyrs longer (635-650 ka) by mistake. The reason for a gap in the stack during that period is still valid — it's where two portions of the stack, based on absolutely dated targets (0-650ka) and astronomically tuned ice volume modeling (>650 ka), are joined together. Oct. 7th, 2026 update : we present a new version of BIGSTACK magrev that updates the age of the Brunhes/Matuyama boundary to 773 ka (Suganuma et al., 2018; Singer et al., 2019). We thank Prof. Brad Singer for bringing to our attention the evidence pointing to 773 ka as the boundary age. Other BIGSTACKs remain the same as the last version. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23220134
